questions.objective: Evaluate increasing bright bleeding with a firm uterus after assisted birth
questions.stem: Twenty minutes after a vacuum-assisted birth, quantified blood loss has risen from 350 mL to 650 mL and the pulse from 86/min to 110/min. The uterus is firm and midline, but bright-red blood continues to trickle. The patient denies rectal or perineal pressure, and no bulging mass is visible. Which action plan has priority?
questions.clue: Good uterine tone redirects the source assessment; it does not make increasing blood loss reassuring.
questions.rationale: Continue quantifying blood loss and assessing circulation, notify the obstetric clinician, and prepare for inspection and repair of a possible genital-tract laceration. The visible bright-red trickle with a firm midline uterus differs from the pain, pressure, or bulging mass that would make a concealed hematoma more prominent.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner uses the bleeding trend, rising pulse, firm uterus, assisted-birth exposure, and absent hematoma features to redirect assessment toward laceration. The clues are strongly aligned, so the item is level 2 rather than level 3.

options.text: Continue hemodynamic and blood-loss assessment, notify the obstetric clinician promptly, and prepare for genital-tract inspection and repair.
options.reason: Increasing bright bleeding with a firm uterus after assisted birth points toward genital-tract trauma and requires prompt source evaluation while circulation and blood loss are reassessed.

options.text: Treat uterine atony by repeating fundal massage and requesting another uterotonic before evaluating another source.
options.reason: The uterus is already firm and midline. Repeating an atony-focused sequence before evaluating trauma does not fit the bleeding pattern.

options.text: Treat a concealed hematoma with ice and analgesia, then inspect if severe perineal pressure develops.
options.reason: Hematoma is more strongly associated with pain, pressure, or a bulging mass, whereas this patient has visible increasing bright bleeding that requires source assessment now.

options.text: Continue pad checks for 30 minutes because a firm midline uterus makes active postpartum hemorrhage less likely.
options.reason: Firm uterine tone makes atony less likely but does not make active hemorrhage unlikely. The rising blood loss and pulse require prompt evaluation rather than delayed observation.

questions.objective: Communicate assisted-birth risks to the newborn team
questions.stem: A newborn's initial examination is reassuring after a vacuum-assisted birth. During handoff, which report best supports ongoing risk-focused surveillance?
questions.clue: Some birth-related injuries become apparent over time, so a normal first examination is a baseline rather than an endpoint.
questions.rationale: Communicate that vacuum assistance was used, the documented procedure course, current scalp and perfusion findings, and the need for serial observation for evolving swelling and bruising-related jaundice. An initially reassuring examination does not make targeted surveillance unnecessary.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must choose the handoff that connects an intrapartum exposure to a newborn baseline and forward surveillance rather than merely listing isolated facts. This is applied interprofessional communication at level 2.

options.text: Report vacuum use and procedure course, current scalp and perfusion findings, and serial surveillance for evolving swelling and jaundice.
options.reason: The handoff connects the assisted-birth exposure and current baseline to complications that can evolve after an initially reassuring examination.

options.text: Report vacuum use and initial Apgar scores, then use routine observations because the first scalp check is reassuring.
options.reason: Apgar scores and the initial scalp examination provide a baseline but do not remove the need for targeted ongoing assessment after vacuum exposure.

options.text: Report current feeding and scalp findings, and direct the newborn team to the maternal chart for vacuum details.
options.reason: The maternal chart can validly contain procedure documentation, but directing the receiving team there does not communicate the vacuum exposure and course during handoff. That context helps the team interpret later changes.

options.text: Report the vacuum course and current vital signs, and repeat the scalp examination if feeding becomes poor.
options.reason: The procedure and vital signs are relevant, but a poor-feeding trigger does not replace planned surveillance for scalp and perfusion changes that may evolve after the initial examination.

questions.objective: Coordinate bedside support when birth precedes clinician arrival
questions.stem: A fetal head is crowning in a triage room, and the birth clinician is still en route. The bedside nurse remains with the patient while the charge nurse and two additional nurses arrive. Which assignment plan best coordinates the next minute of care?
questions.clue: Help is already present, so the decision is how to distribute simultaneous maternal and newborn work without removing bedside support.
questions.rationale: Keep the bedside nurse with the patient and use the arriving staff to prepare for newborn support and begin maternal bleeding and trauma surveillance. This role-allocation decision differs from merely recognizing that the nurse should stay and summon help.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner coordinates limited personnel across simultaneous bedside, newborn, and maternal needs after help has arrived. That applied delegation task supports level 2.

options.text: Keep the bedside nurse supporting the patient; assign one nurse to newborn readiness and another to maternal bleeding and trauma surveillance.
options.reason: The plan preserves continuous bedside support while using newly arrived staff for newborn preparation and maternal postbirth surveillance.

options.text: Send the bedside nurse for delivery supplies; assign one arriving nurse to reassurance and the other to admission questions.
options.reason: The problem is not that the original nurse may never hand off to qualified staff; this plan uses available staff for supplies and routine history while failing to assign newborn readiness and maternal bleeding and trauma surveillance.

options.text: Keep the bedside nurse with the patient; assign one arriving nurse to maternal vital signs and the other to event documentation.
options.reason: Maternal assessment and documentation matter, but this allocation uses both additional nurses for maternal tasks and leaves newborn readiness unassigned during the imminent birth.

options.text: Assign both arriving nurses to the newborn station; begin maternal bleeding and trauma assessment after the placenta delivers.
options.reason: Newborn readiness is important, but the plan leaves maternal surveillance deferred rather than coordinating concurrent needs.

questions.objective: Sequence fetal-fibronectin collection before an interfering examination
questions.stem: At 30 weeks, a patient with preterm-labor symptoms has intact membranes. The clinician confirms all other Rapid fFN for the TLiIQ System eligibility criteria and orders the specimen, cervical cultures, and a digital cervical examination. Which sequence follows the assay collection instructions?
questions.clue: The specimen most vulnerable to cervical manipulation and abrasive culture collection must be obtained first.
questions.rationale: For the named Rapid fFN TLiIQ assay, collect the cervicovaginal specimen during a speculum examination before collecting cervical cultures and before performing a digital cervical examination. The clinician has already confirmed that the patient meets the assay's other eligibility requirements, including intact membranes.
questions.difficultyReason: The item asks for direct recall of a named manufacturer's specimen sequence after eligibility is established. It remains level 1.

options.text: Collect Rapid fFN during the speculum examination, obtain cultures, then perform the digital examination.
options.reason: The manufacturer instructs collection of the cervicovaginal fFN specimen during a speculum examination before culture collection and before digital cervical manipulation.

options.text: Obtain the cervical cultures, collect the Rapid fFN specimen, and then perform the digital examination.
options.reason: Culture collection can abrade cervical or vaginal mucosa and interfere with sample preparation, so the fFN specimen comes before the cultures.

options.text: Perform the digital examination, collect the Rapid fFN specimen, and then obtain the cervical cultures.
options.reason: Digital cervical manipulation before collection can cause fetal fibronectin release and interfere with interpretation of the specimen.

options.text: Perform the digital examination, obtain the cervical cultures, and then collect the Rapid fFN specimen.
options.reason: This sequence places both potentially interfering steps before the assay specimen instead of protecting the specimen as directed by the manufacturer.

questions.objective: Escalate new suspected active genital HSV before planned induction
questions.stem: A patient at 39 weeks with recurrent genital HSV is admitted for a planned oxytocin induction. Before the infusion starts, the patient reports new burning and tingling at the usual outbreak site, and the nurse observes tender genital vesicles. No lesion test has resulted. Which plan has priority?
questions.clue: The nurse has current symptoms and an observed lesion finding before a planned intervention begins; a laboratory result is not required to communicate that change.
questions.rationale: Hold the start of oxytocin and promptly report the patient's prodromal symptoms and observed genital vesicles so the obstetric clinician can reassess the route and timing of birth. CDC guidance calls for symptom questioning and lesion examination at labor onset; the nurse describes findings and facilitates review rather than independently confirming HSV or choosing the operative plan.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must interrupt a previously appropriate induction workflow when a new infectious-risk assessment changes the birth-plan context. This is an applied level-2 decision.

options.text: Hold oxytocin, document symptoms and lesions, and notify the obstetric clinician to reassess the delivery plan.
options.reason: New prodromal symptoms and visible genital lesions can change the delivery plan because of neonatal exposure risk. The nurse should communicate the findings before carrying out the planned induction without claiming a confirmed diagnosis.

options.text: Begin oxytocin while a lesion swab is processed and notify the clinician after a result is available.
options.reason: CDC guidance bases onset-of-labor assessment on symptoms and examination; waiting for a test result before communicating the new findings can allow an outdated plan to proceed.

options.text: Administer the scheduled suppressive antiviral and proceed because the prior induction plan already addressed HSV risk.
options.reason: Suppressive treatment can reduce recurrences but does not make current prodromal symptoms or lesions irrelevant. The delivery plan still requires reassessment.

options.text: Pause oxytocin and repeat the genital assessment before deciding whether the new findings change the planned induction.
options.reason: Repeat assessment can supplement care, but it is not the priority because current prodromal symptoms and observed vesicles are already relevant to the delivery plan. The obstetric clinician should reassess before induction.

questions.objective: Support urgent surgery and hemorrhage readiness for suspected rupture
questions.stem: At 39 weeks, a patient with one prior low-transverse cesarean birth is in active TOLAC. Oxytocin is infusing at 8 mU/min through a dedicated line, and a separate 18-gauge IV is patent. After a contraction, the fetal heart rate falls from 140/min to 75/min and remains there; the presenting part was at +1 station and is now at -2. The patient reports sudden constant abdominal pain, the pulse is 128/min, and blood pressure is 82/44 mm Hg. The obstetrician calls a category 1 cesarean birth for suspected uterine rupture, prescribes an immediate lactated Ringer's bolus through the patent IV, and directs hemorrhage preparation. Which actions should the nurse take during immediate preparation for transfer? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: A scarred uterus plus sustained fetal bradycardia, abrupt loss of station, constant pain, and maternal shock supports action for suspected rupture before imaging confirmation.
questions.rationale: Treat the cue cluster as suspected uterine rupture with an immediate threat to the patient and fetus, and support the already-activated category 1 cesarean response. Discontinue oxytocin because fetal distress is present, give the case-specific prescribed isotonic-fluid bolus through the patent IV, and transfer the prior-surgery history and exact deterioration timeline to the receiving team. Beginning the prescribed bolus supports circulation in parallel with operative transfer; completing it is not a prerequisite for transfer. Obtaining confirmatory ultrasonography before the transfer would add a diagnostic step when urgent birth has already been directed. The item does not import the neighboring uterine-inversion assessment or replacement sequence.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a concordant rupture pattern and the supplied surgical and fluid orders to distinguish parallel supportive actions from treatment-completion and diagnostic-confirmation transfer gates. Surgery is already organized, and the case contains no competing trend, contraindication, treatment-response reversal, or calculation, so the estimate is level 2 rather than level 3.

options.text: Discontinue the oxytocin infusion as the surgical team prepares.
options.reason: Persistent fetal bradycardia requires immediate discontinuation of oxytocin. Stopping the infusion removes ongoing uterine stimulation while the category 1 birth proceeds.

options.text: Begin the prescribed lactated Ringer's bolus through the patent 18-gauge IV.
options.reason: The patient is hypotensive and has a patent large-bore IV. Implementing the stated isotonic-fluid order supports maternal circulation while the team prepares definitive surgical care.

options.text: Give the receiving team the prior-cesarean history and times of the abrupt fetal, station, and maternal changes.
options.reason: The prior uterine surgery and the linked timing of persistent bradycardia, station loss, pain, and shock are the information the receiving team needs to continue the time-critical response without reconstructing the event.

options.text: Complete the prescribed fluid bolus before transferring the patient to the surgical team.
options.reason: The prescribed bolus should begin through the patent IV while urgent operative transfer proceeds. Making completion of the bolus a prerequisite would delay definitive care and is not part of the case order.

options.text: Request bedside ultrasonography to identify a rupture site before completing the transfer handoff.
options.reason: The combined acute findings have already prompted a category 1 decision for suspected rupture. Current guidance directs expedited birth for acute bradycardia with suspected rupture; imaging confirmation should not be inserted before the urgent transfer.

questions.objective: Recognize possible newborn infection without requiring fever
questions.stem: A 14-hour-old newborn has become difficult to arouse and feeds poorly. Axillary temperature is 35.8 C after the newborn was rewarmed once, and maternal membranes were ruptured for 25 hours before birth. Which action has priority?
questions.clue: Newborn infection can present with low temperature, feeding difficulty, and altered responsiveness; those same findings also require rapid assessment for concurrent metabolic and respiratory problems.
questions.rationale: Do not require fever before considering newborn infection. Promptly assess airway and breathing, oxygenation and perfusion, temperature, and glucose while notifying the neonatal team. Prolonged membrane rupture increases risk, but the history and signs trigger evaluation rather than proving sepsis or excluding environmental and metabolic causes.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a maternal risk plus several subtle newborn findings and coordinates infection escalation with an urgent glucose differential. The cues point in the same direction and require no probability calculation, supporting level 2.

options.text: Assess breathing and perfusion, obtain a bedside glucose while restoring thermal support, and notify the neonatal team for possible infection or another systemic cause.
options.reason: Prolonged rupture of membranes plus persistent hypothermia, poor feeding, and altered responsiveness warrants immediate physiologic assessment and escalation. Glucose disturbance is an urgent alternative or concurrent problem and can be assessed without dismissing infection.

options.text: Repeat controlled warming and use the next temperature result to decide whether the behavior and feeding changes require neonatal evaluation.
options.reason: Environmental heat loss is possible, but waiting on another temperature response delays assessment of the newborn's altered responsiveness, feeding difficulty, and infection risk.

options.text: Obtain a blood culture before assessing glucose or cardiorespiratory status because prolonged membrane rupture makes infection the leading concern.
options.reason: A culture may be ordered, but specimen collection should not precede immediate assessment of breathing, perfusion, and glucose in an unwell newborn or make infection the only urgent differential.

options.text: Perform a brief oral feeding-readiness trial and use improved arousal with sucking to distinguish sleepiness from systemic illness.
options.reason: Difficult arousal and physiologic instability make oral intake an unsafe diagnostic trial. Feeding behavior does not rule out infection or hypoglycemia.

questions.objective: Coordinate ordered specimens and timely empiric therapy
questions.stem: A newborn with suspected infection has temperature instability, tachypnea, and delayed capillary refill. The neonatal clinician orders a blood culture, baseline laboratory tests, and empiric IV antibiotics while stabilization continues. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Diagnostic yield matters, but specimens, stabilization, and empiric treatment must be coordinated so no single step creates an unsafe delay.
questions.rationale: Obtain the ordered blood culture before the first antibiotic dose when feasible, then give empiric therapy promptly without awaiting results or holding the ready first dose for a later routine collection round. Continue system-focused reassessment during treatment. The specimen list depends on the clinical setting and orders, and one response to warming does not supersede the treatment plan.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies timing and role constraints across specimens, empiric therapy, and systemic monitoring while evaluating five independent options. The order and clinical cues are explicit, so this remains level 2.

options.text: Obtain the ordered blood culture before the first antibiotic dose when this can occur without unsafe treatment delay.
options.reason: A pretreatment blood culture improves diagnostic yield, but the qualification prevents specimen collection from becoming a barrier to urgent care.

options.text: Administer the empiric IV antibiotics as ordered without waiting for culture or other laboratory results.
options.reason: Empiric treatment addresses possible infection before organism identification; final results guide later team decisions rather than the timing of the initial ordered dose.

options.text: Continue reassessing respiratory effort, oxygenation, perfusion, glucose, and urine output during specimen collection and treatment.
options.reason: Newborn infection can affect respiratory, circulatory, metabolic, neurologic, and renal status, so treatment coordination includes continued physiologic surveillance.

options.text: After collecting the blood culture, hold the ready first antibiotic until the next routine collection round obtains the remaining ordered baseline specimens.
options.reason: Once the ordered blood culture is collected and the first antibiotic is ready, routine scheduling of other baseline specimens should not postpone empiric therapy for a symptomatic newborn.

options.text: Use normalization of temperature after warming to postpone the first dose until the next full assessment clarifies whether infection remains likely.
options.reason: One improving sign does not negate tachypnea, delayed refill, and the clinician's empiric-treatment order. Reassessment continues while timely treatment proceeds.

questions.objective: Prioritize breathing and withhold unsafe oral intake during deterioration
questions.stem: A newborn born at 30 weeks is now 35 weeks postmenstrual age and has been taking partial oral feedings. Over the past hour, oxygen support has increased, retractions have become more pronounced, and the newborn tires with routine care. An oral feeding is scheduled now. Which nursing plan should be prioritized?
questions.clue: The newborn's support need and work of breathing are worsening before the feeding begins; apparent rest alone does not show that the trend has resolved.
questions.rationale: Prioritize breathing and withhold oral intake during respiratory deterioration. Maintain ordered support and monitoring and obtain team reassessment before selecting an oral or alternate nutrition route. The cues indicate compromise and reduced feeding safety; they do not by themselves prove respiratory failure or prescribe a new device, oxygen concentration, or gavage volume.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a one-hour respiratory trend and feeding demand to distinguish immediate stabilization from plausible alternate-route, readiness-assessment, and rest-first plans. The aligned trend supports level 2.

options.text: Withhold the oral attempt, maintain prescribed respiratory support and monitoring, and notify the neonatal team for reassessment.
options.reason: Increasing support needs, work of breathing, and fatigue indicate deterioration and make an oral feeding attempt unsafe until respiratory stability and feeding readiness are reassessed.

options.text: Replace the oral attempt with the full planned gavage volume now while leaving the respiratory plan unchanged.
options.reason: A gavage route may later be appropriate, but completing nutrition before reassessing the respiratory deterioration assumes feeding tolerance and leaves the changing support need unaddressed.

options.text: Complete a full oral-readiness score and observed sucking trial before reporting the increased retractions to the neonatal team.
options.reason: Readiness assessment is useful in stable infants, but an oral trial should not delay escalation when breathing and support needs are already worsening.

options.text: Cluster care and allow a rest period, then retry the scheduled oral feeding if the newborn appears less tired on the same support.
options.reason: Energy conservation is supportive but does not establish respiratory stability or feeding readiness after a trend of increasing support and retractions.

questions.objective: Reassess ordered support after surfactant response
questions.stem: A mechanically ventilated preterm newborn with respiratory distress syndrome receives intratracheal poractant alfa (CUROSURF). A standing order authorizes oxygen titration to a prescribed saturation range; ventilator-pressure changes require the neonatal clinician. Ten minutes later, saturation is above the ordered range on unchanged settings, heart rate is stable, and breath sounds are equal. Which action is best?
questions.clue: The formulation can change oxygenation and compliance quickly, but the standing order authorizes only target-based oxygen titration.
questions.rationale: After intratracheal poractant alfa, frequent assessment is needed because oxygenation and lung compliance can change rapidly. Use the standing order to titrate the oxygen setting toward the prescribed saturation range, continue close respiratory monitoring, and alert the respiratory/neonatal team so any ventilator change is made by the authorized clinician. Neither a scheduled blood gas nor otherwise stable findings replace response to the monitored saturation target.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner evaluates a treatment response while applying an explicit target and role constraint. The values and authorization are aligned rather than conflicting, so this remains level 2 despite treatment-response language.

options.text: Coordinate the authorized oxygen titration toward the ordered range, continue close monitoring, and notify the respiratory and neonatal team of the rapid response.
options.reason: Poractant alfa can rapidly improve oxygenation and lung compliance. The nurse should use the authorized target-based order, watch the response, and communicate because ventilatory needs may also change.

options.text: Leave the oxygen concentration unchanged until the next scheduled blood gas because an early saturation response may not persist.
options.reason: Laboratory assessment may be ordered, but postponing an already authorized response leaves the newborn above the prescribed oxygen target despite a known rapid treatment effect.

options.text: Reduce both oxygen concentration and ventilator pressure now, then report the combined change to the neonatal clinician.
options.reason: The standing order authorizes oxygen titration, not an independent ventilator-pressure change. Treatment response requires monitoring and role-bounded coordination rather than changing both settings at once.

options.text: Reduce the oxygen setting once, then use stable heart rate and equal breath sounds rather than the saturation trend to judge whether support is appropriate.
options.reason: Heart rate and breath sounds remain important, but they do not replace the prescribed oxygen-saturation range as the response variable for oxygen titration. The saturation trend must guide and verify the authorized adjustment.

questions.objective: Connect procedural heat loss with metabolic assessment
questions.stem: A 31-week preterm newborn undergoes a prolonged central-line dressing change that requires extended torso exposure. Immediately afterward, axillary temperature is 35.9 C, down from 36.7 C before the procedure, and the newborn is jittery. Respirations are unlabored and oxygen saturation is unchanged. Which plan is most appropriate?
questions.clue: The axillary temperature is below the expected range after prolonged exposure, and jitteriness adds an urgent metabolic assessment need despite stable oxygenation.
questions.rationale: Prolonged procedure exposure can destabilize temperature in a preterm newborn. Restore the prescribed thermoneutral environment while checking bedside glucose and reassessing axillary temperature, breathing, oxygenation, and heart rate. A normal glucose result would not correct the thermal problem, and stable oxygenation would not exclude glucose disturbance. The case relies on an independent measured temperature trend rather than an assumed warmer or probe malfunction.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner links a measured postprocedure temperature decline and jitteriness to concurrent thermal and metabolic care while weighing reassuring respiratory findings and plausible one-domain responses. This remains an applied level 2 decision.

options.text: Restore the prescribed thermoneutral environment, check bedside glucose, and continue axillary temperature and cardiorespiratory reassessment.
options.reason: The measured temperature decline after prolonged exposure establishes a thermal concern. Cold stress increases metabolic demand, and jitteriness warrants concurrent glucose assessment while controlled thermal support and monitoring continue.

options.text: Restore thermal support and repeat the axillary temperature before deciding whether jitteriness warrants a bedside glucose check.
options.reason: Thermal support is appropriate, but waiting for a temperature response postpones assessment of a concurrent glucose problem signaled by jitteriness.

options.text: Check bedside glucose now and use a normal result to decide whether the temperature change needs active correction.
options.reason: Glucose assessment is important, but a normal result would not negate the independently measured temperature decline or the need to restore thermal stability.

options.text: Provide containment and repeat the temperature at the next care interval because stable oxygenation makes acute metabolic assessment less urgent.
options.reason: Stable oxygenation does not rule out cold stress or glucose disturbance. Containment does not replace prompt thermal correction and metabolic assessment after the measured decline.

questions.objective: Recognize IDM screening risk despite appropriate birth weight
questions.stem: A term newborn is appropriate for gestational age, has normal vital signs, and is feeding without difficulty. The birth parent had gestational diabetes. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?
questions.clue: The screening indication comes from the pregnancy history, not only the newborn's size or current behavior.
questions.rationale: Infants of parents with diabetes require glucose screening according to the local newborn pathway even when they are appropriate for gestational age and initially asymptomatic. Early feeding and continued clinical observation belong to that risk-based plan. The case does not establish hypoglycemia or a need for IV treatment.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recalls one direct risk-based screening rule and distinguishes maternal diabetes from size- or symptom-only triggers, supporting level 1.

options.text: Begin the facility's glucose-screening pathway for infants of diabetic parents and support early feeding.
options.reason: Maternal diabetes is itself a neonatal hypoglycemia risk factor. Appropriate birth weight and an initially well appearance do not remove the indication for protocol-based screening and feeding support.

options.text: Use routine well-newborn care and add glucose testing only if clinical signs develop.
options.reason: Clinical observation remains important, but symptom-triggered testing alone misses the stated maternal-diabetes screening indication.

options.text: Defer risk-based glucose screening unless the newborn begins taking less milk than expected.
options.reason: Poor intake can accompany hypoglycemia, but waiting for it would substitute a later clinical change for the already established maternal risk factor.

options.text: Apply the glucose pathway only if a later weight measurement places the newborn above the gestational-age range.
options.reason: Large size is one screening risk, but it is not required when maternal diabetes is already present.

questions.objective: Escalate after glucose treatment failure with reduced responsiveness
questions.stem: A term newborn is 3 hours old and is being treated under the unit hypoglycemia pathway. After a feeding and prescribed dextrose gel, glucose remains below the pathway's treatment target. The newborn is now difficult to arouse and cannot suck safely. Which action has priority?
questions.clue: The newborn has both failed initial therapy and lost the ability to use the oral route safely.
questions.rationale: Escalate immediately when glucose remains below the local treatment target and the newborn develops reduced responsiveness with unsafe sucking. The neonatal plan should move toward prescribed IV glucose while airway, breathing, circulation, and glucose response are monitored. Additional gel can be a directed bridge during IV access in some protocols, but it must not become a reason to delay definitive rescue.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate treatment failure, neurologic change, and loss of a safe oral route to choose the next rescue pathway over believable delay strategies, supporting level 2.

options.text: Notify the neonatal team immediately and prepare to administer prescribed IV glucose with continuous clinical monitoring.
options.reason: Persistent low glucose with reduced responsiveness and an unsafe oral route requires urgent reassessment and parenteral rescue under the neonatal plan.

options.text: Attempt another feeding before notifying the team, using stimulation to maintain sucking.
options.reason: The newborn cannot suck safely and has neurologic deterioration after initial treatment, so another oral attempt would delay the needed escalation.

options.text: Give another gel dose and defer the IV plan until the response to gel is known.
options.reason: Gel may be used as a temporary bridge when directed while IV access is being established, but it should not postpone parenteral rescue in a symptomatic newborn who cannot feed safely.

options.text: Obtain a laboratory confirmation and wait for that result before escalating treatment.
options.reason: Confirmatory testing may be obtained within the pathway, but treatment of a symptomatic newborn should not be held while awaiting the result.

questions.objective: Monitor local and systemic deterioration during NEC care
questions.stem: A preterm newborn with suspected necrotizing enterocolitis is NPO with gastric decompression and IV support. Which new assessment trends should the nurse report promptly as possible deterioration? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Worsening NEC may appear in the abdomen, cardiorespiratory pattern, temperature, neurologic state, or perfusion.
questions.rationale: Ongoing NEC care requires serial surveillance for both local abdominal progression and systemic decline. Increasing girth or discoloration, tenderness with abnormal stool or drainage, apnea or bradycardia with temperature instability, and worsening perfusion all merit prompt escalation. Stable, unchanged findings still require routine trending but do not themselves demonstrate deterioration.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner distinguishes four independent local and systemic deterioration clusters from two stable comparison patterns during an already established care plan, supporting level 2.

options.text: Increasing abdominal girth with new dusky discoloration of the abdominal wall
options.reason: Progressive distention and abnormal abdominal color are concerning local changes that can accompany worsening bowel injury.

options.text: New apnea and bradycardia accompanied by temperature instability
options.reason: Apnea, bradycardia, and temperature instability are systemic deterioration findings described with NEC and possible sepsis.

options.text: Falling blood pressure with delayed capillary refill and decreasing urine output
options.reason: This trend suggests worsening perfusion and possible shock, requiring prompt neonatal reassessment.

options.text: New abdominal tenderness with bloody stool or bilious gastric drainage
options.reason: Tenderness and new bloody or bilious gastrointestinal findings are concerning local changes during NEC surveillance.

options.text: Unchanged abdominal girth with a soft abdomen and stable gastric drainage
options.reason: These findings do not describe a new deterioration trend, although serial assessments should continue because NEC can evolve.

options.text: Quiet sleep with arousal during care and stable temperature, breathing, and perfusion
options.reason: Normal arousal with stable systemic findings differs from new lethargy or cardiorespiratory compromise.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Postterm Infants: Meconium aspiration; Neonatal resuscitation procedure.
questions.stem: A newborn is born through meconium-stained fluid. After initial warming, positioning, and stimulation, the infant remains apneic with a heart rate of 80/min. There is no evidence of airway obstruction. What has priority?
questions.clue: The infant needs ventilation, not routine suction solely because meconium is present.
questions.rationale: Current AHA/AAP guidance prioritizes effective ventilation. This corrects older lecture wording that could imply routine deep suction before resuscitation.
questions.difficultyReason: Apply the neonatal ventilation algorithm and reject routine suction for meconium alone.

options.text: Begin effective positive-pressure ventilation.
options.reason: Apnea and heart rate below 100/min require ventilation.

options.text: Delay ventilation for routine endotracheal suctioning.
options.reason: Meconium alone does not justify delaying ventilation when there is no obstruction.

options.text: Begin chest compressions before providing ventilation.
options.reason: Ventilation is the initial priority at this heart rate.

options.text: Provide supplemental oxygen while continuing tactile stimulation.
options.reason: Persistent apnea requires effective ventilation; oxygen and repeated stimulation do not replace it.

questions.objective: Escalate after chest-moving ventilation fails to restore heart rate
questions.stem: During delivery-room resuscitation of a term newborn, the team completes positive-pressure ventilation corrective steps and places an alternative airway. Ventilation produces visible chest movement, but after 30 seconds the heart rate is 50/min. Which action should the nurse anticipate next?
questions.clue: Adequate lung inflation has been established, the 30-second ventilation step is complete, and the heart rate remains below 60/min.
questions.rationale: Begin chest compressions coordinated with ventilation when the newborn's heart rate remains below 60/min after at least 30 seconds of ventilation that inflates the lungs, preferably through an alternative airway after corrective steps. Ventilation continues during compressions. Epinephrine belongs later in the algorithm if the heart rate remains below 60/min after adequate coordinated ventilation and compressions.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must verify adequacy and duration of ventilation, interpret the heart-rate response, and select the next algorithm step over realistic sequencing errors, supporting level 2.

options.text: Begin chest compressions coordinated with ventilation while the team follows the neonatal resuscitation algorithm.
options.reason: A heart rate below 60/min after 30 seconds of ventilation that inflates the lungs calls for coordinated chest compressions and ventilation.

options.text: Continue effective ventilation alone for another full cycle before considering compressions.
options.reason: Once adequate lung inflation has been provided for 30 seconds and the heart rate remains below 60/min, ventilation alone is no longer the next algorithm step.

options.text: Pause ventilation and start chest compressions without coordinated breaths.
options.reason: Neonatal compressions are performed with continued coordinated ventilation because ventilation remains central to newborn resuscitation.

options.text: Prepare epinephrine as the immediate next intervention before beginning compressions.
options.reason: Medication is considered later if the heart rate remains below 60/min despite adequate ventilation and a coordinated compression cycle; it does not precede the indicated compressions here.

questions.objective: Connect stable cephalohematoma to bilirubin follow-up
questions.stem: A term newborn has a stable, localized cephalohematoma that does not cross suture lines and otherwise meets discharge criteria. A bilirubin follow-up has been scheduled. Which teaching is most important to include in the follow-up plan?
questions.clue: A stable scalp collection can still contribute bilirubin as the trapped blood breaks down.
questions.rationale: Cephalohematoma is a subperiosteal blood collection and is a risk factor for significant hyperbilirubinemia. The newborn should complete the risk-based bilirubin follow-up plan and be evaluated sooner if jaundice or feeding and arousal concerns increase.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner makes a direct mechanism-to-follow-up connection between a stable cephalohematoma and bilirubin surveillance, supporting level 1.

options.text: Keep the scheduled bilirubin follow-up and seek earlier evaluation for increasing jaundice, poor feeding, or unusual sleepiness.
options.reason: Blood breakdown within a cephalohematoma increases bilirubin risk. Timely bilirubin follow-up and earlier assessment for concerning changes are appropriate even when the swelling is stable.

options.text: Use skin color at home to decide whether the planned bilirubin measurement is still necessary.
options.reason: Visual observation can prompt concern but should not replace an already indicated bilirubin follow-up plan.

options.text: Focus follow-up on skull imaging because the non-crossing swelling predicts an underlying fracture.
options.reason: A cephalohematoma is defined by its subperiosteal, non-crossing pattern. The stated stable finding does not make routine skull imaging the priority over bilirubin surveillance.

options.text: Delay bilirubin follow-up while the swelling remains confined by the suture lines.
options.reason: The stable non-crossing boundary supports the cephalohematoma assessment but does not remove bilirubin risk from blood breakdown in the collection.

questions.objective: Link incomplete eyelid closure to eye protection and feeding assessment
questions.stem: After a forceps-assisted birth, a newborn has facial asymmetry when crying, cannot fully close one eyelid, and loses milk from the affected side during feeding. Which plan is most appropriate?
questions.clue: The same facial weakness creates two functional risks: corneal exposure and an ineffective feeding seal.
questions.rationale: Facial weakness after birth can leave one eye incompletely closed and alter the newborn's mouth seal. Assess the eye and provide lubrication or covering only as prescribed by the neonatal team, with reassessment of the ocular surface. Separately evaluate suck, seal, swallowing, and cardiorespiratory feeding tolerance before selecting feeding modifications.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner integrates two manifestations of facial weakness into one individualized protection-and-function plan rather than treating only appearance or intake volume, supporting level 2.

options.text: Assess the exposed eye, provide prescribed lubrication or protection, and evaluate suck, seal, and swallowing during feeding.
options.reason: Incomplete eyelid closure can expose the cornea, while facial weakness can impair the feeding seal. Both functions require assessment and individualized protective care.

options.text: Observe for spontaneous recovery and begin eye care only if redness develops, while continuing the usual feeding method.
options.reason: Waiting for visible irritation leaves an incompletely closing eye unprotected and does not address the stated loss of feeding function.

options.text: Cover the eye continuously without reassessment and judge feeding safety only by the volume taken.
options.reason: Eye protection should be prescribed and reassessed, and intake volume alone does not evaluate seal, coordination, swallowing, or respiratory tolerance.

options.text: Modify the nipple first and leave the eye uncovered so pupillary responses remain visible.
options.reason: A feeding-device change requires an individualized assessment, and leaving an eye exposed because the eyelid does not close fails to protect the ocular surface.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Cleft lip and palate.
questions.stem: A newborn with an unrepaired cleft palate tires during feeds and coughs when milk flows rapidly. Which interventions should be included? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: A structural gap interferes with suction and coordinated intake.
questions.rationale: Adapt equipment and technique to the infant's anatomy and endurance, with objective monitoring of nutrition.
questions.difficultyReason: Apply coordinated feeding adaptations for anatomy, endurance, and growth.

options.text: Use the prescribed specialized feeding system and assess milk flow.
options.reason: The infant may be unable to create normal suction.

options.text: Hold the infant upright with head support and offer frequent burping.
options.reason: This supports feeding and reduces swallowed-air discomfort.

options.text: Track intake and weight and consult feeding specialists.
options.reason: Feeding effectiveness and growth require ongoing evaluation.

options.text: Increase milk flow so the infant finishes before tiring.
options.reason: The observed coughing shows that rapid flow is not tolerated and can increase aspiration risk.

options.text: Feed supine to use gravity to fill the mouth.
options.reason: This increases aspiration risk.

questions.objective: Stop feeding and escalate respiratory symptoms suggesting EA/TEF
questions.stem: During a newborn's first oral feeding, the nurse observes repeated coughing, cyanosis, respiratory distress, and frothy oral secretions. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.clue: The first feed triggers respiratory compromise in a newborn who also cannot manage oral secretions.
questions.rationale: Stop oral intake and address airway and breathing when a first feeding triggers coughing, cyanosis, respiratory distress, and frothy secretions. Notify the neonatal team urgently for evaluation of possible esophageal atresia with or without tracheoesophageal fistula and follow the ordered NPO and secretion-management plan. The symptom cluster supports suspicion, not a confirmed anatomic diagnosis.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a condition-specific feeding-and-secretion cluster to stop intake and escalate, while rejecting plausible rechallenge and route-substitution choices, supporting level 2.

options.text: Stop the feeding, support airway and breathing, and notify the neonatal team for urgent evaluation of possible EA/TEF.
options.reason: Feeding-associated respiratory compromise with excessive secretions requires immediate interruption of oral intake and urgent airway-focused evaluation; the pattern suggests but does not prove EA/TEF.

options.text: Pause the feeding and attempt a smaller oral volume after the color and breathing recover.
options.reason: Recovery from the immediate episode does not make another oral challenge safe before the cause of this high-risk pattern is assessed.

options.text: Replace the bottle feeding with an orogastric feeding while respiratory coordination is evaluated.
options.reason: Changing the feeding route before urgent evaluation may be unsafe when esophageal continuity and a tracheoesophageal connection are in question.

options.text: Clear the oral secretions and resume with a slower-flow nipple under continuous monitoring.
options.reason: Secretion management may support the airway when ordered, but it does not justify resuming oral intake after this combined cyanotic and respiratory event.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Omphalocele, gastroschisis.
questions.stem: A newborn has an omphalocele with an intact sac. Which proposed action should the nurse question?
questions.clue: The visible defect needs protection, not bedside forceful reduction.
questions.rationale: Preserve the sac and physiologic stability while the surgical team determines management.
questions.difficultyReason: Identify an unsafe bedside action for a known abdominal wall defect.

options.text: Press the organs firmly into the abdomen before surgical evaluation.
options.reason: Uncontrolled reduction may injure tissue and compromise circulation or ventilation.

options.text: Protect the sac with the prescribed sterile covering.
options.reason: Protection reduces injury, contamination, and fluid or heat loss.

options.text: Maintain warmth and monitor fluid status.
options.reason: Thermal support and careful fluid balance remain part of stabilization, although an intact sac limits evaporative loss.

options.text: Keep the infant NPO and prepare ordered decompression.
options.reason: These measures support stabilization before repair.

questions.objective: Escalate a new change in neural-defect dressing drainage
questions.stem: A newborn with an unrepaired myelomeningocele is positioned off the lesion, which is covered with the prescribed saline-moistened nonadherent dressing. At the next assessment, new clear fluid is pooling beyond the lesion margin and soaking the outer protective layer. Which action has priority?
questions.clue: The baseline covering was intentionally moist, but the new pooling and outer-layer soak-through represent a change beyond that baseline.
questions.rationale: Protect an unrepaired myelomeningocele from pressure, drying, contamination, and trauma. New clear fluid extending beyond an intentionally damp dressing may indicate leakage and should be reported promptly to the neonatal and neurosurgical teams for assessment. The nurse should not expose the lesion or wait for fever before escalating the local change.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must distinguish expected dressing moisture from a new drainage pattern and prioritize lesion protection plus escalation despite stable systemic findings, supporting level 2.

options.text: Keep pressure off the lesion, protect the covering, and notify the neonatal and neurosurgical teams promptly about possible leakage.
options.reason: A new clear-fluid change beyond the expected damp dressing may indicate sac or cerebrospinal-fluid leakage and requires prompt specialist assessment while the lesion remains protected.

options.text: Re-moisten the dressing and wait until the next scheduled assessment before deciding whether to report the drainage.
options.reason: The new pooling and outer-layer soak-through differ from the expected moist dressing and should not be dismissed or left to routine reassessment.

options.text: Remove the covering and leave the lesion exposed briefly to determine whether the fluid continues.
options.reason: Leaving the lesion exposed risks drying, contamination, and injury; the newborn needs protected assessment and escalation rather than an exposure test.

options.text: Mark the drainage edge and continue routine observation because the newborn has no fever or vital-sign change.
options.reason: Absence of systemic illness does not make a new possible lesion leak harmless; the local change itself requires prompt reporting and evaluation.

questions.stem: An infant with hydrocephalus has head circumference measured each shift. Which practice provides the most useful trend?
questions.clue: Useful trends pair comparable measurements with the infant's clinical assessment.
questions.rationale: Combine head-growth data with feeding, behavior, fontanel, and eye findings when assessing possible progression.
questions.difficultyReason: Identify consistent measurement technique and its role in trend interpretation.

options.text: Record consistently measured circumferences alongside neurologic findings.
options.reason: Reliable serial measurement supports detection of changing head growth and pressure signs.

options.text: Use the most comfortable tape position at each assessment.
options.reason: Changing the measurement path between assessments can create a misleading trend.

options.text: Attribute one higher reading to worsening intracranial pressure.
options.reason: Circumference contributes to a trend but does not by itself diagnose a pressure change.

options.text: Use an unchanged circumference to downgrade new neurologic findings.
options.reason: An unchanged measurement does not make new neurologic changes unimportant.

questions.rationale: Teach caregivers practical observation and handling skills, including when to call for urgent circulation or skin concerns.
questions.difficultyReason: Recall routine harness handling and monitoring instructions.

options.text: Inspect skin and feet regularly for pressure injury and circulation changes.
options.reason: Early detection prevents unnoticed skin or neurovascular injury.

options.text: Place diapers beneath the straps as taught.
options.reason: This supports hygiene without changing therapeutic alignment.

options.text: Leave strap adjustments to the prescribed orthopedic plan.

options.text: Bind the legs tightly together during swaddling.

options.text: Schedule harness-free periods when the infant becomes fussy.
options.reason: Fussiness needs assessment; removal and reapplication must follow the orthopedic plan, with concerns reported.

questions.objective: Escalate new perfusion abnormalities after casting
questions.stem: In the pediatric orthopedic clinic, a newborn is reassessed 2 hours after a serial clubfoot cast was applied. The exposed toes were pink and warm earlier but are now pale and cool with capillary refill of 4 seconds. Which action has priority?
questions.clue: The toes have changed from a documented warm, pink baseline to a cluster of impaired-perfusion findings after casting.
questions.rationale: Serial clubfoot casting requires repeated neurovascular assessment. New pale, cool toes with prolonged capillary refill indicate possible cast-related perfusion compromise and require immediate orthopedic notification and urgent evaluation before discharge. Warming, waiting for a scheduled check, or arranging later follow-up can delay correction of a time-sensitive device complication.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner compares a prior and current neurovascular assessment, recognizes a device-associated deterioration pattern, and selects the urgent team pathway over plausible delay strategies, supporting level 2.

options.text: Keep the newborn under observation, notify the orthopedic team immediately, and repeat the documented neurovascular assessment while the cast is urgently evaluated.
options.reason: New pallor, coolness, and delayed refill after casting suggest impaired perfusion and require immediate cast and neurovascular evaluation by the responsible team.

options.text: Compare both feet at the next scheduled check and notify the team only if the asymmetry persists.
options.reason: The current change from a previously pink, warm baseline already indicates possible compromise; delaying until the next routine check is unsafe.

options.text: Warm the exposed toes and use return of color as confirmation that the cast remains safe.
options.reason: External warming could change skin appearance without evaluating whether the cast is impairing circulation; the cast and neurovascular status still require urgent assessment.

options.text: Complete discharge teaching and arrange an expedited outpatient cast check later the same day.
options.reason: Pale, cool toes with delayed refill represent a current perfusion concern that should be evaluated before discharge, not deferred to a later visit.

questions.objective: Recognize neurologic warning signs in a jaundiced newborn
questions.stem: A jaundiced 38-week newborn is 72 hours old and remains admitted for bilirubin monitoring. The newborn now feeds poorly, has a high-pitched cry, and intermittently arches the neck and back. Which action has priority?
questions.clue: Jaundice is now accompanied by a cluster of abnormal feeding, cry, and posture findings.
questions.rationale: Escalate immediately when a jaundiced newborn develops poor feeding with neurologic warning signs such as a high-pitched cry and abnormal arching. The team should urgently reassess the newborn; after escalation, obtain bilirubin measurement and carry out intensified treatment as directed according to gestational age, postnatal age, measurements, risk factors, and clinical status. Call the condition possible acute bilirubin encephalopathy unless the evaluation establishes more; the stem does not prove permanent kernicterus.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner integrates gestational age, postnatal age, jaundice surveillance, and a neurologic change to prioritize urgent escalation over feeding, routine monitoring, or an alternate differential, supporting level 2.

options.text: Activate urgent neonatal evaluation for possible acute bilirubin encephalopathy and prepare for immediate bilirubin measurement and intensified treatment.
options.reason: A high-pitched cry and abnormal arching are neurologic warning signs in a jaundiced newborn; poor feeding adds clinical concern. The cluster requires urgent evaluation and treatment escalation but does not by itself prove permanent kernicterus.

options.text: Offer a feeding and reassess the cry and arching before notifying the neonatal team if intake remains poor.
options.reason: A feeding trial would delay escalation of a neurologic warning cluster and may be unsafe if the newborn's neurologic function is worsening.

options.text: Continue the current monitoring plan and wait for the next scheduled bilirubin measurement because the findings are nonspecific.
options.reason: The findings can have other causes, but their combination with jaundice requires immediate evaluation rather than routine scheduling.

options.text: Request a routine reflux evaluation first because reflux can also cause arching.
options.reason: Reflux may enter the differential later, but it does not take priority over urgent assessment for possible bilirubin-related neurologic dysfunction in this context.

questions.objective: Reassess persistent functional impairment despite withdrawal support
questions.stem: A newborn receiving scheduled oral morphine for opioid withdrawal also receives swaddling, low stimulation, and frequent small feedings. Cardiorespiratory findings are stable, but the newborn still cannot feed adequately, sleep between care periods, or be consoled. What should the nurse do next?
questions.clue: Both medication and first-line environmental support are already in use, yet all three functional domains remain impaired.
questions.rationale: Withdrawal care is evaluated through the infant's function and clinical response, not cardiorespiratory stability alone. Because prescribed morphine and supportive measures have already started and the newborn still cannot eat adequately, sleep between care periods, or be consoled, the nurse should summarize the pattern and seek neonatal-team reassessment. The case does not independently authorize a dose increase or other medication change.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must distinguish stable vital functions from persistent treatment failure across eating, sleeping, and consolability and choose team reassessment over delay or a single-domain dose request, supporting level 2.

options.text: Report the persistent functional findings and response to current therapy so the neonatal team can reassess the plan.
options.reason: Medication and supportive care have already begun, yet eating, sleeping, and consolability remain impaired. Reporting the pattern supports timely team reassessment while current safety monitoring and comfort measures continue.

options.text: Continue the same plan until routine rounds because stable cardiorespiratory findings show the treatment is effective.
options.reason: Stable breathing and circulation do not resolve the stated functional treatment failure. Waiting for routine rounds would discount persistent inability to eat, sleep, and be consoled.

options.text: Request a higher morphine dose based on poor sleep alone and leave the supportive-care plan unchanged.
options.reason: Focusing only on sleep is incomplete for this case because feeding and consolability are also impaired. Requesting a higher dose while leaving supportive care unchanged bypasses reassessment of the full clinical response and current plan.

options.text: Add more frequent waking and feeding attempts before reporting the pattern because withdrawal care should remain nonpharmacologic.
options.reason: Nonpharmacologic care remains important, but those measures are already in place and repeated stimulation may add workload. The ongoing functional impairment should be reported rather than treated as a reason to defer reassessment.

questions.objective: Withhold a scheduled opioid and support breathing with new depression
questions.stem: A newborn receiving oral morphine for opioid withdrawal is difficult to arouse. Before the next scheduled dose, respirations have fallen from 44/min to 18/min and are shallow. What should the nurse do first?
questions.clue: The concerning findings appeared before a scheduled dose and are recognized adverse effects of morphine.
questions.rationale: The scheduled-dose conflict requires applied medication safety: withhold the opioid, support airway and breathing, continue close cardiorespiratory monitoring, and obtain immediate neonatal-team assessment. The neonatal morphine monograph identifies respiratory depression and sedation as safety concerns but does not provide a universal respiratory-rate hold parameter for this case. Rescue medication and dose adjustment remain team- and protocol-directed.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies current pre-dose assessment findings to interrupt a standing medication schedule and prioritize breathing support and urgent reassessment, supporting level 2 rather than level 3.

options.text: Withhold the dose, support airway and breathing, and obtain immediate assessment by the neonatal team.
options.reason: New marked sedation and respiratory depression before a scheduled opioid dose require immediate medication-safety action. The nurse should not give the dose while supporting breathing and escalating for neonatal assessment.

options.text: Apply continuous pulse oximetry, give the scheduled dose, and reassess after its expected effect.
options.reason: Monitoring does not make opioid administration safe in the presence of new shallow bradypnea and marked sedation. Giving the dose could worsen respiratory depression.

options.text: Delay the dose until the next withdrawal score, then use that score instead of the respiratory change.
options.reason: Withdrawal scoring does not replace immediate assessment of a potentially adverse opioid effect. The current breathing change requires action before the next routine score.

options.text: To avoid interrupting withdrawal treatment, give a reduced dose and reassess sedation and breathing afterward.
options.reason: Avoiding an interruption in withdrawal treatment does not justify giving even a reduced opioid dose during new respiratory depression. Withhold the scheduled dose, support airway and breathing, and obtain immediate neonatal assessment.

questions.objective: Resolve failed home-equipment return demonstration before discharge
questions.stem: A medically stable preterm infant is scheduled for discharge with prescribed home oxygen. During return demonstration, the caregiver connects the flowmeter incorrectly and cannot state what to do if breathing worsens. Which plan is best?
questions.clue: The infant is physiologically stable, but the person expected to use a safety-critical therapy has not demonstrated readiness.
questions.rationale: Discharge readiness includes caregiver competence with prescribed equipment and a workable response plan for deterioration. The team should pause discharge completion, provide further supervised teaching, and verify the caregiver's technique and emergency understanding through repeat demonstration. Written material, a home visit, or another person's skill can support but cannot erase the current gap.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner weighs several feasible teaching and transition supports and identifies which one actually resolves the demonstrated equipment and emergency-plan gap before discharge, supporting level 2.

options.text: Pause discharge completion, coordinate hands-on reteaching, and repeat the equipment and emergency-plan demonstration.
options.reason: A failed safety-critical demonstration is an unresolved readiness gap. Supervised practice, coordinated teaching, and a successful repeat demonstration should occur before discharge is completed.

options.text: Review the written guide and discharge once the caregiver can describe the steps without reconnecting the equipment.
options.reason: Verbal teach-back can clarify understanding, but it does not resolve the demonstrated hands-on equipment error. Another supervised return demonstration remains necessary.

options.text: Confirm a next-day home nursing visit and discharge after staff assemble the equipment for transport.
options.reason: A prompt home visit is useful follow-up, but it does not make an unprepared caregiver ready to manage oxygen or respiratory worsening during the transition home.

options.text: Use another family member's successful demonstration as clearance while the designated caregiver observes once more.
options.reason: Another competent caregiver may be part of a safe plan, but their performance cannot substitute for assessing the availability and competence of the person expected to provide care.

questions.objective: Respond to expressed fear with supported contact at the family's pace
questions.stem: A parent stands beside the incubator and says, "I am afraid I will hurt her." The preterm infant is stable enough for supported contact. Which nursing response is best?
questions.clue: The parent names fear as the barrier, and the infant can safely participate in graded contact.
questions.rationale: The nurse should acknowledge the parent's concern, offer a concrete low-pressure way to participate, and let the family set the pace. Watching, kangaroo care, and further discussion may all become useful, but none should be imposed or used to postpone every safe form of contact until fear is absent.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes the response that combines assessment, instruction, choice, and family-paced involvement in a straightforward therapeutic-communication situation, supporting level 1.

options.text: "Let's start with what feels manageable. I can show you safe touch, and you can decide whether to try."
options.reason: The response acknowledges the stated fear, offers concrete support, and allows the parent to choose a comfortable level of participation.

options.text: "Many parents feel that way. Watch me provide care today, and you will probably feel ready tomorrow."
options.reason: Normalization may reduce isolation, but the response predicts readiness and leaves the parent as an observer instead of exploring and supporting a manageable choice now.

options.text: "Kangaroo care often builds confidence. I will arrange it now so you can see that holding is safe."
options.reason: Kangaroo care may be beneficial when clinically appropriate and desired, but arranging it immediately assumes the parent's pace rather than first offering graded choices.

options.text: "Tell me what worries you most. We can wait to discuss contact until you feel completely confident."
options.reason: Exploring fear is therapeutic, but requiring complete confidence before supported contact can unnecessarily postpone safe, confidence-building involvement.

questions.objective: Offer individualized support and choices after neonatal death
questions.stem: After a neonatal death, the parents decline to hold the infant now and ask for time before making other decisions. Which nursing actions support individualized care? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: The family has expressed a current preference and a need for time, not a permanent refusal of every support.
questions.rationale: Individualized bereavement care offers contact, memory-making, cultural or spiritual support, and follow-up resources without requiring any one response. The nurse should respect a refusal, explain available choices, and revisit them only as the family wishes and policy permits. Well-intentioned predictions about regret or staff-selected keepsakes can still become pressure.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes three direct family-centered actions and distinguishes them from two subtle but well-intentioned forms of pressure, supporting foundational level 1.

options.text: Acknowledge the current choice and offer to revisit available contact options if the parents wish.
options.reason: Respecting the present refusal while leaving room to reconsider preserves choice without pressuring the family.

options.text: Ask whether the parents want specific cultural or spiritual practices supported.
options.reason: The nurse should ask rather than infer which beliefs or practices matter to this family and then coordinate available support.

options.text: Offer available memory-making choices without assuming which keepsakes the parents want.
options.reason: Offering rather than selecting keepsakes allows the family to accept or decline each available memory-making option.

options.text: Explain that holding the infant usually prevents regret, then return soon for a final decision.
options.reason: The intent may be reassuring, but predicting regret and setting pressure for a final decision promotes one grieving response over the family's stated need for time.

options.text: Choose the unit's usual keepsakes for the parents so they do not have to make more decisions.
options.reason: Reducing decision burden can be compassionate, but selecting keepsakes without first offering a choice may impose staff assumptions and conflict with family preferences.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Newborn Screening for Disease.
questions.stem: A newborn's screening result suggests congenital hypothyroidism. The family says the infant looks normal and wants to wait several months. Which response is best?
questions.clue: An apparently well newborn can still have a time-sensitive screening abnormality.
questions.rationale: A screening program works only when abnormal findings lead to prompt evaluation and appropriate therapy.
questions.difficultyReason: Distinguish an abnormal screening result from visible disease while preserving timely follow-up.

options.text: Explain that prompt confirmatory testing determines whether treatment is needed.
options.reason: Newborns may appear well; prompt confirmation allows indicated treatment without symptom-based delay.

options.text: Suggest waiting for feeding or growth problems before arranging follow-up.
options.reason: Early findings can be subtle, so visible symptoms are not a safe trigger for follow-up.

options.text: Suggest an iodine supplement as the initial thyroid treatment.
options.reason: Iodine supplementation does not replace confirmatory testing or prescribed thyroid hormone when indicated.

options.text: Tell the family the screening result establishes congenital hypothyroidism.
options.reason: Screening identifies newborns needing follow-up; confirmation is required before treating the result as a diagnosis.

questions.objective: Explain developmental follow-up after prematurity without predicting disability
questions.stem: A caregiver of an infant born at 28 weeks asks why developmental follow-up is needed after discharge. Which explanation by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: Longitudinal follow-up supports contextual assessment and early help; it is not a one-visit prediction of disability.
questions.rationale: Developmental follow-up after prematurity tracks progress over time, interprets findings in light of gestational history, and connects the infant and family with support if concerns emerge. It should be framed as surveillance and access to help, not as proof that disability is expected or as a single final test.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner selects a routine family explanation that accurately describes longitudinal, contextual follow-up without a prediction or fixed cutoff, supporting level 1.

options.text: "The team will interpret development with the birth history, follow progress over time, and arrange support if concerns emerge."
options.reason: Follow-up uses prematurity and serial development together to recognize needs and connect the infant with appropriate support without predicting a fixed outcome.

options.text: "The first visit should determine whether any developmental differences are permanent, so later visits may not be necessary."
options.reason: One early assessment cannot establish a permanent outcome. The purpose of follow-up is to observe development over time and respond to emerging needs.

options.text: "Follow-up mainly repeats the discharge examination after the infant has had time to recover from hospitalization."
options.reason: Developmental follow-up is not merely a delayed repeat of discharge stability checks; it evaluates progress and support needs across time.

options.text: "Services are usually considered only after the infant consistently misses milestones expected for term newborns of the same age."
options.reason: This explanation ignores gestational history and delays support until repeated difficulty is established. Follow-up is intended to interpret findings in context and connect services when concerns emerge.

questions.objective: Adjust clustered care when physiologic stress cues emerge
questions.stem: During clustered care, a preterm infant extends the limbs, hiccups, and has an oxygen saturation decrease from 95% to 87%. Which action should the nurse take?
questions.clue: The infant develops both recognized stress behaviors and an objective cardiorespiratory change during care.
questions.rationale: Clustered care should reduce stimulation and energy use, but it remains responsive to the infant. When stress cues accompany desaturation, pause nonessential handling, support the existing respiratory plan and positioning, reassess cardiorespiratory status, and resume only necessary care after recovery. The findings should not be treated as a reason to rush or to delay all prescribed care automatically.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies behavioral and oxygenation changes to modify an otherwise appropriate care strategy and distinguish a responsive pause from rushing, blanket deferral, or escalation solely to finish tasks, supporting level 2.

options.text: Pause nonessential handling, support prescribed positioning and respiratory care, and reassess before resuming necessary tasks.
options.reason: The behavioral and oxygenation changes indicate that the infant is not tolerating the current workload. Care should pause while cardiorespiratory status and recovery are assessed.

options.text: Finish the remaining tasks at a faster pace to avoid another handling episode, then complete the assessment.
options.reason: Clustering is intended to conserve energy, but it should not override new physiologic intolerance. Continuing the tasks delays assessment and adds stimulation during desaturation.

options.text: End the care cluster and let the infant rest undisturbed, reassessing at the next routine care period.
options.reason: Protecting rest is important, but the current desaturation and stress cues require assessment and individualized supportive care now. Reassessment should not wait for the next routine care period.

options.text: Request more respiratory support so the planned cluster can continue while the saturation is monitored.
options.reason: Additional support may be required after assessment, but using it only to push through nonessential care ignores the infant's stress cues and current intolerance.

questions.objective: Coordinate chronic lung disease nutrition, equipment and follow-up
questions.stem: A former 29-week infant with chronic lung disease is preparing for discharge with prescribed oxygen, slow weight gain, and fatigue during feedings. Which elements belong in the coordinated home-care plan? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: The home plan must integrate persistent respiratory support with feeding endurance, growth, caregiver skill, and access to follow-up.
questions.rationale: The coordinated plan should align the ordered feeding strategy with fatigue and nutritional needs, verify caregiver preparation for prescribed oxygen equipment, and establish both follow-up assessment and between-visit contacts. Tracking feeding volume while postponing an existing fatigue problem, or relying on an equipment vendor for clinical concerns, leaves important needs unresolved.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner selects four linked but individually assessable discharge-plan elements and rejects two plausible but incomplete nutrition and follow-up plans for an infant with ongoing respiratory and nutritional needs, supporting level 2.

options.text: An ordered feeding plan adjusted for fatigue while meeting the infant's prescribed nutritional needs
options.reason: Chronic respiratory effort can compete with feeding endurance. The plan should make feeding manageable while meeting the infant's prescribed nutritional needs.

options.text: Caregiver return demonstration with the prescribed home oxygen equipment before discharge
options.reason: Safe home care requires hands-on preparation for the prescribed oxygen equipment the infant will continue to need.

options.text: Scheduled follow-up that reviews respiratory status, feeding tolerance, and growth
options.reason: Ongoing respiratory support, feeding fatigue, and slow growth require planned reassessment after discharge.

options.text: A clearly identified contact for breathing, feeding, or equipment concerns between scheduled visits
options.reason: The family needs a defined route for timely help when clinical or equipment concerns occur before the next appointment.

options.text: A feeding log centered on total prescribed volume, with fatigue reviewed at the first scheduled clinic visit
options.reason: Volume tracking is useful, but the infant already has fatigue and slow growth; the discharge plan must address feeding endurance and nutritional delivery before relying on later review.

options.text: Scheduled respiratory and growth visits, with the oxygen-equipment vendor as the between-visit contact for breathing or feeding concerns
options.reason: The vendor can address equipment problems but cannot replace a clinical contact for breathing or feeding changes; the plan needs the appropriate route for each concern.
