questions.objective: Recognize EC opportunity after a blanket 72-hour cutoff
questions.stem: A patient calls 96 hours after intercourse without contraception and says, "Urgent care told me emergency contraception works only within 72 hours. I want to avoid pregnancy." Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The call occurs on day four, so the older blanket cutoff should trigger prompt method-specific counseling rather than closure.
questions.rationale: Emergency contraception remains time sensitive after 72 hours. A copper IUD may be placed within five days of the first act of intercourse, and emergency-contraceptive pills should be taken as soon as possible within five days. UPA has been observed to be more effective than LNG on days three through five, while LNG effectiveness can decline with later use. The nurse should preserve prompt access and facilitate method-specific selection without claiming that every method is equally effective at every point in the window.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes one foundational timing correction from a direct 96-hour cue. No competing clinical priorities or multistep regimen must be reconciled, supporting level 1.

options.text: Seek method-specific emergency-contraception counseling today; some options remain usable within 5 days, and timing and method affect the choice.
options.reason: Ninety-six hours is within the five-day window for some emergency-contraception options. Prompt selection matters because the methods do not have identical timing or effectiveness profiles.

options.text: Accept the 72-hour cutoff and arrange a later visit to discuss contraception for future intercourse.
options.reason: A blanket 72-hour cutoff would discard a current time-sensitive opportunity because some emergency-contraception options can be used within five days.

options.text: Start a regular combined-pill pack today with seven days of backup because that replaces the remaining need for emergency contraception.
options.reason: Starting an ongoing method addresses later risk but is not itself the method-specific emergency-contraception decision for the intercourse that already occurred.

options.text: Prefer LNG pills at 96 hours because they become more effective than UPA later in the five-day window.
options.reason: This reverses the observed later-window comparison: UPA is more effective than LNG on days three through five. Actual selection still requires normal eligibility, access and preference assessment.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: hormonal and emergency contraception context (P318–P333; P371–P372; P388–P400). The older blanket 72-hour limit is not current guidance.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — contraception passages: combined-pill and emergency-contraception background (bounded reading; older blanket 72-hour wording excluded).

CDC — Emergency Contraception, U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use: some methods remain available within five days; timing and method affect the choice, and UPA has been observed to be more effective than LNG on days 3–5 (page dated November 19, 2024).

questions.objective: Apply UPA-specific hormonal restart and backup instructions
questions.stem: A patient took ulipristal acetate today and has an eligible combined-pill prescription ready at home. Which restart and backup plan should the nurse teach?
questions.clue: UPA and LNG emergency-contraception pills have different hormonal-restart instructions, and the backup interval does not end when the five-day delay ends.
questions.rationale: After UPA, starting or resuming hormonal contraception should wait at least five days because exogenous progestin can reduce UPA's effect. For this self-administered combined pill, condoms or abstinence are needed during the delay and after restart until seven days of pill use or the next menses, whichever comes first. This plan is specific to UPA; it should not be replaced by the immediate-restart instructions used after LNG emergency-contraception pills.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a named-drug distinction and links a pre-restart delay to a separate post-restart protection interval. The cues are aligned and the prescription is supplied, supporting level 2 rather than advanced reasoning.

options.text: Wait 5 days before restarting; use condoms or abstain through the delay and for 7 days after restart, unless menses comes first.
options.reason: UPA requires delaying progestin-containing hormonal contraception for at least five days. Protection is then needed until seven days after restart or the next menses, whichever occurs first.

options.text: Restart the pill today and use condoms or abstain until 7 consecutive pill days have been completed.
options.reason: Immediate hormonal restart is the LNG-ECP approach. Starting a progestin-containing pill too soon after UPA can reduce UPA's ability to delay ovulation.

options.text: Wait at least 5 days before restarting the pill; use condoms or abstain only during that five-day delay.
options.reason: The restart delay is correct, but protection is still needed after the pill is resumed until the post-restart interval is completed or the next menses occurs first.

options.text: Wait at least 5 days before restarting the pill; stop condoms or abstinence 7 calendar days after today's UPA dose.
options.reason: Counting seven total days from the UPA dose supplies only two pill days after a five-day delay. The post-restart interval is anchored to resuming regular contraception.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: hormonal and emergency contraception context (P318–P333; P371–P372; P388–P400; not the complete UPA restart algorithm).

questions.objective: Activate emergency evaluation for new focal neurologic symptoms during CHC use
questions.stem: A 29-year-old using a combined hormonal vaginal ring has no migraine-with-aura diagnosis. During a telephone call, the patient reports a sudden blind spot, new left-arm weakness and difficulty finding words that began 15 minutes ago. Which instruction should the nurse give first?
questions.clue: The symptoms are new, focal and occurring now; they cannot safely be classified as benign aura during a contraception call.
questions.rationale: Sudden visual change, unilateral weakness and speech difficulty are stroke warning signs. The immediate response is to activate emergency medical services, record the onset time and avoid self-transport. A new or markedly changed headache or focal neurologic pattern also warrants later contraceptive reassessment. Migraine with aura is a category 4 condition for CHC use, but this undiagnosed acute event should not be declared to be aura before emergency evaluation.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner prioritizes active focal neurologic red flags over the relevant but secondary CHC-eligibility question. The current symptom status makes the priority clear, supporting level 2.

options.text: Call 911 now, note when the symptoms began and do not drive; reassess combined-hormonal eligibility after the acute evaluation.
options.reason: Sudden visual, unilateral motor and speech symptoms are stroke warning signs. Emergency assessment takes priority; method eligibility can be revisited after the acute cause is evaluated.

options.text: Remove the ring now and arrange a same-day contraception visit to determine whether this is migraine aura.
options.reason: CHC eligibility does require reassessment, but a contraception visit cannot substitute for emergency evaluation of current focal neurologic deficits.

options.text: Ask a friend to drive to urgent care after the visual symptom clears, then discuss a non-estrogen method.
options.reason: Transient improvement would not exclude a stroke or transient ischemic event. The patient should use emergency medical services rather than delay or travel by car.

options.text: Continue the ring until a migraine diagnosis is confirmed and send the prescriber a portal message today.
options.reason: Waiting for a routine diagnostic label or portal response is unsafe while focal neurologic symptoms are occurring. Acute evaluation comes first.

ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — combined-hormonal contraception background (bounded reading; current CDC emergency and eligibility guidance controls).

CDC — Signs and Symptoms of Stroke: sudden visual change, one-sided weakness or numbness, speech difficulty, and severe headache are warning signs; call 911, note symptom onset, and do not drive (page dated May 19, 2026).

CDC — U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Combined Hormonal Contraceptives: new or markedly changed headaches require evaluation; accurate migraine/aura diagnosis matters, and migraine with aura is category 4 for CHC use (page dated November 19, 2024; later eligibility context only).

questions.objective: Prioritize acute cardiopulmonary symptoms over method counseling
questions.stem: A patient using a norelgestromin/ethinyl estradiol patch calls while alone and reports sudden chest pressure and difficulty breathing. The symptoms began 10 minutes ago and are continuing. Which instruction should the nurse give first?
questions.clue: The cardiopulmonary symptoms are sudden, ongoing and occurring while the patient is alone.
questions.rationale: The official patch label identifies sudden shortness of breath and severe chest pressure as serious warning symptoms associated with possible blood clots. Other cardiopulmonary emergencies can present similarly, so the nurse should not diagnose the cause during the call. Activate 911, avoid self-driving and defer patch-removal or alternative-method counseling until emergency care is underway.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies the acute symptom pattern to choose the correct level and route of care while rejecting reasonable-sounding but slower method-focused plans. The cues align, supporting level 2.

options.text: Call 911 now and wait for emergency medical services; do not drive, and report the patch use and symptom onset to responders.
options.reason: Continuing chest pressure and dyspnea require emergency assessment for thromboembolism or another acute cardiopulmonary cause. EMS provides the appropriate transport route.

options.text: Remove the patch, rest for 20 minutes and call again if the chest pressure or breathing difficulty continues.
options.reason: Removing the patch does not treat a possible clot or another acute cause. A watch-and-wait interval delays emergency assessment of symptoms that are already continuing.

options.text: Ask a friend to drive to urgent care now and bring the patch package for the clinician to review.
options.reason: Seeking prompt care is appropriate, but ongoing chest pressure and breathing difficulty call for 911 and EMS rather than transport by private car to a lower-acuity setting.

options.text: Call the contraception clinic for a same-day method change and seek emergency care only if the symptoms worsen.
options.reason: Method counseling is secondary while potentially life-threatening symptoms are present. Waiting for worsening would delay evaluation of the current emergency.

questions.objective: Differentiate worsening post-insertion findings from improving cramps
questions.stem: Five days after Kyleena insertion, a patient who was specifically taught how to check the threads calls the clinic. Which reports require prompt same-day clinician contact or emergency evaluation? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Select worsening infection, pregnancy-location or displacement findings, not improving expected effects or an unchanged taught baseline.
questions.rationale: After insertion of the named levonorgestrel IUD, fever with worsening pelvic pain or abnormal discharge warrants prompt contact. Pregnancy with lower abdominal pain requires urgent evaluation for an ectopic pregnancy. A new inability to feel previously palpable threads or feeling the device warrants location assessment and nonhormonal backup or abstinence until confirmation. Mild cramps and spotting that are steadily improving are different from worsening or severe findings. The stem makes prior thread teaching explicit; it does not impose a universal self-check schedule on every IUD user.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner independently classifies five post-insertion reports by trend and warning category, including both prompt clinic contact and emergency evaluation. No competing treatment response or unstable trend is present, supporting level 2.

options.text: A fever with worsening pelvic pain and unusual vaginal discharge
options.reason: Fever with increasing pelvic pain and abnormal discharge can indicate a serious post-insertion infection and warrants prompt clinician contact; severe illness may require emergency care.

options.text: A positive pregnancy test with new one-sided lower abdominal pain
options.reason: Pregnancy with Kyleena in place requires evaluation for ectopic pregnancy, and lower abdominal pain raises concern for this medical emergency.

options.text: Previously palpable threads can no longer be felt, or firm plastic is felt at the cervix
options.reason: A thread change or feeling the device can reflect displacement or expulsion. The patient should contact the clinician and avoid intercourse or use nonhormonal backup until location is confirmed.

options.text: Mild cramps and light spotting that have both steadily decreased since insertion
options.reason: Mild cramps and spotting can occur after placement, and a clearly improving trend without warning signs does not itself require prompt escalation.

options.text: Threads feel the same length as demonstrated, with no new pain, bleeding, discharge or fever
options.reason: An unchanged taught finding without symptoms does not indicate expulsion, perforation, pregnancy or infection and does not require prompt evaluation.

ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — IUD passages: post-insertion and contraception background (bounded reading; overbroad monthly string-check language excluded).

DailyMed — Official Kyleena levonorgestrel intrauterine-system labeling: pregnancy with lower abdominal pain, fever with worsening pelvic symptoms, and changed or absent threads require the labeled evaluation or contact pathway; mild early cramps and spotting can occur (device-specific; label date not established in the checked scope).

questions.objective: Identify the need for a method-specific missed-pill and EC plan
questions.stem: After a seven-day hormone-free interval, a patient missed the first two active pills of a 21-active-pill combined oral contraceptive pack. It is now the third pill day before today's dose, and intercourse without a condom occurred yesterday. After method-specific screening, the clinician selects levonorgestrel emergency contraception. Which complete plan should the nurse teach?
questions.clue: The branch is defined by two missed active pills in the first week, recent intercourse and a selected LNG—not UPA—emergency-contraception method.
questions.rationale: With two or more consecutive active COC pills missed, take the most recent missed pill as soon as possible, discard earlier missed pills, take the current pill at its usual time even if this means two pills in one day, and continue the pack. Use condoms or abstain until seven consecutive days of hormonal pills have been taken. Because the misses occurred in week one after the hormone-free interval and intercourse occurred within five days, emergency contraception should be considered; the stem supplies the method-specific selection of LNG, which permits immediate COC continuation.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies the first-week two-missed-pill branch and integrates the selected LNG EC plan with catch-up and backup sequencing. The cues are explicit and aligned, so the published level 3 is corrected to level 2.

options.text: Take the LNG EC now; discard the earlier missed pill, take the most recent missed pill and today's pill today, continue the pack, and use condoms or abstain until 7 consecutive active-pill days.
options.reason: For two missed first-week active pills, catch up only the most recent missed pill and keep today's scheduled dose, then continue daily. LNG EC can be taken now, and protection is needed until seven consecutive active-pill days are completed.

options.text: Take the LNG EC now; take one active pill today, two tomorrow and two the next day to replace both misses, then continue daily and use condoms or abstain until 7 consecutive active-pill days.
options.reason: This spreads replacement of both missed pills over later days. The recommended branch is to take the most recent missed pill now, discard the earlier miss and continue the remaining pills at their usual time, even if two are taken today.

options.text: Take the LNG EC now; discard both missed pills, take only today's scheduled pill, continue the pack, and stop condoms or abstinence after the seventh pack day.
options.reason: This omits the most recently missed pill and counts protection by pack position rather than seven consecutive days of active-pill use after resumption.

options.text: Take the LNG EC now; wait 5 days, start a new combined-pill pack, and use condoms or abstain during the delay and for 7 days after restart.
options.reason: The five-day hormonal delay belongs to UPA, not the selected LNG EC. Delaying the combined pill would unnecessarily extend the hormone-free interval.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: combined-hormonal and emergency-contraception context (P318–P333; P371–P372; P388–P400). The older blanket 72-hour limit is not the current algorithm.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — combined-pill and emergency-contraception passages (bounded reading; current CDC missed-pill and product-specific instructions control).

CDC — Combined Hormonal Contraceptives, U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations: after two or more consecutive missed active pills, take the most recent missed pill, discard earlier misses, continue the remaining pills, and use condoms or abstain until seven consecutive hormonal-pill days (page dated November 18, 2024).

CDC — U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use, 2024: LNG emergency-contraception pills permit immediate regular-method restart, unlike the delayed hormonal restart after UPA (published August 8, 2024).

questions.objective: Continue backup until follow-up confirms vasectomy success
questions.stem: Several weeks after a vasectomy, a patient reports that the incision is healed and many ejaculations have occurred, but the prescribed post-vasectomy semen analysis is still pending. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: Recovery findings and an ejaculation count do not answer the laboratory question of whether the procedure has achieved contraceptive success.
questions.rationale: Current CDC guidance advises abstinence or barrier protection until post-vasectomy semen analysis confirms success. The analysis is generally scheduled by the treating service, and the number of ejaculations after surgery is not a reliable clearance measure. Incision healing, absence of pain or an unprescribed home substitute should not end backup early.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes the single clearance criterion in a direct follow-up scenario. There is no multistep calculation or competing instability, supporting level 1.

options.text: Continue condoms or the current contraceptive method until the prescribed semen analysis confirms vasectomy success.
options.reason: Vasectomy is not considered reliable immediately, and ejaculation count alone is not an adequate indicator of success. Backup continues until post-vasectomy semen analysis provides confirmation.

options.text: Stop backup now because a healed incision and absence of pain indicate that the vas deferens is fully cleared.
options.reason: Wound healing and comfort describe recovery, not whether sperm remain in the ejaculate. They do not replace the prescribed semen analysis.

options.text: Use one negative home semen test as clearance and cancel the prescribed laboratory follow-up.
options.reason: The planned post-vasectomy semen analysis and clinician interpretation establish follow-up; an unsupervised substitute should not cancel that confirmation step.

options.text: Stop backup after reaching the suggested ejaculation count even if the semen-analysis result is not available.
options.reason: The number of ejaculations after surgery is not a reliable indicator of vasectomy success and should not replace the semen-analysis result.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: permanent contraception and vasectomy context (P341–P367; older or erroneous sterilization wording excluded).
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — vasectomy teaching passages (bounded reading; fixed ejaculation-count and two-zero-sample rules excluded).

CDC — Permanent Contraception, U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations: continue abstinence or barrier contraception until post-vasectomy semen analysis confirms success; ejaculation count is not a reliable indicator (page dated November 18, 2024).

questions.objective: Reassess LAM after the menstrual and feeding pattern changes
questions.stem: At 4 months postpartum, a patient who has relied on the lactational amenorrhea method reports a menstrual period last week. Formula now replaces several daily breastfeeds, with some feeding intervals longer than 6 hours. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: LAM depends on all three criteria at the same time; being less than six months postpartum is not sufficient by itself.
questions.rationale: LAM can be relied on only when the patient is amenorrheic, is less than six months postpartum, and is fully or nearly fully breastfeeding with intervals no longer than four hours during the day or six hours at night. The return of menses already means the criteria are not met, and several formula substitutions with longer intervals add a second reason. Counseling should support selection of another appropriate method while respecting the patient's breastfeeding preference.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies the complete three-part LAM criteria to a changed postpartum pattern and identifies the needed transition. Two aligned failed criteria do not create advanced reasoning, supporting level 2.

options.text: LAM criteria are no longer met; discuss another contraceptive method now that fits the patient's preferences and breastfeeding plans.
options.reason: Return of menses alone ends the amenorrhea criterion, and the changed feeding pattern also no longer meets the fully or nearly fully breastfeeding criterion. Another method should be selected without requiring breastfeeding to stop.

options.text: Continue LAM until 6 months postpartum because age under 6 months outweighs the menstrual and formula-feeding changes.
options.reason: Being under six months postpartum is only one of three required conditions. Return of menses and the feeding changes independently prevent reliance on LAM here.

options.text: Resume fully breastfeeding and rely on LAM again once one month passes without another menstrual period.
options.reason: A return to frequent breastfeeding does not erase the documented return of menses or create a new evidence-based waiting interval that restores LAM eligibility.

options.text: Continue LAM until a second menstrual period confirms regular ovulation, while recording each formula feed.
options.reason: LAM requires amenorrhea; a second period or proof of ovulation is not needed before recognizing that the criterion has changed.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: breastfeeding, fertility awareness, and contraceptive-choice context (P300–P310; P352–P360; not the complete current LAM criteria).
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — breastfeeding and contraception passages (bounded reading; current CDC LAM criteria control).

CDC — U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria, Lactational Amenorrhea Method: all three criteria are required—amenorrhea, fully or nearly fully breastfeeding with intervals no longer than four hours by day or six hours by night, and less than six months postpartum (page dated September 26, 2025).

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Barrier methods.
questions.stem: Which condom-use statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Correct technique and realistic protection expectations matter together.
questions.rationale: Teach practical risk reduction without promising complete protection or combining barrier devices in a way that can increase breakage.
questions.difficultyReason: Recall correct condom-use principles and their protection limits.

options.text: "I will use a new condom for each act of intercourse."
options.reason: Reuse increases failure and exposure risk.

options.text: "I will choose lubricant compatible with the condom material."
options.reason: Oil-based products can damage latex condoms.

options.text: "Condoms reduce STI risk but do not eliminate every skin-to-skin infection risk."
options.reason: Uncovered skin can still transmit some infections.

options.text: "Using an internal condom together with an external condom gives extra protection."
options.reason: Friction between devices can increase failure risk.

options.text: "An IUD makes condoms unnecessary even when STI exposure is possible."
options.reason: IUDs prevent pregnancy but do not reduce STI transmission.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: barrier methods (P311–317, P337, P355).
Course lecture topic locator — Week 6 Contraception & Abortion, slide 3 (barrier-method heading only; not technique verification).
Supplemental reading — ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11, chapter 1, Contraception (background; current CDC guidance controls technique and protection limits).
CDC — Condom Use: risk reduction, a new condom for each act, and latex-compatible lubricant.
CDC — Internal Condoms: do not use with an external condom and do not reuse.
CDC — Contraception and Birth Control Methods: pregnancy prevention does not replace STI protection.

questions.objective: Respect an informed eligible contraceptive preference
questions.stem: An adult patient is medically eligible for both a contraceptive implant and depot medroxyprogesterone acetate. After comparing effectiveness, bleeding changes, follow-up, return to fertility and procedures, the patient chooses the injection and accurately restates its tradeoffs. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: Eligibility, comparison and understanding are all supplied; the remaining task is to respect the patient's informed weighting of the tradeoffs.
questions.rationale: Person-centered contraceptive care provides accurate method information, checks clinical eligibility, elicits preferences and supports voluntary informed choice. Greater duration, fewer visits, ease of discontinuation and bleeding effects are reasonable counseling topics, but none automatically overrides this patient's understood preference. With no unresolved question or contraindication in the stem, the nurse should document and support the selected plan.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes the foundational autonomy principle after the stem explicitly supplies eligibility, counseling and understanding. No unresolved conflict or method calculation is present, supporting level 1.

options.text: Confirm any remaining questions, document the informed preference and proceed with the selected injection plan.
options.reason: The patient has received comparative counseling, is eligible and demonstrates understanding. Supporting the informed selection preserves reproductive autonomy.

options.text: Recommend another implant visit before providing the injection because longer duration and fewer return visits should carry more weight.
options.reason: Those are legitimate comparison points, but the patient has already considered them. Elevating the clinician's weighting above an informed eligible preference creates an unnecessary barrier.

options.text: Suggest a one-month combined-pill trial first because a daily method is easier to stop if bleeding changes occur.
options.reason: Ease of discontinuation is a legitimate comparison point, but suggesting a new pill trial does not respond to the informed injection preference already established in the stem.

options.text: Schedule a second decision visit because the injection cannot be removed if the patient later dislikes an effect.
options.reason: Duration of an administered dose is important counseling, but the patient already understands that tradeoff. A mandatory delay is not supported by the stated assessment.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: individualized contraceptive choice, preferences, and informed consent (P352–P367; no universal method preference).

CDC — U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use, 2024: person-centered, noncoercive counseling should respect patient preferences and reproductive autonomy (published August 8, 2024).

questions.objective: Coordinate pregnancy syphilis therapy despite immediate allergy
questions.stem: A patient at 18 weeks of pregnancy has confirmed syphilis and a documented immediate penicillin reaction with hives and wheezing. The outpatient prenatal clinic is not equipped for desensitization. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?
questions.clue: The allergy changes the setting and preparation for therapy, not the requirement for effective fetal and maternal treatment during pregnancy.
questions.rationale: Penicillin G is the only known effective antimicrobial for treating fetal infection and preventing congenital syphilis. When a pregnant patient has a true penicillin allergy, CDC guidance calls for desensitization and treatment with penicillin G. Because the current clinic cannot provide that monitored process, the nursing plan is prompt coordination with an equipped service; the item intentionally does not invent a desensitization protocol or a stage-specific dose.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner reconciles two explicit constraints—pregnancy requires effective penicillin therapy, while immediate allergy requires monitored desensitization—and chooses coordinated care. This supports level 2.

options.text: Promptly coordinate care in a monitored setting for penicillin desensitization followed by stage-appropriate penicillin G treatment.
options.reason: Penicillin G is the only known effective antimicrobial for treating fetal infection and preventing congenital syphilis. A pregnant patient with true penicillin allergy should be desensitized and treated with the appropriate penicillin regimen.

options.text: Replace penicillin with outpatient ceftriaxone because another parenteral antibiotic avoids the immediate allergy risk.
options.reason: Available evidence is insufficient to define an optimal ceftriaxone regimen for maternal infection and fetal treatment. It is not a proven substitute for desensitization and penicillin G in pregnancy.

options.text: Use an oral macrolide with serial maternal titers because oral therapy can be given without monitored allergy care.
options.reason: Azithromycin and erythromycin are not reliable for treating fetal infection. Monitoring does not turn them into effective pregnancy therapy.

options.text: Send separate routine referrals to allergy and infectious disease and let each service arrange its part before the prenatal team schedules treatment.
options.reason: Both specialties may participate, but fragmented sequential referrals risk delaying time-sensitive treatment and do not establish the coordinated monitored desensitization pathway required for this high-risk history.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: syphilis in pregnancy, placental transmission, penicillin treatment, and education (P127–P134; current CDC allergy guidance controls).

CDC — Syphilis During Pregnancy, STI Treatment Guidelines: penicillin G is the only known effective antimicrobial for fetal treatment and prevention of congenital syphilis; pregnant patients with penicillin allergy should be desensitized and treated with penicillin G (page last reviewed July 22, 2021).

CDC — Managing Persons Who Have a History of Penicillin Allergy, STI Treatment Guidelines: when penicillin is the only effective therapy, desensitization requires specialist care in a monitored inpatient environment; high-risk histories should not undergo ambulatory challenge (page last reviewed September 21, 2022).

questions.objective: Explain prescribed therapy and partner care to reduce reinfection
questions.stem: An adult woman with confirmed trichomoniasis is prescribed metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. Which statements by the patient show correct understanding of treatment and reinfection prevention? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: The prescription defines a full multidose course, and reinfection prevention depends on what both partners do before intercourse resumes.
questions.rationale: Complete the prescribed seven-day oral metronidazole regimen even if symptoms improve. Current sex partners should be referred for presumptive treatment, and intercourse should wait until the patient and partners have completed treatment and symptoms have resolved. Vaginal metronidazole gel should not replace the prescribed oral regimen, and recurrent symptoms require reassessment rather than self-directed medication reuse.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes three direct, regimen-specific teaching statements without interpreting competing clinical findings; the multiple-response format does not by itself raise the item above level 1.

options.text: "I will finish every prescribed dose even if my symptoms resolve before day 7."
options.reason: Symptom improvement does not replace completion of the prescribed multidose oral regimen.

options.text: "My current sex partner should seek treatment now even if no symptoms are present."
options.reason: Current partners should receive presumptive treatment because asymptomatic infection can sustain transmission and reinfection.

options.text: "We will avoid intercourse until we have both completed treatment and any symptoms have resolved."
options.reason: Waiting until both partners have completed therapy and symptoms have resolved reduces immediate transmission and reinfection risk.

options.text: "I can replace the prescribed oral tablets with vaginal metronidazole gel if the tablets upset my stomach."
options.reason: Vaginal metronidazole gel is less effective for trichomoniasis and is not a substitute for the prescribed oral regimen; medication intolerance should be discussed with the clinician.

options.text: "If my symptoms return later, I can restart metronidazole on my own without another assessment."
options.reason: Recurrent symptoms can reflect reinfection, nonadherence, or treatment failure, so the cause and next regimen require clinical reassessment rather than self-directed reuse.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: trichomoniasis therapy and partner-care teaching (P99–P116, P140–P175, and P209–P228; current CDC guidance controls).
Week 6 GYN, STIs, and Infertility lecture — slide 25: trichomoniasis heading (topic locator from the text layer, not detailed treatment guidance).
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — bounded trichomoniasis and STI teaching passages (supplemental course context; current CDC therapy and partner guidance controls).

CDC — Trichomoniasis, STI Treatment Guidelines: seven-day oral metronidazole for women, no equivalent substitution with vaginal gel, presumptive treatment of current partners, abstinence until treatment is complete and symptoms resolve, and cause assessment for recurrence (last reviewed September 21, 2022).

questions.objective: Escalate absent improvement after outpatient PID therapy
questions.stem: A patient being treated as an outpatient for pelvic inflammatory disease reports taking every prescribed dose for 72 hours. Temperature remains 38.2 C (100.8 F), and lower abdominal pain and pelvic tenderness have not improved. The patient is alert, can drink fluids and has no new instability. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?
questions.clue: The patient has adhered to outpatient therapy but has not shown the expected clinical improvement by the defined response checkpoint.
questions.rationale: Clinical improvement in fever and pelvic tenderness should be evident within three days of PID treatment. No improvement by 72 hours after outpatient IM or oral therapy calls for same-day reevaluation, with hospital care, antimicrobial-plan review and additional diagnostics considered together. A single repeat test, an unexamined medication change or imaging in isolation is not an adequate response assessment. New deterioration before 72 hours would also require prompt reassessment rather than waiting for the checkpoint.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a corroborated time-to-response threshold and distinguishes comprehensive reassessment from three plausible same-day but incomplete actions.

options.text: Arrange same-day in-person reevaluation and anticipate hospital-level assessment of the diagnosis, antimicrobial plan and need for additional diagnostics.
options.reason: Absent clinical improvement by 72 hours after outpatient therapy warrants reevaluation that can include hospitalization, regimen assessment and investigation of complications or alternative diagnoses.

options.text: Arrange a same-day repeat gonorrhea and chlamydia NAAT, then continue the outpatient plan unchanged until those results return.
options.reason: Repeat pathogen testing alone does not assess the failed clinical response, complications, alternative diagnoses or need for parenteral care.

options.text: Request a same-day telephone switch to a different oral regimen and schedule the next examination after that new course is completed.
options.reason: Changing outpatient antibiotics without examining the patient bypasses the recommended reassessment of diagnosis, severity and possible complications.

options.text: Send the patient to outpatient radiology for pelvic ultrasonography first and decide whether clinical reevaluation is needed after the report is available.
options.reason: Imaging may become part of the evaluation, but an imaging-first detour should not replace or delay same-day clinical reassessment after no response at 72 hours.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: PID symptoms, ascending infection, complications, treatment, and follow-up teaching (P129–P148; the endometriosis wording error is excluded).

CDC — Pelvic Inflammatory Disease, STI Treatment Guidelines: clinical improvement is expected within three days; failure to improve within 72 hours after outpatient IM or oral therapy warrants reevaluation, including hospitalization and additional diagnostics (2021 STI guideline).

questions.objective: Explain pregnancy test-of-cure separately from reinfection retesting
questions.stem: A pregnant patient completed treatment for chlamydia today. The follow-up plan includes a NAAT about 4 weeks after the last dose and another chlamydia test about 3 months after treatment. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
questions.clue: One test is scheduled soon after therapy because of pregnancy; the later test addresses what can happen after successful treatment.
questions.rationale: In pregnancy, a NAAT at approximately four weeks after treatment completion is a test of cure used to verify chlamydial eradication. Retesting about three months after treatment is still recommended to detect repeat infection. The two appointments therefore have separate purposes; a negative early result does not substitute for the later check.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recalls and distinguishes two explicitly named follow-up purposes and time anchors without resolving competing patient findings.

options.text: The four-week NAAT checks that treatment eradicated the infection during pregnancy; the later test looks for repeat infection after treatment.
options.reason: Pregnancy calls for a test of cure at approximately four weeks, while the later retest serves the distinct purpose of detecting repeat infection.

options.text: The four-week NAAT looks only for reinfection; the three-month test is the first check that the antibiotic worked.
options.reason: This reverses the purposes of the two tests: the earlier pregnancy test documents cure, and the later test detects repeat infection.

options.text: A negative four-week NAAT makes the later retest unnecessary as long as symptoms do not return.
options.reason: A negative test of cure does not remove the separate recommendation to retest for repeat infection, which can be asymptomatic.

options.text: Both appointments are duplicate tests of cure, so one combined test at an intermediate date would serve the same purpose.
options.reason: The scheduled tests answer different questions at different times and should not be merged into an invented compromise interval.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: chlamydia treatment and follow-up context (P99–P116, P140–P175, and P209–P228; current CDC pregnancy follow-up guidance controls).
Week 6 GYN, STIs, and Infertility lecture — slide 15: chlamydia heading (topic locator from the text layer, not a pregnancy follow-up algorithm).
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — bounded chlamydia and STI passages (supplemental context; the older three-week pregnancy retest statement is excluded).

CDC — Chlamydial Infections, STI Treatment Guidelines: during pregnancy, a test of cure at about four weeks after therapy verifies eradication; retesting at three months is a separate reinfection check (last reviewed July 22, 2021).

questions.objective: Distinguish antiviral control from eradication of genital HSV
questions.stem: A patient without HIV has symptomatic recurrent genital HSV-2 and a partner who does not have HSV-2. The patient is considering daily suppressive valacyclovir instead of episodic treatment. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
questions.clue: The regimen is daily suppression for symptomatic recurrent HSV-2, and clinical control is not the same as eliminating latency.
questions.rationale: Systemic antivirals partially control genital-herpes manifestations but do not eradicate latent HSV. In symptomatic recurrent HSV-2, daily suppressive therapy reduces recurrences and can lower transmission risk in supported contexts; it does not make transmission impossible, and asymptomatic shedding remains relevant. Episodic treatment instead targets the duration and severity of individual recurrences.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner identifies the foundational distinction between control and cure while recognizing the named suppressive regimen's bounded benefit.

options.text: Daily suppression can reduce recurrences and lower transmission risk in this HSV-2 context, but it does not eradicate latent virus or eliminate asymptomatic shedding.
options.reason: Suppressive antiviral therapy controls recurrent symptomatic HSV-2 and can reduce transmission risk, but HSV remains latent and transmission risk is not zero.

options.text: Daily suppression gradually clears latent virus from sensory nerves, so recurrence risk remains reduced after the medication is stopped.
options.reason: Antivirals do not eradicate latent HSV or change the later recurrence pattern once suppressive therapy is discontinued.

options.text: Episodic treatment provides the same reduction in between-outbreak transmission as daily suppression; the approaches differ only in pill frequency.
options.reason: Episodic treatment shortens a recurrence, whereas the supported transmission-reduction benefit is tied to daily suppressive therapy in defined HSV-2 contexts.

options.text: A negative swab from healed genital skin after suppression confirms that latent infection is absent and ongoing therapy is no longer relevant.
options.reason: Viral shedding is intermittent, and a negative swab—especially without an active lesion—does not establish eradication of latent HSV.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: genital herpes therapy and transmission teaching (P99–P116, P140–P175, and P209–P228; current CDC guidance controls).
Week 6 GYN, STIs, and Infertility lecture — slide 20: genital herpes heading (topic locator from the text layer, not detailed suppressive-therapy guidance).

CDC — Genital Herpes, STI Treatment Guidelines: antivirals control but do not eradicate latent HSV; recurrent HSV-2 may shed between outbreaks, and daily suppressive therapy reduces recurrences and can lower—but not eliminate—transmission risk in supported contexts (2021 STI guideline).

questions.objective: Explain why vaccination does not replace indicated screening
questions.stem: An adult whose HPV vaccination is complete sees that routine cervical cancer screening is due according to the clinic's guideline-based plan and asks to cancel it because of the vaccination. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: Vaccination prevents selected future infections, whereas screening looks for clinically silent cervical precancer according to a separate risk-based plan.
questions.rationale: HPV vaccination substantially reduces the risk of vaccine-type infection and disease, but it does not cover every oncogenic type or replace detection of asymptomatic cervical precancer. Current screening recommendations do not differ by HPV-vaccination status. Follow the patient's age-, history- and result-based screening plan rather than using vaccination timing, symptoms or antibody testing as substitutes.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner distinguishes the foundational purposes of primary prevention and screening without calculating an age-specific interval.

options.text: Keep the scheduled screening; HPV vaccination prevents many new vaccine-type infections, but screening recommendations currently do not differ by vaccination status.
options.reason: Vaccination and screening have complementary preventive roles, and completing vaccination does not remove guideline-based cervical screening.

options.text: Cancel the screening if the vaccine series was completed before sexual activity because that timing determines whether screening is needed.
options.reason: Vaccination timing can affect preventive benefit, but current cervical-screening recommendations do not exempt vaccinated people on that basis.

options.text: Delay screening until genital symptoms appear because vaccination makes asymptomatic precancer unlikely to need detection.
options.reason: Cervical precancer is often asymptomatic, which is why indicated screening is performed before symptoms appear.

options.text: Replace screening with a serum HPV antibody test and resume cervical testing only if the antibody level falls.
options.reason: No clinical antibody threshold determines cervical-screening need, and serology is not a replacement for guideline-based screening.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: HPV and cervical-screening context (P99–P116, P140–P175, and P209–P228; age-specific wording and Pap-as-diagnosis shortcuts are excluded).
Week 6 GYN, STIs, and Infertility lecture — slide 19: HPV heading (topic locator from the text layer, not a screening interval).
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — bounded HPV and STI passages (supplemental context; fixed vaccine schedules and Pap-as-diagnosis wording are excluded).

CDC — Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases, Chapter 5: Human Papillomavirus: cervical screening detects asymptomatic precancer, recommendations evolve, and current screening recommendations do not differ based on vaccination status (page updated July 6, 2026).

questions.objective: Prioritize unstable systemic illness after tampon exposure
questions.stem: At a student health clinic, a patient who has had a tampon in place since yesterday develops a temperature of 39.5 C (103.1 F), diffuse erythematous rash, vomiting, BP 82/46 mmHg and pulse 128/min. The tampon is still in place. Which action plan has priority?
questions.clue: The patient already has measured hypotension and multisystem findings, and the suspected retained source can be addressed while transfer begins.
questions.rationale: This pattern raises concern for toxic shock or another sepsis-like shock syndrome after tampon exposure. Activate emergency transport to a hospital and begin available airway/circulation support immediately. Remove the tampon promptly if this can be done without delaying transfer; source removal is part of the coordinated response, not a step that must wait until stabilization is complete. Do not postpone escalation for oral fluids, organism identification or additional organ-system findings.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner integrates exposure, measured hypotension and multisystem illness to prioritize simultaneous emergency transfer, supportive care and source removal over three plausible but unsafe sequences.

options.text: Activate EMS for emergency-department transfer, begin available airway and circulation support, and have the tampon removed promptly without delaying transfer.
options.reason: Hypotension with rapid systemic illness is a medical emergency; hospital-level support and prompt source removal should proceed together.

options.text: Remove the tampon, give oral fluids while the patient rests supine, and decide about transfer after repeating the blood pressure in 15 minutes.
options.reason: Removing the tampon is appropriate, but a fluid trial and repeat reading must not become prerequisites that delay emergency transport for current shock findings.

options.text: Obtain vaginal and blood cultures at the clinic, then choose the destination after the organism is identified.
options.reason: Cultures may be obtained during evaluation, but organism confirmation is not required before emergency transfer and supportive care.

options.text: Arrange the first same-day gynecology appointment, remove the tampon while waiting, and use emergency care only if confusion or dyspnea develops.
options.reason: The existing hypotension, fever, rash, tachycardia and vomiting already justify emergency hospital evaluation; additional organ symptoms are not required.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: toxic shock syndrome as a life-threatening complication associated with prolonged tampon use and requiring emergency treatment (P229–P231; not a full stabilization or antibiotic protocol).

Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition — bounded older-textbook background on toxic shock syndrome systemic findings, shock, hospitalization, and abnormal-bleeding assessment; current direct guidance controls acute routing.

NHS — Toxic shock syndrome: symptoms can progress quickly and require urgent hospital treatment; remove a tampon if one is in use, and hospital care can include fluids, blood-pressure support, and antibiotics (last reviewed June 6, 2023; review date shown as June 6, 2026).

questions.objective: Assess perfusion during acute heavy bleeding
questions.stem: A patient arrives at a gynecology clinic after soaking about one pad each hour for 4 hours and passing several large clots. Pulse is 118/min, and the patient reports becoming lightheaded when standing. No blood pressure has yet been obtained. Which focused assessment should the nurse perform first?
questions.clue: Tachycardia and lightheadedness during active heavy bleeding raise an immediate circulation question before the cause is classified.
questions.rationale: Acute abnormal uterine bleeding should first trigger prompt assessment for hypovolemia and potential hemodynamic instability. Obtain blood pressure and assess other perfusion findings while confirming ongoing loss, then continue with bleeding quantification, pregnancy and medication history, coagulation history and pelvic/source evaluation. Reported lightheadedness on standing is a symptom; the stem does not claim that formal orthostatic hypotension has been measured.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner prioritizes one assessment domain among four legitimate acute evaluations and must not let useful etiologic or quantification tasks precede perfusion assessment.

options.text: Assess blood pressure, mental status, skin temperature and capillary refill immediately while confirming whether heavy bleeding is continuing.
options.reason: The acute blood-loss pattern, tachycardia and positional lightheadedness make current perfusion and hemodynamic stability the first assessment priority.

options.text: Count and weigh all available used pads and clots before checking blood pressure or mental status.
options.reason: Quantifying blood loss is useful, but it should not precede assessment of current perfusion when systemic symptoms and tachycardia are already present.

options.text: Complete the pregnancy, medication, bleeding-disorder and menstrual history before obtaining the remaining vital signs.
options.reason: These details are important for etiology and treatment, but immediate perfusion assessment comes first in an acute heavy-bleeding presentation.

options.text: Prioritize abdominal and pelvic findings to localize the bleeding source, then assess circulation after the examination.
options.reason: Source evaluation is necessary, but it follows the prompt assessment for hypovolemia and hemodynamic instability.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: abnormal uterine bleeding terms and assessment context (P66–P89 and P444–P446; not a complete acute-resuscitation protocol).
Week 6 GYN, STIs, and Infertility lecture — slide 5: metrorrhagia heading (topic locator from the text layer, not acute hemodynamic guidance).

Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition — bounded older-textbook background on bleeding assessment and systemic hypovolemia or shock findings; current professional guidance controls the initial priority.

ACOG Committee Opinion No. 557 abstract, via PubMed — Management of Acute Abnormal Uterine Bleeding in Nonpregnant Reproductive-Aged Women: initial evaluation begins with prompt assessment for hypovolemia and possible hemodynamic instability (2013).

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Amenorrhea.
questions.stem: A previously menstruating patient reports two missed periods and asks for medication to "restart the cycle." Which step should come first?
questions.clue: A potentially pregnant patient requests treatment before the cause is assessed.
questions.rationale: Start with a relevant history and pregnancy evaluation, then investigate endocrine, nutritional, medication, and other causes as indicated.
questions.difficultyReason: Identify pregnancy assessment as an initial step in secondary amenorrhea.

options.text: Assess the possibility of pregnancy before pursuing other causes or treatment.
options.reason: Pregnancy is a common cause of secondary amenorrhea and changes management.

options.text: Recommend cycle-restarting medication as the initial management approach for missed periods.
options.reason: Cycle-directed treatment is premature until pregnancy has been assessed.

options.text: Prioritize thyroid testing as the first step for the missed periods.
options.reason: Thyroid disease can disrupt menstruation, but pregnancy remains an initial consideration.

options.text: Recommend stress-reduction strategies as the initial management approach for missed periods.
options.reason: Stress can affect cycles, but assuming it explains this presentation does not address possible pregnancy.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: amenorrhea, pregnancy as a common cause, and other possible contributors (P17–P31; extract paragraph locators).
Course lecture topic context — Week 6 GYN, STIs, and Infertility, slide 2: amenorrhea heading only (text layer only; not pregnancy-first guidance).

Supplemental reading — Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition: pregnancy exclusion as an important initial step in amenorrhea evaluation, with later assessment as indicated (bounded passage; no duration criterion or full workup algorithm).
ASRM — Current evaluation of amenorrhea (2024): pregnancy is the first consideration in secondary amenorrhea, followed by other evaluation as indicated.

questions.objective: Assess new unexplained bleeding while using menopause hormones
questions.stem: A postmenopausal patient with an intact uterus has taken an unchanged continuous-combined oral estradiol/norethindrone regimen for 18 months. Spotting stopped after the first 4 months, and there has been no bleeding for a year. The patient now reports two new spotting episodes this week. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The regimen has been unchanged well beyond its initiation period, and bleeding has newly returned after a prolonged amenorrheic interval.
questions.rationale: Unscheduled bleeding can occur during the early months of continuous-combined MHT, but this patient has a first new episode after 18 months on an unchanged regimen and a year without bleeding. Begin with a structured review of the bleeding, regimen, adherence and risk factors and arrange prompt clinical evaluation. Do not treat MHT as the diagnosis, defer all assessment for a medication trial or substitute routine cervical screening for evaluation of the symptom.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies regimen type, time since initiation and a change from established amenorrhea to distinguish prompt assessment from reasonable-sounding early-adjustment approaches.

options.text: Review the bleeding pattern, adherence, exact hormone regimen and cancer risk factors, and arrange prompt clinician evaluation rather than assuming the medication explains it.
options.reason: New bleeding after an established amenorrheic interval and well beyond initiation requires assessment; MHT is part of the history, not a benign diagnosis.

options.text: Document the episodes and continue routine follow-up because light spotting remains an expected medication effect at any point on this regimen.
options.reason: Early spotting can occur, but new bleeding after 18 months and a year without bleeding should not be classified as expected solely because the patient uses MHT.

options.text: Request a progestogen adjustment for the next 6 months and pursue diagnostic assessment only if bleeding continues after that trial.
options.reason: An adjustment-first observation pathway applies to selected early or recently changed regimens, not a first bleed long after treatment started and stabilized.

options.text: Arrange cervical screening as the sole first test and pursue other causes only if that screening result is abnormal.
options.reason: Cervical screening has a defined preventive purpose and cannot by itself evaluate every source of postmenopausal bleeding.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: menopause-hormone management and reproductive-tract symptoms requiring follow-up (P66–P89 and P444–P446; not a diagnostic test sequence).

British Menopause Society — Management of Unscheduled Bleeding on Hormone Replacement Therapy: review the bleeding pattern, HRT preparation, adherence, and cancer risk factors; a first bleed more than six months after starting or more than three months after changing HRT is not an early-adjustment-only pattern (guideline reviewed May 2026).

DailyMed — Official estradiol/norethindrone acetate tablet labeling: bleeding tends to decrease with continued use, but postmenopausal bleeding should be reported and assessed; the label also addresses endometrial risk with systemic estrogen and an intact uterus (record updated June 26, 2026; product-specific).

questions.objective: Explain endometrial protection with systemic estrogen and an intact uterus
questions.stem: A postmenopausal patient with an intact uterus is prescribed systemic oral estradiol together with a progestogen. The patient asks why both hormones are included. Which explanation by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The prescription is systemic estrogen, and the patient still has the endometrial tissue that estrogen can stimulate.
questions.rationale: Unopposed systemic estrogen can stimulate the endometrium and increase the risk of hyperplasia, which may be a precursor to endometrial cancer. Adding an appropriate progestogen lowers that risk by opposing the estrogen effect. This explains the uterus-dependent combination but does not guarantee zero risk or replace individualized monitoring and assessment of unexplained bleeding.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recalls the direct mechanism linking systemic estrogen, an intact uterus and endometrial protection.

options.text: The progestogen opposes estrogen-driven endometrial growth and lowers the risk of endometrial hyperplasia that can occur with unopposed systemic estrogen.
options.reason: In a patient with a uterus using systemic estrogen, progestogen provides endometrial protection by reducing estrogen-induced hyperplasia risk.

options.text: The progestogen increases intestinal absorption of estradiol so the same estrogen dose controls hot flashes more quickly.
options.reason: Endometrial opposition—not improved estradiol absorption—is the uterus-specific reason to add a progestogen.

options.text: The progestogen supplies most of the bone-protective effect, while systemic estrogen is included mainly to prevent uterine bleeding.
options.reason: This reverses the roles relevant to the prescription; systemic estrogen treats menopause symptoms and affects bone, while progestogen protects the estrogen-exposed endometrium.

options.text: The progestogen stimulates the postmenopausal ovaries to resume endogenous cyclic hormone production while estradiol is tapered.
options.reason: The added progestogen is not intended to restart ovarian cycling; its relevant role is opposing estrogen's endometrial effect.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: menopause hormone therapy and uterus-dependent systemic estrogen/progestogen selection (P66–P89 and P444–P446).

DailyMed — Official estradiol/norethindrone acetate tablet labeling: unopposed systemic estrogen can stimulate the endometrium, and adding an appropriate progestogen lowers endometrial-hyperplasia risk in a patient with an intact uterus (record updated June 26, 2026; product-specific).

questions.objective: Escalate abrupt unilateral pain in a patient with an ovarian cyst
questions.stem: A patient with an ultrasound-documented right ovarian cyst is scheduled for repeat imaging in 6 weeks. The patient calls now with sudden severe right-sided pelvic pain and repeated vomiting. Which instruction should the nurse give?
questions.clue: A cyst that was appropriate for surveillance has developed a sudden severe symptom change with vomiting.
questions.rationale: Watchful waiting applies to selected stable cysts, but sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with vomiting requires prompt emergency assessment. Torsion, rupture or bleeding are possibilities, along with other acute pelvic or abdominal causes; the nurse should not diagnose one by telephone. Do not wait for routine imaging, analgesic response, office availability or vaginal bleeding before escalating.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a major change from stable surveillance to an acute disposition decision while keeping several possible causes open.

options.text: Obtain emergency evaluation now because torsion, cyst rupture or bleeding and other acute pelvic causes must be assessed promptly.
options.reason: Sudden severe unilateral pain with vomiting in a patient with an ovarian cyst requires urgent acute evaluation; the cause is not established by telephone.

options.text: Ask the imaging center to move the surveillance ultrasound earlier and use that report to decide whether emergency evaluation is needed.
options.reason: Routine outpatient imaging should not become a gate before clinical evaluation of sudden severe pain with vomiting.

options.text: Use the prescribed as-needed analgesic and reassess after one dosing interval because a previously documented cyst is already being monitored.
options.reason: Existing surveillance applies to the prior stable cyst, not to a new acute symptom pattern that could reflect a complication or another emergency.

options.text: Wait for the gynecology office to offer a same-day appointment and seek emergency care only if vaginal bleeding also begins.
options.reason: Vaginal bleeding is not required for torsion, rupture or another acute pelvic cause, and office-call delay is unsafe with current severe pain and vomiting.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: ovarian-cyst topic and general symptom follow-up (P435–P449; not acute torsion, rupture, disposition, or procedural guidance).

NHS — Ovarian cyst: sudden severe pelvic pain, or abdominal pain with nausea or vomiting, requires urgent help; follow-up depends on symptoms and cyst features (last reviewed June 21, 2023; review date shown as June 21, 2026).

questions.objective: Acknowledge grief before offering fertility solutions
questions.stem: After another unsuccessful fertility treatment, a patient says, "My body keeps failing us." Which response is most therapeutic?
questions.clue: The patient is expressing grief and self-blame rather than requesting a new treatment schedule.
questions.rationale: Attend to emotional needs before offering solutions. Explore support and counseling when the patient is ready.
questions.difficultyReason: Select an open, validating response over reassurance or unsolicited solutions.

options.text: "This has been painful. What part of this experience feels hardest right now?"
options.reason: This acknowledges distress and invites the patient's perspective.

options.text: "Are you feeling discouraged because this fertility treatment did not work as hoped?"
options.reason: This recognizes a likely emotion, but the closed question supplies the feeling instead of inviting the patient to describe the experience.

options.text: "Would you like information about infertility support groups available through the clinic?"
options.reason: A support group may be useful later, but offering a resource before exploring the grief moves prematurely to a solution.

options.text: "Many patients describe unsuccessful fertility treatment as a major source of stress."
options.reason: Normalization may reduce isolation, but this general statement shifts away from the patient's individual grief and does not invite further expression.

refs.label: Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI Instructor Notes — P237–P241 (goals of care and emotional support); P282–P285 (therapeutic communication, referrals and counseling).

ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11, chapter 2: Infertility — printed p. 14 / supplied text extract 1568–1586 (bounded support for expression of feelings, decision support and grief/infertility support-group referral; not a universal response script).

Supplemental reading locator: ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11, chapter 2: Infertility; Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition, chapter 5: Infertility, Contraception, and Abortion. Chapter-level background, not verification of every item detail.

questions.objective: Explain why both partners may need fertility assessment
questions.stem: At an initial infertility visit, a patient says, "My menstrual cycles are irregular, so why does my partner need a history and semen analysis now?" Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: A possible factor in one partner does not exclude a simultaneous factor in the other.
questions.rationale: Initial infertility assessment considers both partners when a male partner is contributing to pregnancy. Irregular cycles can warrant evaluation, but they do not establish a single cause or make the partner's history and semen analysis unnecessary. Presenting evaluation as a concurrent clinical process avoids delay, blame, and false certainty.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes a direct shared-assessment principle from a clearly stated initial infertility visit; no test interpretation or competing clinical data are required.

options.text: "Irregular cycles may be one contributor, but they do not rule out others; evaluating both partners together helps guide the plan."
options.reason: A possible ovulatory factor does not exclude a concurrent male factor, so initial evaluation can proceed for both partners without assigning fault.

options.text: "We should finish the entire ovulation evaluation first; partner testing is useful only if those results are normal."
options.reason: A recognized possible female factor is not a reason to postpone the partner's initial assessment; guidance supports concurrent evaluation.

options.text: "The semen analysis will determine whether your irregular cycles are causing the difficulty conceiving."
options.reason: Semen analysis evaluates semen parameters; it does not establish the cause of the patient's irregular menstrual cycles.

options.text: "If the first semen analysis is within reference ranges, it will confirm that no male contribution needs further consideration."
options.reason: A semen result is interpreted within the couple's complete evaluation, and individual semen parameters do not by themselves prove fertility or infertility.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: infertility support, female and male factors, hysterosalpingography, semen analysis, treatment, and nursing actions (P239–P285).
Week 6 GYN, STIs, and Infertility lecture — slides 28–30: male infertility and female/male assessment headings (topic locators; the text layer does not supply a detailed assessment sequence).
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — infertility chapter: bounded passages on assessment of female and male factors and semen-analysis purpose (book pages 13–14; supplemental context).

Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition — bounded older-textbook passages on joint infertility assessment and semen analysis (supplemental course context; current professional guidance controls interpretation).

AUA/ASRM Guideline Part I — Diagnosis and Treatment of Infertility in Men: initial infertility evaluation includes concurrent assessment of both partners; male evaluation includes reproductive history and one or more semen analyses, and individual semen parameters do not alone predict fertility or infertility (2020 guideline; published in 2021).

questions.objective: Reassess HSG readiness when infection symptoms appear
questions.stem: At radiology check-in for a scheduled hysterosalpingography, a patient reports a new fever and purulent vaginal discharge that began yesterday. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.clue: New infection findings can change the safety of a previously scheduled intrauterine procedure.
questions.rationale: HSG uses a catheter and contrast material to examine the uterus and fallopian tubes. Active pelvic infection is a reason not to perform the procedure, and patients should report signs of pelvic infection before it begins. Fever and purulent discharge suggest a possible infection but do not identify an organism; the nurse should pause preparation and coordinate assessment before a proceed-or-defer decision.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must apply a new change in clinical status to a scheduled diagnostic procedure and coordinate reassessment rather than follow the original plan automatically.

options.text: Pause preparation and notify the ordering or radiology clinician so pelvic infection can be assessed before any decision to proceed.
options.reason: Possible pelvic infection must be assessed before HSG because uterine and tubal instrumentation can worsen an active infection.

options.text: Give the planned preprocedure analgesic, repeat the temperature in 30 minutes, and proceed if the fever decreases.
options.reason: A lower temperature after an analgesic would not resolve the new infection concern or establish that HSG is safe to perform.

options.text: Obtain a vaginal specimen, then continue the HSG while results are pending because an infection has not yet been confirmed.
options.reason: The findings do not prove a specific infection, but signs of pelvic infection still require assessment before the procedure rather than instrumentation while results are pending.

options.text: Reschedule the HSG for the next cycle and advise routine follow-up only if the fever or discharge persists.
options.reason: Deferring the image alone does not address current fever and purulent discharge; the patient needs timely clinical evaluation of the new symptoms.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: infertility testing, hysterosalpingography, treatment, and nursing actions (P239–P285; not an infection contraindication protocol).
Week 6 GYN, STIs, and Infertility lecture — slides 29 and 32: infertility assessment and medical-therapy headings (topic locators, not HSG infection guidance).
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — infertility chapter: bounded hysterosalpingography-purpose passage (book pages 13–14; does not establish the infection contraindication).

Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition — bounded older-textbook passages on infertility assessment and hysterosalpingography purpose (supplemental context, not the controlling infection-safety source).

ACR/RSNA RadiologyInfo — Hysterosalpingography: HSG uses catheter-delivered contrast and should not be performed with active pelvic infection; patients should report possible pelvic-infection or untreated-STI findings because instrumentation can worsen infection (last reviewed August 25, 2024).

questions.objective: Stop further clomiphene exposure and escalate new visual symptoms
questions.stem: A patient taking a prescribed course of clomiphene reports new blurred vision and flashes of light and asks whether to finish the course. Which instruction by the nurse is most appropriate?
questions.clue: A new visual disturbance is a medication warning, not evidence that ovulation induction is working.
questions.rationale: Blurred vision and flashes can occur with clomiphene and may make driving or operating machinery hazardous. The prescribing information directs patients with any visual symptoms to discontinue treatment and undergo prompt complete ophthalmologic evaluation. The patient should not finish, reduce, or later restart the medication without clinician direction.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a medication-specific warning to a two-part safety response: stop further exposure and arrange prompt specialty evaluation.

options.text: Do not take another dose; contact the prescriber now for prompt ophthalmologic evaluation, and do not restart clomiphene on your own.
options.reason: The label directs discontinuation for any visual symptoms and prompt complete ophthalmologic evaluation; later treatment decisions belong to the prescriber.

options.text: Hold the tablets only until vision clears, then restart the remaining doses without contacting the fertility team.
options.reason: Symptom improvement is not permission for an unsupervised restart; visual symptoms require discontinuation and prompt ophthalmologic evaluation.

options.text: Finish the current course while avoiding driving in variable light, then report the symptoms at the next routine visit.
options.reason: Avoiding hazardous activity does not replace stopping clomiphene and obtaining prompt evaluation of the visual symptoms.

options.text: Reduce the next dose by half and arrange a routine vision screening after the fertility treatment is complete.
options.reason: The patient should not self-adjust and continue therapy; the label calls for discontinuation and prompt ophthalmologic evaluation.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: infertility medical therapy and nursing actions (P239–P285; not a clomiphene visual-warning protocol).
Week 6 GYN, STIs, and Infertility lecture — slide 32: medical-therapy heading (topic locator, not detailed clomiphene safety guidance).

ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — infertility chapter: bounded clomiphene ovarian-stimulation and adverse-effect-monitoring context (book pages 13–14; the official product label controls the visual-symptom response).

DailyMed — Official clomiphene citrate prescribing information: blurred vision, spots, or flashes are visual warnings; any visual symptoms require discontinuation and prompt complete ophthalmologic evaluation, and may create driving hazards (label issued August 2025 and revised December 2025).

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: General Women's Health Promotion & Maintenance: Breast cancer; Breast Disorders.
questions.stem: A patient reports a persistent new breast lump despite a screening mammogram described as normal six months ago. What should the nurse recommend?
questions.clue: Screening history does not negate a new persistent symptom.
questions.rationale: Distinguish routine screening from diagnostic evaluation and support timely follow-up without premature certainty.
questions.difficultyReason: Separate routine breast screening from evaluation of a persistent new finding.

options.text: Arrange diagnostic evaluation of the new finding.
options.reason: A prior normal screening study does not rule out a subsequently noticed abnormality.

options.text: Continue routine screening on the currently planned schedule.
options.reason: A persistent new lump needs evaluation outside routine screening intervals.

options.text: Assume the lump is benign because it is painless.
options.reason: Lack of pain does not exclude malignancy.

options.text: Arrange another screening mammogram to address the current lump.
options.reason: Routine screening alone does not replace diagnostic evaluation of a persistent breast finding.
