Week 6 GYN, STIs, and Infertility lecture — slide 11 breast-cancer topic heading (extracted text layer only).
Supplemental reading: Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition — chapter 4, Reproductive System Concerns (verified breast-condition supplied-text passages).
National Cancer Institute — Breast Cancer Signs and Symptoms (updated 2 December 2025).
National Cancer Institute — Mammograms (updated 2 December 2025).

questions.objective: Recall prescribed rehabilitation and complication reporting after node surgery
questions.stem: A patient is reviewing an individualized discharge plan after axillary lymph-node dissection. Which statements show correct understanding of recovery and complication prevention? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Safe recovery pairs gradual movement with skin protection and reporting of new lymphatic or infection findings.
questions.rationale: After axillary node surgery, the patient should follow the surgical team's exercise plan and rebuild activity gradually, protect the skin, care for cuts, and report new or worsening swelling or infection findings. A closed incision does not end rehabilitation, and heat is not a substitute for assessment of swelling. The exact exercise schedule and activity limits remain individualized.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes routine postoperative teaching across several independent statements; the SATA format does not add competing cues or advanced reasoning.

options.text: "I will contact my healthcare provider if the affected side becomes warmer, redder, more painful, or more swollen, or if I develop a fever."
options.reason: New or worsening warmth, redness, pain, swelling, and fever can indicate infection or a lymphatic complication and should be reported.

options.text: "I will start the prescribed arm exercises when my care team says it is safe and build activity back gradually."
options.reason: Team-directed exercises and gradual progression support range of motion while respecting the individual surgical plan.

options.text: "I will protect the skin during chores and promptly clean and cover a cut while watching for signs of infection."
options.reason: Skin protection and prompt care of minor injuries reduce infection risk in an area with altered lymph drainage.

options.text: "If the arm feels tight or puffy, I will place a heating pad over the shoulder to encourage drainage."
options.reason: Heating pads and hot packs are not recommended on the affected arm, shoulder, or torso; swelling should be managed according to the care plan and reported when indicated.

options.text: "Once the incision closes, I can stop the prescribed exercises even if my shoulder movement is still limited."
options.reason: Incision closure is not the endpoint for rehabilitation; limited range of motion requires continued team-directed exercise and follow-up.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: breast surgery, lymph-node removal, reconstruction, accurate information, psychosocial support, and therapeutic communication (P422–P432; not an axillary rehabilitation protocol).
Week 6 GYN, STIs, and Infertility lecture — slide 11: breast-cancer heading (topic locator; text and prior visual review did not supply detailed axillary-care guidance).
Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition — bounded older-textbook breast-surgery and support passages (supplemental course context; current institutional guidance controls arm-care details).

Memorial Sloan Kettering — Hand and Arm Guidelines After Axillary Lymph Node Dissection: report new or worsening swelling or infection findings, protect skin and care for cuts, follow team-directed exercise with gradual activity, and avoid heating pads on the affected area (updated July 7, 2026).

Memorial Sloan Kettering — Axillary Lymph Node Dissection Checklist: review individualized home exercises and care-team instructions and report fever, redness, warmth, drainage, discomfort, breathing difficulty, or increasing arm or incision swelling (updated April 3, 2026).

questions.objective: Support an informed reconstruction preference
questions.stem: Before a planned mastectomy, a patient says, "People keep assuming I will want reconstruction, but I am still unsure." Which response by the nurse best supports informed decision-making?
questions.clue: Uncertainty calls for values exploration and balanced information, not a predetermined outcome.
questions.rationale: A patient may choose immediate reconstruction, delayed reconstruction, or no reconstruction. The nurse should explore what matters to the patient, provide accurate and balanced information, and help bring questions and preferences to the surgical team. Uncertainty does not mean the patient lacks decision-making capacity, and neither clinician nor partner preference should replace the patient's choice.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner identifies a direct therapeutic-communication response that supports autonomy from a clearly expressed preference and uncertainty.

options.text: "What matters most to you about reconstruction? I can explain the options and help you discuss your preferences."
options.reason: An open question plus balanced information centers the patient's values and supports discussion of more than one acceptable pathway.

options.text: "Would reviewing only the surgeon's preferred reconstruction make the choice feel less overwhelming?"
options.reason: Limiting information to one clinician-preferred approach narrows informed choice before the patient's goals and eligible options are explored.

options.text: "Because reconstruction can be delayed, let's avoid the topic until after mastectomy so today's plan stays simple."
options.reason: Delayed reconstruction may be an option, but automatically ending the discussion withholds support and information the patient is asking for now.

options.text: "Let's first identify which option would be easiest for your partner to support at home, then discuss your concerns."
options.reason: A support person can participate if the patient wishes, but the partner's convenience should not precede or determine the patient's informed preference.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: breast surgery, reconstruction, accurate information, psychosocial support, and therapeutic communication (P422–P432).
Week 6 GYN, STIs, and Infertility lecture — slide 11: breast-cancer heading (topic locator, not detailed reconstruction decision guidance).

Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition — bounded older-textbook passages on breast-surgery decisions, supportive communication, and the possibility of choosing no reconstruction (supplemental course context).

National Cancer Institute — Breast Reconstruction After Mastectomy: immediate reconstruction, delayed reconstruction, and no reconstruction are possible pathways, and patients may weigh personal goals and clinical factors when choosing timing or method (updated December 2, 2025).

questions.objective: Escalate possible GI bleeding during NSAID self-treatment
questions.stem: A patient calls the clinic after using over-the-counter ibuprofen for menstrual cramps for 3 days. The patient reports two black, tarry stools and feeling lightheaded when standing. Which instruction should the nurse give first?
questions.clue: The new stool and perfusion findings are not routine dysmenorrhea symptoms or simple gastric discomfort.
questions.rationale: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can cause gastrointestinal bleeding. Black, tarry stools and lightheadedness are warning findings, so the patient should stop ibuprofen and obtain urgent clinical evaluation rather than mask symptoms, switch to another NSAID, or restart independently. The scenario signals possible bleeding; it does not establish the amount, source, or final diagnosis.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must connect a common dysmenorrhea self-treatment to a new bleeding-and-perfusion pattern and choose immediate escalation over familiar comfort advice.

options.text: Stop taking ibuprofen and seek urgent clinical evaluation now for possible gastrointestinal bleeding, especially given the lightheadedness.
options.reason: Black, tarry stools and positional lightheadedness are concerning for acute gastrointestinal bleeding and possible circulatory compromise, requiring prompt evaluation without further NSAID exposure.

options.text: Take the next ibuprofen dose with food, increase oral fluids, and call back tomorrow if the stool remains dark.
options.reason: Food can reduce gastric discomfort but does not make continued ibuprofen appropriate when bleeding warning signs and lightheadedness are present.

options.text: Change from ibuprofen to over-the-counter naproxen and mention the stool color at the next scheduled visit.
options.reason: Naproxen is also an NSAID, and switching products does not address current signs of possible GI bleeding.

options.text: Hold ibuprofen until the lightheadedness resolves, then restart the labeled dose and arrange routine stool testing.
options.reason: Symptom improvement is not a safe restart criterion; the bleeding-warning pattern requires prompt evaluation before any further NSAID plan.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: dysmenorrhea, prostaglandin activity, NSAID medication, and heat comfort measures (P32–P44; the empty peptic-ulcer heading is not clinical support).

ATI RN Pharmacology for Nursing — Non-Opioid Analgesics: bounded ibuprofen/NSAID teaching for dysmenorrhea, gastric-mucosal injury, gastrointestinal bleeding, and black or dark stool warning findings (book pages 283–284; no dose or treatment protocol imported).

Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition — bounded older-textbook dysmenorrhea passages identifying NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and dark stool as a possible gastrointestinal-bleeding sign (supplemental context).

DailyMed — Official OTC ibuprofen 200 mg tablet labeling: ibuprofen is used for menstrual cramps but can cause severe stomach bleeding; stop use and seek medical advice for faintness or bloody or black stools (record updated June 9, 2026; product-specific).

questions.objective: Observe resting infant respirations for a full minute before disturbing the child during a routine assessment.
questions.stem: A sleeping 8-month-old with no signs of acute distress is due for a routine assessment. Which action should the nurse take first to obtain the resting respiratory rate?
questions.clue: The infant is already calm and can be observed without equipment or contact.
questions.rationale: For this stable routine assessment, count respirations before touching the child and observe for a full minute. Beginning with temperature, pulse, or equipment can change the resting pattern. This sequence is not an emergency rule: visible distress or deterioration would require immediate assessment and intervention rather than preserving the routine order.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes the directly taught low-distress vital-sign sequence for a stable sleeping infant.

options.text: Observe chest and abdominal movement for one full minute before touching the infant.
options.reason: The calm pre-touch period provides resting respiratory data, and the full-minute count screens for the irregularity expected in infants and toddlers.

options.text: Take the axillary temperature first, then count respirations after the infant settles.
options.reason: An axillary temperature can be appropriate, but touching or repositioning the infant can change the resting pattern. The available quiet observation should be used first.

options.text: Auscultate the apical pulse first, then count respirations for 30 seconds and double.
options.reason: The course sequence places respirations before the apical pulse and specifies a full-minute respiratory count for infants and toddlers.

options.text: Apply the pulse-oximetry probe first, then count respirations after the waveform stabilizes.
options.reason: Applying equipment can disturb the infant and alter the available resting pattern. The direct full-minute observation should occur before contact in this routine assessment.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: count infant respirations before touching and count respiratory and apical rates for a full minute (P571–P619, especially P609–P610; stable routine assessment only).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapter 2, printed p. 7: adapt the examination to developmental needs, involve family, observe readiness, explain steps, and organize the sequence when possible (does not supply the exact respiration-before-touch sequence).

questions.objective: Assess and reassess postoperative pain with a consistent behavioral tool when a toddler cannot report a reliable numeric rating.
questions.stem: Two hours after surgery, a 2-year-old gives inconsistent answers when shown a numeric pain scale. The child grimaces, guards the incision, and is difficult to console. Which nursing plan is best?
questions.clue: The numeric response is unreliable, but the postoperative behaviors can be assessed and compared over time.
questions.rationale: Inability to provide a reliable numeric rating does not remove the need to assess and treat pain. FLACC provides a structured behavioral baseline for this toddler. After medication-safety checks and the ordered intervention, repeating FLACC supports comparison while caregiver observations add context and the nurse monitors function, adverse effects, and the broader clinical picture. An unstructured caregiver estimate, an unchanged unreliable numeric scale, or heart rate alone cannot replace that comparable behavioral assessment. No exact score, dose, route, or fixed reassessment interval is supplied.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies postoperative behavioral cues and a demonstrated communication limitation to select both an appropriate tool and a comparable reassessment plan.

options.text: Score pain with FLACC, give ordered relief, and reassess with FLACC.
options.reason: FLACC uses observable behavior appropriate to this child's demonstrated communication limits. Using the same tool before and after the ordered intervention supports comparison of response.

options.text: Use the caregiver's estimate as baseline, give ordered relief, and reassess with FLACC.
options.reason: Caregiver observations can improve the assessment, but using an unstructured estimate instead of a pretreatment FLACC score leaves no comparable behavioral baseline for the later FLACC reassessment.

options.text: Score pain with FLACC, give ordered relief, and reassess with the numeric scale.
options.reason: The numeric scale has already produced inconsistent answers, and the case supplies no improved communication or changed context. A tool change can be appropriate when ability or context changes, but this switch would weaken the comparison here.

options.text: Use heart rate as the pain measure, give ordered relief, and reassess after it decreases.
options.reason: Heart rate can change with pain, anxiety, activity, or other factors and cannot measure pain in isolation. Behavioral assessment is available and should be used before and after the intervention.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: pediatric postoperative pain assessment and FLACC for ages 2 months through 7 years (P655–P682; no score, dose, route, or fixed reassessment interval).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapter 9, printed pp. 43–44: toddler pain behavior, behavioral and self-report measures, tool selection, caregiver input, reassessment, and FLACC components (age-only rules and scale graphics excluded).

Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne — Pain assessment and measurement: cognitive and contextual assessment, caregiver observations, behavioral tools when self-report is not attainable, before-and-after reassessment, and limits of physiologic indicators alone (updated August 2022; local workflows excluded).

Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Trauma Service — Pain Management: systematic developmentally appropriate assessment, consistent-tool comparison, reassessment, FLACC when a young child cannot self-report, and caregiver context (page date not established; trauma-specific treatment content excluded).

questions.objective: Explain responsive care and infant trust
questions.stem: During a 2-month well visit, a parent says, "I wait before responding when the baby signals hunger or discomfort because I do not want to spoil the baby." Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The parent identifies recognizable need cues; responsive care can be paired with practical caregiver support.
questions.rationale: Infants communicate needs through behavior, and dependable responses to hunger, comfort, stimulation, and care support trust and security. Responsive care means assessing and answering the cue; it does not mean feeding for every sound, imposing one response delay, or requiring the same caregiver for every interaction. A tired caregiver can use safe relief and support while the infant's needs continue to be met. This developmental framework supports care; it does not predict a deterministic personality outcome.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes the foundational connection between cue-responsive infant care and trust. The case contains direct, aligned cues and does not require competing priorities or a protocol decision, supporting level 1.

options.text: Respond consistently to hunger and comfort cues, and arrange caregiver relief when you need rest.
options.reason: Cue-responsive feeding and comfort support a dependable caregiver-infant relationship. Planning relief also supports the caregiver without asking the infant to tolerate unmet needs.

options.text: Offer a feeding whenever the infant fusses so every episode receives the same response.
options.reason: A consistent response begins by assessing the cue; fussing can signal needs other than hunger. Automatically feeding for every episode is not individualized responsive care.

options.text: Use a fixed waiting period before responding so the infant practices calming without help.
options.reason: The case identifies hunger or discomfort cues and does not establish a reason for a fixed response delay. The sources support dependable response, not a universal sleep- or feeding-training interval.

options.text: Have one caregiver provide every feeding and comfort response so the infant experiences consistent care.
options.reason: Consistency does not require one exhausted caregiver to provide every response. Multiple familiar caregivers can respond dependably while sharing care and protecting caregiver rest.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: infant attachment, caregiver safety, cue response, feeding experiences, and trust (P37–P47; T2R1–T2R3; no feeding, sleep-training, or response-delay protocol).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapter 3, printed p. 16: infant crying as communication, caregiver-infant relationships, comfort and feeding needs, attachment, and caregiver rest (the before-vocalization mistrust claim is excluded).

questions.objective: Evaluate declining growth with feeding fatigue
questions.stem: At an infant follow-up visit, the nurse confirms that three serial weights were obtained with the same calibrated scale and show a continuing downward growth pattern. The caregiver reports prolonged feeds and that the infant tires before finishing. The infant is alert and has no acute respiratory distress. Which plan is most appropriate?
questions.clue: The measurements are verified, and both the serial trajectory and feeding function are concerning now.
questions.rationale: A verified downward growth pattern plus prolonged, fatiguing feeds requires timely assessment rather than reassurance or a one-factor trial. Review accurate serial anthropometrics, feeding history and difficulties, medical and developmental history, physical findings, family and social context, and other concerns; then coordinate focused evaluation and support. Faltering weight is multifactorial, so the case does not establish feeding technique, disease, neglect, or another single cause. No single old percentile cutoff is used as the complete current definition.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies two aligned findings—verified serial decline and impaired feeding endurance—to a focused assessment and coordination decision. The cues do not conflict and no treatment response or differential ranking is required, supporting a retag from level 3 to level 2.

options.text: Assess feeding and health factors now, review the serial measurements, and coordinate further evaluation based on the findings.
options.reason: The verified downward pattern and feeding fatigue warrant a current, nonjudgmental feeding and health assessment followed by focused evaluation based on what is found.

options.text: Continue the current plan and wait for the next routine visit to repeat the weight and apply a percentile cutoff.
options.reason: Waiting for one percentile threshold discounts the already confirmed trajectory and functional feeding concern. Current evaluation should integrate serial measurements, feeding, history, and examination.

options.text: Increase the length of every feeding, recheck the weight in one week, and use worsening fatigue to trigger broader evaluation.
options.reason: The infant already tires during prolonged feeds. Extending feeds without assessing feeding function and health factors delays evaluation and assumes a solution without identifying the problem.

options.text: Begin feeding-technique coaching, recheck the weight after coaching, and add medical assessment if the decline continues.
options.reason: Feeding coaching can be appropriate after assessment, but using it as the sole first explanation prematurely assigns a cause and postpones evaluation of other contributing factors.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: causes and assessment of faltering growth, standard growth measurements, plotting, and attention to trends (P99–P107; P602–P606; an isolated percentile cutoff is not used as the definition).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapter 2, printed p. 8: weight, length or height, BMI, head circumference, and age-appropriate growth charts as assessment tools (not a faltering-weight definition or feeding-fatigue workup).

American Academy of Pediatrics and NASPGHAN — Clinical Practice Guideline for Diagnosis and Management of Faltering Weight: accurate serial measurement, multifactorial causes, broad feeding and health assessment, and focused evaluation (published March 16, 2026; numeric criteria and treatment algorithms excluded).

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Infants: Sleep and activity.
questions.stem: Which home sleep plans for a 3-month-old should the nurse reinforce? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Comfort products can introduce hazards into an infant's sleep space.
questions.rationale: Keep sleep recommendations simple and consistent, including for infants who spit up. Follow individualized medical instructions when a specific clinical exception exists.
questions.difficultyReason: Recall the standard safe-sleep environment without a medical exception.

options.text: Place the infant on the back for sleep.
options.reason: Supine placement is the recommended initial sleep position.

options.text: Use a firm, flat, noninclined approved sleep surface with a fitted sheet.
options.reason: This avoids soft surfaces and positional airway hazards.

options.text: Keep pillows, loose blankets, and stuffed toys out of the sleep space.
options.reason: These create suffocation hazards.

options.text: Use a wedge to hold the infant on the side after feeds.
options.reason: Inclined devices and side positioning are not routine safe-sleep solutions.

options.text: Sleep with the infant on a sofa if the caregiver is tired.
options.reason: Sofas are especially hazardous shared sleep surfaces.

refs.label: Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes — Infants: Sleep and activity.
Supplemental reading: ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11 — infant back-sleep positioning and clear sleep-space safety (targeted passages).
NIH/NICHD Safe to Sleep® — Safe Sleep Environment
American Academy of Pediatrics (HealthyChildren.org) — safe sleep for babies with reflux

questions.objective: Use readiness cues before escalating toilet training
questions.stem: At a health visit, the caregiver of an 18-month-old plans an intensive toilet-training weekend. The child walks to the bathroom but does not signal the need to void and is usually wet at hourly diaper checks. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The child has mobility but lacks the communication and dry-period cues that make an intensive plan timely.
questions.rationale: Toilet-training readiness is based on a pattern of developing physiologic, communication, motor, and behavioral abilities rather than one skill or chronological age alone. This child can approach the bathroom but does not signal a need and remains wet at short intervals, so postponing intensive training while using neutral, supportive routines is appropriate. The history does not diagnose delay, set a universal training age, or make one isolated dry period sufficient for intensive training.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner weighs present and absent readiness cues to advise against escalation while preserving supportive learning. This is a specific teaching application rather than simple recall, supporting level 2.

options.text: Postpone intensive training, use neutral toilet routines, and watch for communication and longer dry periods.
options.reason: Walking to the bathroom is only one skill. The absent communication and dry-period cues support waiting before intensive training while keeping toilet learning familiar and nonpunitive.

options.text: Begin the weekend plan because walking to the bathroom is enough evidence of readiness.
options.reason: Motor access alone does not demonstrate awareness, communication, or physiologic readiness. The case supplies two important cues that are not yet present.

options.text: Begin scheduled toilet sitting because bladder awareness usually develops only after training starts.
options.reason: The plan treats training as the prerequisite for awareness even though readiness assessment should guide when focused training begins. A schedule does not replace the missing cues.

options.text: Begin the intensive plan after one dry nap because a single dry period confirms readiness.
options.reason: One dry nap is encouraging but does not establish a stable readiness pattern, especially while communication and usual daytime dry periods remain absent.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: toddler independence, readiness communication, dry periods, toilet training, and normal developmental context (P116–P130; P152–P166; no universal training age).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapter 4, printed p. 21: autonomy, toilet sensation and readiness, patience, routines, and consistent boundaries (not a diagnostic rule or intensive training protocol).

American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org — Cognitive and Verbal Skills Needed for Toilet Training: multiple physical, cognitive, and communication skills plus supportive familiarity (updated July 31, 2026; adapted from a 2016 AAP guide; family education, not a research trial).

questions.objective: Recognize expected parallel play
questions.stem: Which observation of children in a toddler play group best illustrates parallel play?
questions.clue: Parallel play combines proximity and similar activity without a shared organized goal.
questions.rationale: Toddlers commonly play beside peers with separate materials and no coordinated objective. Watching or imitating a nearby child can occur without converting the activity into cooperative play. The other observations illustrate a shared organized activity, onlooker behavior, and solitary play. One play-group observation identifies the play pattern; it does not prove or rule out a developmental disorder.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner directly recognizes parallel play from four concrete observations. No care-plan tradeoff or competing clinical cue is present, supporting level 1.

options.text: Two toddlers push separate toy trucks beside each other and occasionally watch the other's play.
options.reason: Playing near another child with similar materials but without a shared goal is parallel play; brief observation of the peer can occur.

options.text: Two toddlers take turns adding blocks to one shared tower after choosing roles.
options.reason: Turn-taking toward one shared product and role organization describe a more interactive cooperative pattern, not separate side-by-side activity.

options.text: One toddler watches another child stack blocks without selecting a toy to use.
options.reason: Watching another child without joining a nearby activity is onlooker behavior rather than parallel play.

options.text: One toddler completes a shape sorter alone without attending to nearby children.
options.reason: Independent play without attention to nearby peers is solitary play, not parallel play.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: toddler independence and parallel play beside peers without a shared goal (P147–P159; T1R8; T4R5; one observation is not diagnostic).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapter 4, printed p. 21: toddler parallel play, autonomy, and routine developmental context (not a universal age cutoff or social diagnosis).

questions.objective: Coach calm safe consistent limits
questions.stem: A caregiver stops a toddler from throwing blocks. The toddler drops to the floor, cries, and kicks toward the caregiver. The nurse observes no injury, breathing difficulty, or new symptom. Which coaching is most appropriate?
questions.clue: The immediate task is to protect safety while keeping the limit calm, brief, and predictable.
questions.rationale: Toddler frustration can intensify when independence is limited. The caregiver should control the unsafe object, state the boundary simply and consistently, remain calmly available, and reconnect with acceptable choices as the child regains control. Immediate limits help connect the behavior with the boundary, and consistency means calm predictable wording—not delayed teaching, lengthy reasoning, or escalating volume. The stated observations make a limit-setting response reasonable now, but they do not prove that every medical or emotional concern has been excluded; new, persistent, or atypical findings require reassessment.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner selects a routine, nonpunitive limit-setting sequence from a direct toddler-behavior vignette. The stem supplies no competing clinical finding or treatment response, supporting level 1.

options.text: Move the blocks away, calmly restate the limit, stay nearby, and reconnect with a safe choice as the child settles.
options.reason: The plan protects immediate safety, keeps the boundary predictable, avoids adding lengthy demands during peak distress, and supports reconnection and an acceptable choice afterward.

options.text: Remove the blocks, then postpone stating the limit until the toddler is fully calm later in the day.
options.reason: Removing the blocks protects safety, but postponing the brief limit weakens the immediate connection between the unsafe behavior and the boundary.

options.text: Remove the blocks, then explain the injury risk in detail until the toddler can repeat the rule.
options.reason: The object is controlled, but a lengthy explanation and required teach-back exceed what is useful during a toddler's peak distress. A short concrete limit is more developmentally appropriate.

options.text: Remove the blocks, restate the limit more loudly with each protest, and keep the wording consistent.
options.reason: Consistent wording is useful, but increasing volume with each protest can intensify the interaction. Firm boundaries can remain calm and brief.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: toddler exploration, tantrums, negativism, volatile behavior, independence, and autonomy versus shame and doubt (P116–P166; T2R3; no restraint or punishment protocol).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapter 4, printed p. 21: autonomy, negativism, routines, consistent expectations for tantrums, and consistent boundaries (not proof that illness is absent).
CDC — Good Directions: clear age-appropriate directions, brief instructions, and a calm tone (page dated April 30, 2026; supplemental parenting guidance, not a universal tantrum-treatment sequence).

questions.objective: Plan routine toddler meals and safe snacks
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing routine feeding with the caregiver of a healthy toddler whose growth follows the expected pattern. The caregiver says the child eats small amounts at meals and asks for snacks. Which plans are appropriate? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Expected growth and variable intake support structured small portions, while choking prevention still applies at every eating time.
questions.rationale: Healthy toddlers often eat variable small amounts. Regular meals, child-sized portions, and planned nutritious snacks provide structure without continuous grazing or coercion. Foods should be prepared in developmentally safe sizes and textures and eaten while seated with adult supervision. Assessment should consider the overall diet and serial growth pattern rather than one meal. The item does not set calorie, milk, juice, or food-introduction targets.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes routine toddler feeding and choking-prevention principles from a stable healthy-child scenario. SATA format and multiple content points do not add competing cues, so the item is retagged from level 2 to level 1.

options.text: Offer child-sized portions at regular meals and planned nutritious snack times.
options.reason: Small portions and planned meals and snacks fit normal toddler appetite variation while preserving structure instead of continuous access to food.

options.text: Seat the child for eating and supervise foods prepared in safe sizes and textures.
options.reason: Seated, supervised eating with appropriately prepared foods reduces choking risk during routine meals and snacks.

options.text: Review the overall diet and serial growth pattern rather than judging intake from one meal.
options.reason: Toddler intake varies from meal to meal. Broader intake and growth context is more informative than pressuring the child to meet one-meal expectations.

options.text: Keep preferred snack foods within reach so the child can graze between planned eating times.
options.reason: Continuous grazing blurs hunger and meal routines. The guidance supports planned nutritious snacks, not unrestricted food access throughout the day.

options.text: Start with adult-sized portions so the child has enough choices at every meal.
options.reason: Offering choices can support autonomy, but an adult-sized portion does not match toddler appetite or developmental portion guidance. Choice does not require excess serving size.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: toddler appetite variation, small meals, snack requests, mealtime supervision, and avoidance of round or otherwise hazardous foods (P162–P167; P561–P564; planned snacks are distinguished from continuous grazing).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapters 2 and 4, printed pp. 8 and 22: longitudinal growth assessment, variable appetite, developmental portions, regular meals, nutritious snacks, seated supervised eating, and bite-size choking prevention (older numeric intake targets excluded).

questions.objective: Withhold a planned vaccine pending severe-reaction review
questions.stem: At a routine visit, a vaccine is scheduled for a child who is well today. The caregiver reports that within minutes of the previous dose of the same vaccine, the child developed wheezing and facial swelling and received emergency treatment; the record does not identify the cause. Which action should the nurse take?
questions.clue: The child is stable now, but the planned re-exposure follows an immediate prior event with respiratory and facial symptoms.
questions.rationale: Before administering the planned vaccine, the nurse should hold it, obtain and document details of the prior event and products involved, and obtain clinician review. CDC guidance calls for characterizing an immediate reaction and generally treats a history of severe allergic reaction as a contraindication to another dose of the same vaccine pending appropriate evaluation. This case reports a possible reaction rather than confirming its cause. It does not create a current anaphylaxis emergency, let absent hives rule out a severe reaction, or let record confirmation alone clear another dose.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a significant prior reaction history to today's otherwise routine administration decision and distinguishes temporary withholding for evaluation from treatment of a current reaction. The cues align and no competing indication or component analysis is supplied, supporting level 2.

options.text: Hold the planned vaccine, clarify and document the prior event, and obtain clinician review before re-exposure.
options.reason: The immediate respiratory and facial symptoms after the prior dose could represent a severe allergic reaction. The history requires evaluation before another dose of the same vaccine is given.

options.text: Give the planned vaccine with extended observation because the child has no symptoms today.
options.reason: Being asymptomatic today does not resolve the possible severe reaction to the previous dose. Observation after re-exposure is not a substitute for evaluating the history first.

options.text: Classify the prior event as nonallergic because no hives were reported, then give the planned vaccine.
options.reason: Immediate wheezing and facial swelling can indicate a severe allergic reaction even when hives are not reported. Their absence does not clear the planned dose.

options.text: Hold today's vaccine, obtain the emergency record, and give the next dose once the symptoms are confirmed.
options.reason: Confirming the reported respiratory and facial symptoms strengthens the need for clinical review; documentation alone does not clear another dose for administration.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: pre-immunization contraindication and precaution review, Vaccine Information Statements, and adolescent participation (P108–P115; P450–P494; no diagnosis, component table, or rescue protocol).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapter 35, printed p. 231: severe allergic reaction after a vaccine, concern about further doses and shared components, and clinician review of precautions (current CDC guidance controls this item).

CDC — Preventing and Managing Adverse Reactions: characterize prior immediate reactions; respiratory compromise may occur without urticaria; and evaluate a suspected severe reaction before another dose of the same vaccine (page dated July 25, 2024; acute treatment and product algorithms excluded).

questions.objective: Give concrete truthful reassurance about bodily integrity
questions.stem: Before a blood draw, a 4-year-old says, "If the needle makes a hole, all my blood will come out." Which response by the nurse best addresses this concern?
questions.clue: The child names a concrete fear that the puncture will let all blood escape.
questions.rationale: The best response answers the child's actual concern with simple truthful language: only a small amount is collected, the puncture site is covered, and play can show what will happen. Distraction, comfort positioning, purpose teaching, or watching may be useful for some children, but none alone corrects the expressed bodily-integrity fear. The nurse should not promise that the procedure will be painless.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner matches one explicit preschool fear to concrete, honest preparation. The direct cue and routine developmental principle support level 1 despite the clinical vignette.

options.text: A small amount goes into the tube, and this bandage covers the spot; let's practice on the doll.
options.reason: The response directly and honestly addresses the fear of bodily contents escaping, uses concrete language, and offers medical play before the procedure.

options.text: You can choose a video to watch while we use a comfort hold for the blood draw.
options.reason: Distraction and a supportive position can help during a procedure, but this response does not correct the child's stated fear that all blood will escape.

options.text: Let me explain what the laboratory will learn from the blood before we begin.
options.reason: Explaining the test's purpose can be useful, but it does not address the concrete concern about the opening and loss of blood.

options.text: You may watch the collection tube so you can see exactly where the blood goes.
options.reason: A child may choose to watch, but viewing the tube neither explains that only a small amount is taken nor reassures the child about bodily integrity.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: preschool bodily-integrity fears, poorly defined body boundaries, medical play, and honest near-term teaching (P187–P213; T3R3; this child's stated fear is not generalized to every preschooler).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapters 5 and 10, printed pp. 25–26 and 49–50: preoperational thinking, bodily-harm fears, bandages, familiar toys, pretend play, clear explanations, choices, and factual preparation.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: School-Age Child: Psychosocial development; Piaget teaching table.
questions.stem: A school-age child will help with a simple home dressing change. Which teaching strategy best evaluates readiness?
questions.clue: A hands-on care task requires observed performance, not only verbal recall.
questions.rationale: Support age-appropriate participation while maintaining the supervision needed for safety.
questions.difficultyReason: Identify return demonstration as the direct way to assess a taught practical skill.

options.text: Demonstrate the steps, then ask the child to show them back with caregiver supervision.
options.reason: Concrete demonstration and return demonstration assess practical understanding.

options.text: Review the illustrated handout, then ask the child to explain the dressing steps.
options.reason: Explaining the sequence checks verbal recall, but it does not show how the child performs the hands-on steps.

options.text: Observe the child arrange the supplies while the caregiver completes the dressing change.
options.reason: Supply setup shows one part of participation, but it does not evaluate the child's performance of the dressing change.

options.text: Ask the child and caregiver to identify changes that should be reported to the clinic.
options.reason: Recognizing when to seek help is important safety teaching, but it does not assess performance of the dressing-change skill.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development instructor notes: school-age concrete thought, demonstration, and supported bandage-placement skill learning (P309–314; teaching table row 4).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapter 6, Health Promotion of School-Age Children: concrete operations, skill acquisition, appropriate tasks, and caregiver influence (developmental background; not a dressing protocol or proof of unsupervised readiness).

questions.objective: Assess social barriers to using a known treatment
questions.stem: At a clinic follow-up, a 14-year-old with a chronic condition correctly demonstrates the prescribed home treatment and explains its purpose. The adolescent reports missing it during activities with friends because the equipment is difficult to use privately. No acute symptoms are present. Which nursing approach is best?
questions.clue: The adolescent knows and can perform the treatment; reliability breaks down in a specific peer-activity context.
questions.rationale: Correct technique does not guarantee that a treatment can be used reliably in daily life. The nurse should explore the adolescent's stated privacy and equipment barriers, include the adolescent in decisions, involve the caregiver as appropriate, and coordinate with the prescriber if timing or regimen changes are considered. Generic reteaching, caregiver-managed equipment transport, or an alarm for a nonmemory barrier can miss the stated privacy problem. Missed-dose instructions and prescribed timing remain individualized; the case does not establish intentional defiance.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner distinguishes demonstrated knowledge from a context-specific implementation failure and selects a collaborative assessment plan. Applying that distinction to care supports level 2 without requiring a drug-specific modification.

options.text: Explore privacy, equipment, and timing barriers, then collaborate with the adolescent, caregiver, and prescriber on a feasible routine.
options.reason: The adolescent has demonstrated knowledge and technique but identifies a real-world barrier. Collaborative assessment can preserve autonomy and safety while any regimen change remains with the prescriber.

options.text: Repeat technique teaching privately and keep the routine unchanged until the adolescent demonstrates it again.
options.reason: The adolescent already demonstrates the skill and explains its purpose. Repeating technique alone does not address privacy, equipment access, or social timing.

options.text: Ask the caregiver to prepare and transport the equipment for each activity while keeping the treatment setting unchanged.
options.reason: Equipment preparation and transport can be helpful, but this plan leaves the stated difficulty using it privately unchanged and does not explore which support is workable.

options.text: Set a phone alarm for activity days and ask whether reminders improve treatment use.
options.reason: An alarm targets forgetting, while the adolescent reports privacy and equipment barriers. Testing a reminder without exploring the stated obstacle does not address the known implementation problem.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: adolescent peer and social barriers, the adolescent perspective, participation in decisions, and health concerns (P440–P474; T3R5; no automatic age-based transfer of all responsibility).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapters 7 and 10, printed pp. 33–34 and 49–50: adolescent reasoning and identity, peer influence, changing parent relationships, independence, family stressors and support, factual information, choices, and inclusion in care planning (no disease-specific adherence protocol).

questions.objective: Offer private adolescent assessment with explained limits
questions.stem: During a routine adolescent health visit, a caregiver answers every question while the 15-year-old remains quiet. No urgent safety concern has been disclosed. The nurse is preparing to complete a sensitive risk assessment. Which plan is best?
questions.clue: A sensitive assessment needs the adolescent's own voice and an honest explanation of privacy before disclosure.
questions.rationale: The nurse should normalize part of the visit alone with the adolescent and explain confidentiality and its applicable limits to the adolescent and caregiver before sensitive assessment. Privacy can support disclosure, but confidentiality is not absolute and its precise boundaries vary by jurisdiction, setting, service, and policy. The stem contains no disclosure or urgent danger, so the nurse should not invent a reportable event or a universal exception.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes routine private adolescent interviewing paired with upfront, qualified confidentiality limits. The principle is direct and no actual disclosure or legal conflict must be resolved, supporting level 1.

options.text: Explain that private time is routine and review applicable confidentiality limits with both, then speak with the adolescent alone.
options.reason: Routine private time supports the adolescent's own account, and explaining limits before sensitive questions avoids promising protection that law or policy might not allow.

options.text: Keep the caregiver present for support and direct each sensitive question to the adolescent in front of them.
options.reason: Directing questions to the adolescent is useful, but caregiver presence can inhibit disclosure during a sensitive assessment. Routine private time should still be offered.

options.text: Have the caregiver complete the risk history, then privately confirm only answers the caregiver marked as concerning.
options.reason: This plan limits the adolescent's private account to concerns recognized by the caregiver and can miss sensitive risks or priorities the caregiver does not know.

options.text: Begin private questioning first and explain confidentiality only if an answer later needs to be shared.
options.reason: Private questioning is appropriate, but the adolescent should understand the scope and applicable limits before deciding what to disclose, not only after a concern arises.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: adolescent perspectives, peer and social context, inclusion in decisions, and health concerns (P440–P474; T3R5; the notes do not define confidentiality law).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapter 2, printed p. 7: developmentally adapted assessment, child and family involvement, privacy, adolescent preference about caregiver presence, rapport, and explanation of examination steps (not a legal source).

American Academy of Pediatrics — Providing Reproductive and Sexual Health Care: private time, confidentiality limits, and supportive trusted-adult communication (page date not established; general adolescent-care principle only, not a consent or reporting determination).

American Academy of Pediatrics — Telehealth and Adolescent Health Care: explain confidentiality limits early to the adolescent and caregiver and include a routine private component (last updated October 5, 2021; general office-care principle only, not a telehealth, portal, billing, or legal workflow).

questions.objective: Use rear-facing product limits rather than foot contact
questions.stem: At a car-seat check, a caregiver points out that a 26-month-old's feet press against the vehicle seat and the child's knees bend. Inspection confirms that the child remains below the restraint's rear-facing height and weight limits, the required head clearance is present, and installation follows the restraint and vehicle instructions. Which recommendation should the nurse make?
questions.clue: The child still meets the actual rear-facing size, clearance, and installation criteria; only leg position concerns the caregiver.
questions.rationale: Rear-facing use is determined by the child's fit within the restraint's stated rear-facing height and weight limits and by correct use under both the restraint and vehicle instructions. Feet touching the vehicle seat or knees bending does not by itself show that the restraint is outgrown. Likewise, visual proximity to the shell does not supersede a clearance requirement that is still met, and a birthday cannot authorize use beyond a product limit. The case does not supply model-specific installation measurements, so no additional product rule should be inferred.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies several supplied fit checks and rejects a familiar but irrelevant visual cue, supporting an intermediate care decision rather than simple recall.

options.text: Continue rear-facing while the child remains within the rear-facing limits and the installation follows both sets of instructions.
options.reason: The stated size, clearance, and installation checks show that the child still fits the rear-facing restraint. Foot contact and bent knees alone do not establish that the rear-facing limits have been reached.

options.text: Change to forward-facing because foot contact and tightly bent knees indicate that the child has outgrown rear-facing use.
options.reason: Foot contact and bent knees do not define rear-facing outgrowth; the restraint's stated limits and fit instructions remain controlling.

options.text: Change to forward-facing because the child's head looks too close to the top of the restraint shell.
options.reason: Visual proximity alone does not establish outgrowth; the supplied clearance check and manufacturer instructions determine whether rear-facing fit remains acceptable.

options.text: Keep rear-facing until the child's third birthday even if a rear-facing limit is reached before then.
options.reason: A fixed birthday cannot override a manufacturer's height, weight, clearance, or installation limit. A child who outgrows rear-facing use needs the next appropriate restraint stage.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: anticipatory guidance and following car-seat instructions (P521–P534; older age-only transitions do not govern this item).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, printed pp. 18 and 23: child-passenger restraint and injury-prevention context (the automatic age-two forward-facing transition is excluded).

National Highway Traffic Safety Administration — Car Seats and Booster Seats: select restraints by age and size, follow both restraint and vehicle instructions, and continue rear-facing until the restraint's rear-facing height or weight limit is reached (current undated page; no foot-contact or model-specific clearance rule).

American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org — Car Seats: Information for Families: follow manufacturer limits and manuals, and do not treat feet touching the vehicle seat as a rear-facing outgrowth criterion (page date not established; no universal birthday, comfort, or injury guarantee).

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Drowning Prevention.
questions.stem: Which caregiver plans reduce drowning risk for a toddler? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Prevention must address access and supervision in ordinary home environments.
questions.rationale: Layer practical protections instead of relying on one skill or one piece of equipment.
questions.difficultyReason: Recognize layered routine drowning-prevention measures.

options.text: Use close, attentive supervision by a responsible adult around water, including bathtubs.
options.reason: Toddlers can drown quickly in small amounts of water.

options.text: Maintain a barrier separating the pool from the house and play area.
options.reason: A physical barrier reduces unintended access.

options.text: Empty buckets and other water containers after use.
options.reason: Standing water creates a hazard beyond pools.

options.text: Rely on swimming lessons instead of supervision.
options.reason: Swimming ability does not remove the need for close supervision.

options.text: Allow an older child to be the sole bathtub supervisor.
options.reason: A responsible adult should provide supervision.

refs.label: Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes — Drowning Prevention.
Supplemental reading: ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11 — toddler water supervision, pool barriers, and household water hazards (targeted passages).
CDC — Preventing Drowning

questions.objective: Secure medicines despite child-resistant packaging
questions.stem: During a home-safety visit, a grandparent says medications stay in their original child-resistant bottles inside a zipped purse on an entry table. The toddler can climb onto the chair beside the table. Which change has priority?
questions.clue: The toddler can reach the purse, and neither its zipper nor the bottle caps are complete access controls.
questions.rationale: Child-resistant packaging is an important layer, but it is not childproof. Medications should remain in their original containers and be returned after use to a locked cabinet or lockbox that is out of the child's sight and reach. Hiding a purse, placing medicines high, relying on a closed interior door, or expecting continuous observation leaves realistic access opportunities.
questions.difficultyReason: The decisive routine-safety principle is directly cued: resistant packaging does not replace locked, inaccessible storage. This remains foundational.

options.text: Move the original containers to a locked cabinet or lockbox out of the child's sight and reach after every use.
options.reason: Locked storage adds an access barrier that a zipper, height, supervision, or child-resistant cap alone does not provide while retaining the original labeled containers.

options.text: Keep the zipped purse on the entry table but place it behind a lamp so the child cannot see it.
options.reason: Reduced visibility does not secure an accessible purse, and the child can already climb to the table.

options.text: Move the original bottles to a high kitchen shelf and rely on the child-resistant caps while adults are in the room.
options.reason: Height, resistant packaging, and general adult presence do not replace locked storage; children can climb and packaging is not childproof.

options.text: Place the closed purse in the bedroom during visits and ask the grandparent to check the door frequently.
options.reason: Moving the purse may reduce immediate visibility, but an unlocked room and intermittent checking do not reliably prevent access.

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, printed pp. 18 and 23: poison-prevention and environmental-safety context (prevention only; no poisoning-treatment protocol).

U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission — Childproofing Your Home: use safety locks to prevent access to medicines, and keep child-resistant packages locked and out of reach because resistant packaging is not childproof (current undated page).

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: General Approaches Toward Examining a Child; medication calculation supplemental practice.
questions.stem: A 22-kg child is prescribed 30 mg/kg/day of a medication in three equal doses. The bottle contains 100 mg/5 mL. What volume should the nurse prepare for each dose after verifying the order?
questions.clue: The prescription states mg/kg/day, not mg/kg per dose.
questions.rationale: Separate the daily calculation from each administration and verify the concentration before converting to volume.
questions.difficultyReason: Convert a weight-based daily amount to a divided dose and then to volume using the available concentration.

options.text: 11 mL.
33 mL.
options.reason: This gives the entire calculated daily volume as one dose.
This divides the already divided dose again.

options.text: 22 mL.
options.reason: This is twice the ordered dose volume.
