questions.objective: Coordinate treatment, partners and reinfection retesting
questions.stem: A nonpregnant adult with uncomplicated chlamydia is starting the prescribed 7-day doxycycline regimen today. Which statements by the patient show an accurate follow-up plan? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: This is a nonpregnant patient on a multidose regimen, so treatment completion, partner care, early test-of-cure rules and later reinfection testing are separate decisions.
questions.rationale: Complete the prescribed course, coordinate evaluation and treatment of recent partners, and avoid intercourse until the regimen is complete, symptoms have resolved if present and partners have been treated. For a nonpregnant person treated with a recommended regimen, an early routine test of cure is not advised unless adherence, persistent symptoms or reinfection is a concern. Retesting at about 3 months addresses the high frequency of repeat infection. Pregnancy would require a separate test-of-cure plan.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies regimen and pregnancy status to distinguish four related but independent follow-up decisions. This is coordinated care application, not advanced synthesis merely because the item is SATA.

options.text: "I will take every prescribed dose even if the discharge resolves before day 7."
options.reason: Symptom improvement does not replace completion of the prescribed multidose regimen.

options.text: "My recent sex partner should be evaluated and treated even if no symptoms are present."
options.reason: Chlamydia is often asymptomatic, and partner treatment helps prevent transmission and reinfection.

options.text: "I will avoid intercourse until I finish the regimen, any symptoms have resolved and my partner has been treated."
options.reason: These treatment, symptom and partner conditions reduce immediate transmission and reinfection risk.

options.text: "I should schedule a NAAT 2 weeks after the last dose as the routine way to prove cure."
options.reason: Routine test of cure is not advised for a nonpregnant patient without adherence concerns, persistent symptoms or suspected reinfection, and testing before 4 weeks can detect nonviable organisms.

options.text: "If my partner completes treatment, I can use that documentation instead of returning for the 3-month retest."
options.reason: Documented partner treatment does not remove the recommendation for retesting or make future reinfection impossible.

options.text: "I will plan repeat chlamydia testing in about 3 months even if I finish treatment and feel well."
options.reason: Retesting at about 3 months is intended to detect repeat infection and is distinct from an early test of cure.

questions.objective: Reassess a changed discharge pattern before reusing medication
questions.stem: A patient calls the clinic about a thin gray discharge with a new fishy odor and no vulvar itching. Six months ago, a clinician treated a thick pruritic discharge with a topical azole. The patient asks the nurse to authorize another azole refill without a visit. Which response is best?
questions.clue: The current odor, consistency and absence of itching differ from the previously diagnosed episode.
questions.rationale: Do not equate all vaginal symptoms or diagnose BV from odor alone. A careful history, examination and appropriate laboratory testing help distinguish BV, candidiasis, trichomoniasis, cervicitis and other causes so treatment can match the etiology. The nurse should facilitate evaluation rather than authorize a leftover or assumed regimen.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner compares the current and prior symptom patterns and chooses reassessment over two plausible empiric-treatment paths. This is a focused applied decision at level 2.

options.text: Arrange evaluation of the new symptoms, including relevant history, examination and testing, before recommending cause-specific treatment.
options.reason: The current pattern differs from the prior episode, and history alone cannot reliably identify the cause of vaginitis or select the correct medication.

options.text: Request the previous azole refill because the prior response to treatment makes recurrent candidiasis the most likely cause.
options.reason: A past response does not establish the cause of a changed discharge pattern, and empiric reuse can delay appropriate evaluation.

options.text: Ask the provider to start empiric metronidazole from the telephone assessment and arrange examination only if the odor persists.
options.reason: The changed pattern can raise suspicion for BV, but telephone history alone does not reliably establish vaginitis etiology or justify making examination contingent on treatment failure.

options.text: Have the patient use an over-the-counter vaginal pH test and restart the azole if the result is within the usual vaginal range.
options.reason: Vaginal pH can contribute to an evaluation, but a home pH result alone cannot identify the cause or establish that the prior azole is appropriate.

questions.objective: Clarify a pregnancy-inappropriate candidiasis prescription
questions.stem: At 10 weeks of pregnancy, a patient has examination and laboratory findings confirming uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis. The medication record contains a new prescription for a single oral fluconazole dose. Which action should the nurse take?
questions.clue: The infection is confirmed, but pregnancy changes both the acceptable route and the recommended duration.
questions.rationale: Recognizing the organism does not make every usual antifungal regimen appropriate. The nurse should hold and clarify the single oral fluconazole order; current guidance recommends a topical azole applied for 7 days during pregnancy. Clarification respects prescriber authority while preventing administration of a pregnancy-inappropriate plan.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies one decisive patient constraint—pregnancy—to a familiar medication order and must preserve both route and duration. That is level-2 medication-safety application.

options.text: Hold the oral dose and contact the prescriber to discuss a topical azole applied for 7 days.
options.reason: Current CDC guidance recommends only 7-day topical azole therapy during pregnancy and advises against the single oral fluconazole dose.

options.text: Administer the oral dose now because laboratory confirmation makes the oral and topical routes equivalent in pregnancy.
options.reason: Confirmation establishes the diagnosis but does not remove the pregnancy-specific route and duration recommendation.

options.text: Hold the prescription until the second trimester, then ask whether the same single oral dose can be administered.
options.reason: The current recommendation is topical azole therapy for 7 days during pregnancy, not delayed single-dose oral fluconazole.

options.text: Ask the prescriber to replace the oral dose with a 3-day topical azole regimen because shorter local therapy limits fetal exposure.
options.reason: Changing to the topical route is not enough; pregnancy guidance specifies a 7-day course rather than a shortened 3-day regimen.

questions.objective: Report incomplete specimen collection without altering the sample
questions.stem: A patient collecting a semen specimen reports that the first portion was spilled and asks whether to add tap water to restore the expected volume. What is the best nursing response?
questions.clue: Part of the specimen was lost; adding another substance would create further collection error.
questions.rationale: Accurate diagnostic results depend on collection quality. Follow the laboratory's instructions for abstinence, collection, transport, and any repeat sample.
questions.difficultyReason: Recognize a compromised specimen, report the collection problem, and follow laboratory-directed disposition.

options.text: Add enough tap water to reach the mark on the container.
options.reason: Adding water changes the specimen and its measured volume and concentration; it cannot replace the lost first portion. Report the collection problem instead.

options.text: Do not add anything; report the lost portion to the laboratory and follow its recollection instructions.
options.reason: Incomplete collection can alter results, especially if the sperm-rich initial fraction was lost.

options.text: Do not add anything; send the specimen with the collection time documented on the label.
options.reason: Recording the collection time does not replace reporting that the first portion was lost; the laboratory should direct disposition.

options.text: Use an ordinary lubricated condom to collect more semen into the same container.
options.reason: Unapproved lubricants or condoms can interfere with sperm testing and do not correct the original collection error.

questions.objective: Distinguish postovulatory BBT evidence from predicting fertility
questions.stem: A patient trying to conceive brings a basal body temperature chart. Temperatures taken immediately on waking have been about 0.6 F higher for the past 3 mornings than earlier in the cycle. Which interpretation should the nurse provide?
questions.clue: The measurements were obtained under basal conditions and show a sustained rise compared with earlier-cycle readings.
questions.rationale: A sustained BBT rise usually reflects progesterone production after ovulation and is therefore retrospective. The method is imperfect and not routinely recommended as a stand-alone fertility test; illness, fatigue and other factors can affect readings. A urine LH kit is an example of a method used to predict ovulation before it occurs.
questions.difficultyReason: The item asks for recognition of the timing meaning of one classic chart pattern. No competing patient instability, treatment response or multistep decision is present, supporting level 1.

options.text: The rise is most useful as evidence that ovulation probably has already occurred.
options.reason: Progesterone released after ovulation produces the temperature rise, so BBT mainly provides retrospective evidence.

options.text: The rise predicts that ovulation is likely to begin after the temperature remains elevated for 2 more days.
options.reason: The sustained rise follows ovulation; waiting for additional elevated readings does not convert BBT into a prospective predictor.

options.text: The rise is the best time to begin intercourse because it identifies the luteinizing-hormone surge before ovulation.
options.reason: Urine ovulation-prediction kits detect the preovulatory LH surge; BBT rise occurs after ovulation and can miss earlier fertile days.

options.text: The rise primarily forecasts the next menstrual period and does not provide information about prior ovulation.
options.reason: The postovulatory temperature pattern can provide imperfect evidence that ovulation occurred, even though it is not a precise prospective tool.

American Society for Reproductive Medicine, ReproductiveFacts — Infertility: an Overview: take basal temperature on waking; a progesterone-related rise indicates ovulation has already occurred, so BBT is retrospective and imperfect rather than predictive.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Menopause; Disorders of the reproductive tract: symptoms that must always have follow-up.
questions.stem: A 58-year-old patient who has had no menstrual periods for four years reports new vaginal spotting. A cervical screening result last year was normal. Which response is most appropriate?
questions.clue: New bleeding occurs years after menses stopped; a prior cervical screen does not evaluate this symptom.
questions.rationale: Distinguish screening in an asymptomatic person from diagnostic evaluation of a new symptom. The new bleeding changes the priority.
questions.difficultyReason: Recognize that a new symptom requires diagnostics despite prior normal screening.

options.text: Arrange prompt diagnostic evaluation of the bleeding even though the previous screening was normal.
options.reason: Postmenopausal bleeding warrants evaluation; cervical screening does not rule out every cause, including endometrial disease.

options.text: Reassure the patient that normal cervical screening excludes gynecologic cancer.
options.reason: Screening has a specific purpose and cannot exclude all sources of bleeding.

options.text: Suggest watching for another episode before arranging diagnostic evaluation of the spotting.
options.reason: New postmenopausal spotting warrants evaluation without waiting for another episode.

options.text: Repeat cervical screening before deciding whether the new bleeding needs diagnostic evaluation.
options.reason: Cervical screening does not replace diagnostic evaluation of a new postmenopausal symptom.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Screening for Uterine Cancer

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: General Women's Health Promotion & Maintenance: Pelvic exam; Informed consent.
questions.stem: During a pelvic examination, a patient becomes tearful, closes the legs, and says, "Stop." The patient signed consent earlier. What should the nurse do first?
questions.clue: The patient explicitly asks to stop during the examination.
questions.rationale: Patient control and safety are essential to trauma-informed care. After stopping, offer choices, explain next steps, and obtain permission before proceeding.
questions.difficultyReason: Recognize the patient's request to stop as withdrawal of ongoing permission.

options.text: Ask the clinician to finish while the nurse uses distraction.
options.reason: Distraction is not a substitute for respecting withdrawal of consent.

options.text: Help stop the examination, provide privacy, and ask what the patient needs before discussing whether to continue.
options.reason: Consent is ongoing; the patient's request to stop must be respected.

options.text: Ask the patient to describe the discomfort before interrupting the examination.
options.reason: The examination should stop before exploring discomfort or discussing possible continuation.

options.text: Remind the patient that the signed form requires completion of the examination.
options.reason: A signed form does not remove the right to withdraw consent.

questions.objective: Reassess secondary causes after menstrual pain changes
questions.stem: A patient whose primary dysmenorrhea was previously controlled with the prescribed NSAID reports that pain now begins several days before menstruation, persists after bleeding stops and occurs with deep intercourse. The usual dose no longer provides relief. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
questions.clue: The pain's timing, associated dyspareunia and response to the established plan have all changed.
questions.rationale: A pattern that extends beyond the prior menstrual window, includes deep dyspareunia and no longer responds to the established plan should be reassessed for a secondary cause. Endometriosis is one possibility, but similar symptoms occur with other conditions. The nurse should facilitate a broad clinical evaluation rather than make response to another symptom plan, one infection test or a normal imaging result the gate for further reassessment.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner compares the current pattern and treatment response with the former primary-dysmenorrhea pattern to decide on reassessment. This is level-2 application without enough evidence to diagnose a specific disorder.

options.text: Arrange gynecologic evaluation for a secondary cause, with endometriosis among the possible explanations.
options.reason: A changed timing pattern, deep dyspareunia and loss of response warrant reassessment for pelvic pathology rather than assuming uncomplicated primary dysmenorrhea.

options.text: Ask the provider to revise the pain-control plan and start a symptom diary, then use the response to decide whether the diagnosis needs reassessment.
options.reason: A diary and symptom control may be useful parts of care, but treatment response should not become a prerequisite for reassessing a diagnosis when the pattern has already changed.

options.text: Arrange STI testing first and pursue other pelvic causes only if the infection testing is negative.
options.reason: Infection may be considered during evaluation, but dyspareunia is not specific; a stepwise STI-first rule can delay assessment of other possible pelvic causes.

options.text: Request pelvic ultrasonography and, if the result is normal, conclude that endometriosis has been excluded.
options.reason: Ultrasonography may show ovarian cysts or other endometriosis evidence, but a normal scan does not rule out the condition; evaluation should not stop solely because imaging is normal.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: primary versus secondary dysmenorrhea, evaluation, and endometriosis-related dysmenorrhea or deep dyspareunia (P32–P44; P62–P65).
Course lecture topic context — Week 6 GYN, STIs, and Infertility, slide 3: dysmenorrhea and endometriosis heading only (text layer; not a diagnostic algorithm).

NHS — Endometriosis: symptoms and reassessment when treatment does not help or symptoms worsen; symptoms can overlap with other conditions, so this supports evaluation rather than diagnosis from symptoms alone (last reviewed August 27, 2024).

Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists — Endometriosis patient information: ultrasound may show evidence, while a normal ultrasound or MRI does not rule out endometriosis (published December 2023; patient information, not a full clinical guideline).

questions.objective: Escalate respiratory and fluid-shift changes during ovarian stimulation
questions.stem: A patient self-administering follitropin alfa during a monitored ovarian-stimulation cycle calls the after-hours triage line. The next dose is due in 1 hour. Over 24 hours, weight increased 1.4 kg (3 lb), abdominal distention worsened, urine output decreased and shortness of breath developed while walking across the room. The fertility clinic cannot examine the patient until morning. What should the nurse advise?
questions.clue: A current named gonadotropin dose is imminent, and new respiratory and low-urine findings accompany a rapid fluid-shift pattern when routine clinic assessment is unavailable.
questions.rationale: Suspect a serious ovarian-stimulation adverse response and prioritize in-person emergency evaluation. The official follitropin alfa label describes rapid fluid accumulation, weight gain, abdominal distention, dyspnea and oliguria with OHSS and directs stopping gonadotropins when serious OHSS occurs. Because the patient is actively symptomatic and the next dose is due, advise against taking it pending urgent evaluation. The in-person team must determine severity and the individualized fluid, laboratory and ongoing medication plan.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a recognizable adverse-response cluster to an after-hours access and medication decision. The cues are aligned rather than competing, so the item remains level 2.

options.text: Do not take the next follitropin dose and obtain emergency evaluation now for a serious stimulation-related complication.
options.reason: The named product's official label and ASRM guidance identify rapid weight gain, distention, dyspnea and oliguria as concerning OHSS findings that require prompt assessment rather than another dose and overnight delay.

options.text: Hold the next dose and arrange the first clinic assessment in the morning, using emergency care only if breathing worsens.
options.reason: Holding the dose addresses one part of the risk, but the current exertional dyspnea, oliguria and rapid weight change already warrant emergency evaluation rather than overnight observation.

options.text: Take the scheduled dose, then go to the emergency department now so a clinician can decide whether later doses should be stopped.
options.reason: Emergency evaluation is appropriate, but administering another dose first conflicts with the named product's serious-OHSS warning to stop gonadotropins.

options.text: Start an urgent video visit with the fertility service and remain home unless the clinician confirms ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.
options.reason: A remote review may help coordination, but requiring diagnostic confirmation before in-person emergency assessment delays care for an already concerning respiratory and fluid-shift pattern.

questions.objective: Distinguish IUD pregnancy prevention from STI prevention
questions.stem: A patient with a levonorgestrel IUD reports a new sexual partner and asks whether another prevention method is needed. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.clue: The patient's IUD and the new-partner question involve two separate prevention goals.
questions.rationale: An IUD is used for pregnancy prevention, not STI prevention. Counsel about consistent and correct condom use to reduce STI risk and about screening based on current risk and applicable recommendations. Do not defer barrier protection until infection is confirmed or substitute another hormonal method for STI prevention.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes one direct dual-protection principle without trends, competing instability or treatment response. The revised author estimate is level 1.

options.text: The IUD provides pregnancy prevention, but consistent condom use is still recommended to reduce STI risk.
options.reason: Hormonal IUDs do not protect against STIs; condom counseling remains appropriate regardless of the contraceptive method used for pregnancy prevention.

options.text: The IUD's local progestin also prevents cervical infection, so condoms add pregnancy protection but not STI protection.
options.reason: The IUD's contraceptive action does not prevent acquisition of chlamydia, gonorrhea, HIV or other STIs.

options.text: Use the IUD alone until STI screening is positive; begin condoms only if an infection is found.
options.reason: Condoms reduce acquisition and transmission risk and should not be deferred until an infection is confirmed.

options.text: Changing to an injectable contraceptive would address both pregnancy prevention and the new STI exposure risk.
options.reason: Changing hormonal contraceptive methods does not supply STI protection; exposure-based prevention and screening remain separate.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 GYN, Infertility and STI instructor notes: IUD pregnancy prevention, lack of STI/HIV protection, and contraceptive choice (P334–P337; P353–P360; not duration, insertion, or removal rules).
Course lecture topic context — Week 6 Contraception and Abortion, slide 6: IUD heading only (text layer; not device-specific procedure guidance).

ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — contraception passages: condom/STI concepts and IUD background (bounded reading; dated prerequisites, duration, string-check, pregnancy-removal, and relationship wording excluded).
CDC — U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use, 2024: IUDs prevent pregnancy but do not protect against STIs; condoms reduce STI risk.

questions.objective: Detect a daily-versus-single-dose calculation error before medication administration.
questions.stem: A child weighs 44 lb (20 kg). A medication order reads 30 mg/kg/day in three equal doses. During the preadministration check, the nurse sees that 600 mg has been prepared as one dose. Which action should the nurse take?
questions.clue: The kilogram conversion is already correct; the unresolved unit is the amount for the whole day versus each administration.
questions.rationale: Read the complete weight-based order before accepting a prepared dose. Here, 20 kg × 30 mg/kg/day = 600 mg/day, and 600 mg/day ÷ 3 doses/day = 200 mg/dose. The nurse should not administer the 600-mg preparation and should clarify the discrepancy while completing the usual drug-specific safety and formulation checks. The arithmetic does not establish a clinical regimen for any named medication.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies one supplied weight conversion to distinguish mg/kg/day from mg/kg/dose and intervenes before administration. The cues align and no linked concentration calculation or competing clinical condition supports level 3.

options.text: Pause administration and verify a 600-mg dose using 20 kg × 30 mg/kg/day.
options.reason: Twenty kilograms times 30 mg/kg/day equals 600 mg for the entire day, not one administration. The calculation leaves the daily time unit unresolved.

options.text: Pause administration and verify a 200-mg dose using 600 mg/day ÷ 3 doses/day.
options.reason: Twenty kilograms times 30 mg/kg/day equals 600 mg/day; dividing that total into three doses gives 200 mg per dose. The nurse should clarify the discrepancy and complete the required safe-range and formulation checks before administration.

options.text: Pause administration and verify a 220-mg dose after converting 44 lb to 22 kg.
options.reason: Using 2 lb/kg produces 22 kg, but the supplied conversion uses 2.2 lb/kg and yields 20 kg. The incorrect weight would produce 660 mg/day and 220 mg per dose.

options.text: Pause administration and verify a 10-mg dose after dividing 30 mg/kg/day by three.
options.reason: Dividing 30 mg/kg/day by three gives 10 mg/kg per dose, not 10 mg per dose. The child's 20-kg weight must still be applied, yielding 200 mg per dose.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Developmental milestones; Growth measurements; Failure to Thrive.
questions.stem: At a well-child visit, which report requires the most prompt developmental follow-up?
questions.clue: One infant has lost a previously acquired skill rather than simply not yet performing a later-age task.
questions.rationale: Regression is more concerning than failure to perform a skill expected at an older age. Assess the whole developmental pattern rather than one rigid cutoff.
questions.difficultyReason: Compare developmental reports and prioritize actual loss of an acquired skill.

options.text: A 10-month-old who previously sat independently now repeatedly falls over and no longer reaches for toys.
options.reason: Loss of previously acquired skills is a concerning change requiring assessment.

options.text: An 18-month-old who needs a hand held while using stairs.
options.reason: Assisted stair use is compatible with this developmental period.

options.text: A 12-month-old who plays beside another child instead of sharing a cooperative game.
options.reason: Mature cooperative play is not expected at this age.

options.text: A 10-month-old who pulls to stand but does not walk independently.
options.reason: Independent walking is not expected of every 10-month-old.

questions.objective: Choose developmentally appropriate play materials for an alert 12-month-old while screening each choice for hazards.
questions.stem: The nurse prepares supervised bedside play for an alert 12-month-old. Which activities are developmentally appropriate and safe in the condition described? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Judge the activity and its present condition separately; awake supervision does not neutralize small parts or an accessible long cord.
questions.rationale: Suitable infant play includes familiar interaction, peekaboo, shared sturdy books, nesting activities, and large intact blocks. Each material still needs an age-appropriate design, intact condition, and active supervision. Small detachable pieces and accessible long cords remain hazards even when the activity might otherwise interest the child.
questions.difficultyReason: Each choice requires routine recognition of an age-appropriate infant activity and a direct hazard screen. SATA formatting does not by itself make the reasoning intermediate.

options.text: Play peekaboo with the caregiver while the infant is awake.
options.reason: Peekaboo supports object-permanence play and familiar social interaction. The awake, supervised context avoids treating the activity as unattended sleep equipment.

options.text: Offer one-piece nesting cups that have been inspected for cracks.
options.reason: Nesting and filling/emptying activities fit purposeful infant play. Intact one-piece cups avoid the stated detachable-part concern but still require supervision.

options.text: Share a sturdy board book and name pictures as the infant looks.
options.reason: Shared books support language and interaction at this age; the nurse is not requiring independent reading or coordinated page turning.

options.text: Provide large washable blocks with no loose or detachable pieces.
options.reason: Large intact blocks support grasping, placing, and purposeful play while addressing the infant's tendency to mouth objects.

options.text: Offer the sibling's miniature building set because an adult will remain nearby.
options.reason: Close supervision does not make small detachable pieces appropriate for an infant who explores with the mouth; an age-appropriate large-piece activity should be chosen instead.

options.text: Place a pull toy with a long dangling cord inside the play area.
options.reason: An accessible long cord creates an entanglement hazard. Developmental interest in a toy does not cancel the need to remove the hazardous feature.

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapter 3, printed pp. 16–18: infant development, interpersonal play, nesting toys, books, blocks, small-object avoidance, and age-appropriate hazard prevention.
CDC Learn the Signs. Act Early. — Milestones by 9 Months: peekaboo, shared reading, and block play (page dated May 15, 2026; milestone guidance is not diagnostic).

questions.objective: Plan predictable, responsive care for an infant during a brief caregiver absence.
questions.stem: A hospitalized 10-month-old has stable findings and controlled pain but cries when the caregiver prepares to leave for 90 minutes. Which plan should the nurse recommend?
questions.clue: The crying begins with a planned separation, while current assessment and pain control do not suggest a new physiologic cause.
questions.rationale: Separation-related protest is expected in late infancy, but it still calls for responsive care. A brief, clear goodbye, familiar routines, consistent staff, and prompt comfort support predictability while the caregiver is away. The nurse should continue to reassess for pain or illness if new cues appear; the stable, pain-controlled scenario only identifies the present care-planning problem.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner uses the timing of distress and the stable assessment to select a developmentally responsive handoff plan among plausible timing and staffing alternatives.

options.text: Use a brief goodbye, continue the familiar routine, and assign the same nurse when possible.
options.reason: A clear goodbye, familiar routine, and consistent responsive caregiver make the separation more predictable. The infant can still cry; the plan supports security rather than promising immediate calm.

options.text: Leave while the infant is distracted so no departure cue is noticed.
options.reason: Leaving without a goodbye removes predictability. Current CDC guidance specifically favors a quick, cheerful goodbye over sneaking away.

options.text: Schedule the departure during the next procedure to combine both upsetting transitions.
options.reason: Combining caregiver departure with an invasive or unfamiliar event adds stress and does not preserve the low-distress preparation described in the course notes.

options.text: Rotate several staff members through the room to increase distraction during the absence.
options.reason: Multiple unfamiliar caregivers reduce continuity during separation. ATI recommends consistency in caregiver assignment and prompt attention to the infant's needs.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: infant attachment, separation and stranger fear, caregiver involvement, predictable care, and trust (P35–P56; P571–P594; T1R5–T1R7; T2R1–T2R3).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapters 3 and 10, printed pp. 16–18 and 49–50: infant attachment and separation, caregiver presence, familiar routines, consistent caregivers, and responsive hospital care.

CDC Learn the Signs. Act Early. — Milestones by 9 Months: a quick cheerful goodbye, predictable routines, and caregiver proximity during separation (page dated May 15, 2026; no promise of immediate calm).

questions.objective: Support toddler autonomy while delivering a verified oral medication dose accurately and safely.
questions.stem: A verified liquid medication dose is due for a hospitalized 2-year-old who turns away from the nurse. Which actions support cooperation and accurate oral administration? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Support limited control and familiar comfort while the nurse controls the measured dose's position and pace.
questions.rationale: Toddler care can preserve autonomy without sacrificing medication accuracy. Use simple immediate teaching, caregiver support, two acceptable choices, and an appropriate measured device while the child is upright. Give small amounts toward the side of the mouth and allow swallowing pauses. Excluding the caregiver without a case-specific reason or pushing the entire syringe at once works against cooperation and safe delivery. Refusal or escalating distress still requires assessment and appropriate help; it does not authorize force, consent override, omission, or automatic redosing.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies toddler autonomy and swallowing safety to several realistic administration actions while preserving dose accountability. No dose calculation or competing physiologic trend supports level 3.

options.text: Explain the medicine in simple words immediately before giving it.
options.reason: Brief, concrete teaching in the present moment matches toddler cognition and prepares the child without a long anticipatory period.

options.text: Offer a choice between sitting with the caregiver or beside the caregiver.
options.reason: Both options keep the needed treatment possible while giving the toddler limited, genuine control over how care occurs.

options.text: Keep the child upright and give small amounts into the side of the mouth.
options.reason: Upright positioning and small side-of-mouth portions support swallowing and reduce aspiration risk during liquid administration.

options.text: Ask the caregiver to step out so the toddler focuses on the nurse's directions.
options.reason: No case cue suggests that caregiver presence is worsening distress. Removing familiar support can reduce cooperation; the caregiver can instead participate in a planned, supervised way.

options.text: Push the full oral-syringe dose in one motion while the child remains upright.
options.reason: Upright positioning is appropriate, but rapidly giving the entire syringe does not allow swallowing pauses and can increase choking or aspiration risk. Small cheek-side portions are safer.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: toddler autonomy, negativism, caregiver presence, simple language, real choices, and immediate teaching (P116–P167; P586–P594; T2R3; T3R2–T3R3).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapters 8 and 10, printed pp. 39 and 49–50: caregiver-supported care, limited choices, oral-syringe use, upright positioning, and small side-of-mouth portions.

Great Ormond Street Hospital — How to give your child liquid medicines: upright positioning, syringe-unit and dose checks, small cheek-side portions, and swallowing pauses (last reviewed December 18, 2024; the displayed next-review date of December 18, 2025 has passed).

questions.objective: Address a preschooler's expressed punishment belief with concrete, honest procedure preparation.
questions.stem: A 4-year-old awaiting wound repair says, "I have to get stitches because I yelled at my sister." Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The child has named a cause for the injury and procedure, not only fear, boredom, or separation.
questions.rationale: Preschool magical thinking and reward-punishment reasoning can link an injury or procedure to prior behavior. The best response identifies and corrects that exact belief, then uses simple concrete preparation such as demonstration on a doll. Comfort, distraction, and general explanation may also help, but they do not replace correcting the expressed guilt-based misconception.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must interpret the child's causal statement and distinguish the response that targets it from three otherwise supportive but incomplete alternatives.

options.text: "The cut is not a punishment for yelling. Let's show the bandage steps on this doll."
options.reason: This response directly corrects the stated punishment belief and uses concrete play to prepare the child for care.

options.text: "Lots of children feel scared. You can choose a cartoon while you wait."
options.reason: The response offers support and a choice but does not assess or correct the child's belief that the injury and procedure are punishment.

options.text: "Your family is nearby. We can put your favorite blanket where you can see it."
options.reason: A familiar object can be comforting, but separation is not the concern the child expressed. The guilt and causation misconception remain unaddressed.

options.text: "I will explain each step when we begin, and you can tell me when you feel worried."
options.reason: Simple preparation and expression are helpful, but this reply still leaves the specific punishment belief intact. The nurse should first correct that misconception honestly.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: preschool punishment beliefs, invasive-experience fears, play therapy, and honest teaching shortly before care (P168–P215; T2R4; T3R3).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapters 2, 5, and 10, printed pp. 7, 25–26, and 49–50: developmentally adapted preparation, magical thinking and guilt, pretend play, clear language, choices, and hospital support.

questions.objective: Support achievable participation and competence for a hospitalized school-age child.
questions.stem: A hospitalized 10-year-old with a leg cast says, "I cannot do anything useful here." Which care plan best supports the child's developmental task?
questions.clue: The child is asking for a sense of usefulness and competence, not complete protection from effort.
questions.rationale: School-age children work toward industry by learning skills, completing meaningful tasks, and seeing their own progress. A reachable self-care goal preserves participation within the child's current physical limits. Peer contact, choices about care, rest, and distraction can all be appropriate, but they target different needs and do not directly answer this child's stated loss of usefulness and competence.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes a direct industry-versus-inferiority need and selects a routine care plan that provides achievable mastery.

options.text: Set a reachable self-care goal and let the child track progress toward it.
options.reason: A meaningful, achievable task gives the child an opportunity to develop skill, contribute to care, and experience competence.

options.text: Schedule daily video calls with classmates to maintain the child's peer connections.
options.reason: Peer contact can be valuable during hospitalization, but this plan does not provide the meaningful task or accomplishment that addresses the child's stated lack of usefulness.

options.text: Offer choices about bath and meal times to increase the child's sense of control.
options.reason: Reasonable choices can support control during hospitalization, but selecting care times does not directly create the achievable skill or contribution requested by this child's statement.

options.text: Plan quiet games between treatments to provide distraction and support needed rest.
options.reason: Rest and distraction can be appropriate, but this plan does not give the child a meaningful role, skill goal, or way to see personal accomplishment.

questions.objective: Separate an emerging two-year-old stair skill from readiness for independent stair safety.
questions.stem: During a home-safety visit, a caregiver reports that a 2-year-old now walks up and down stairs with both feet on each step. Which teaching should the nurse provide?
questions.clue: A motor milestone describes how the child moves on stairs; it does not certify judgment or a barrier's continued fit.
questions.rationale: A 2-year-old may use stairs one step at a time and still need close adult supervision and an appropriate barrier. At the top of stairs, current CPSC guidance calls for a child safety gate that screws to the wall, is installed and re-engaged according to instructions, and meets current safety standards. No safety device is completely childproof, so the gate does not replace supervision.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies the distinction between an expected motor skill and independent safety, then chooses an installation-specific teaching plan among plausible barrier alternatives.

options.text: Supervise stair practice and keep a standards-compliant top gate secured as instructed.
options.reason: The one-step pattern can be developmentally expected, but it does not establish hazard judgment or consistent independent safety. CPSC guidance supports a standards-compliant, wall-secured top gate installed and re-engaged as directed.

options.text: Use a pressure-mounted gate at the top so the wall is not damaged.
options.reason: CPSC guidance specifies a gate that screws to the wall at the top of stairs. Convenience and wall protection do not outweigh secure installation.

options.text: Replace the child gate with a pet gate now that climbing has begun.
options.reason: CPSC states that pet gates should not be used as child safety gates. An emerging skill increases the need for appropriate barriers and supervision rather than a substitute product.

options.text: Remove the gate because the expected milestone confirms independent stair safety.
options.reason: A milestone describes an emerging motor ability, not mature balance, judgment, or consistent safety. Barrier use should follow the child's abilities and product instructions rather than this milestone alone.

questions.objective: Reconcile documented preschool and college-entry vaccine gaps using dated recommendations and product distinctions.
questions.stem: Using the CDC child schedule dated July 2, 2025, the nurse reviews two healthy patients with no identified contraindications. A 4-year-old has valid DTaP doses at 2, 4, 6, and 15 months; IPV doses at 2, 4, and 6 months; and one MMR and one varicella dose at 12 months. An 18-year-old entering a college residence hall received MenACWY only at age 11. Which plans are supported by the documented histories? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: The preschool record contains valid early doses but not the age-4 doses, while the college student has no MenACWY dose at age 16 or later.
questions.rationale: Use the actual documented ages and valid intervals rather than restarting completed series or treating meningococcal products as interchangeable. Under the explicitly dated July 2, 2025 CDC child schedule, the 4-year-old's record supports the DTaP, IPV, MMR, and varicella age-4 plans after exact date/interval and contraindication review. Current CDC meningococcal guidance dated March 30, 2026 continues to distinguish ACWY, B, and ABCWY coverage; a MenB-only dose does not replace the missing MenACWY protection for this residence-hall entrant.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies two explicit records to routine age-based plans and one product distinction. No interval calculation, disputed contraindication, trend, or treatment response makes the reasoning level 3.

options.text: Plan the fifth DTaP dose for the 4-year-old.
options.reason: The dated CDC notes describe a five-dose DTaP series with the later booster at age 4 to 6 years. The documented fourth dose was at 15 months, so the special early-completion exception is not being assumed.

options.text: Plan the final IPV dose after confirming the minimum interval.
options.reason: The dated CDC notes call for the final IPV dose on or after age 4 and at least six months after the previous dose. The supplied history meets the age pattern, but the record should still be checked for exact dates.

options.text: Plan the second MMR dose for the 4-year-old.
options.reason: The dated CDC notes list a two-dose MMR series at 12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 years. The documented record contains only the first valid dose.

options.text: Delay the second varicella dose until age 13 because the early-childhood interval has closed.
options.reason: The dated CDC notes include the second routine varicella dose at age 4 to 6 years. The child's current age is within that interval, so age 13 is not required by this history.

options.text: Plan a MenACWY dose for the 18-year-old before residence-hall entry.
options.reason: CDC recommends the adolescent MenACWY booster at age 16, and the dated schedule specifies one dose for first-year residential college students not vaccinated at age 16 or older. This student received MenACWY only at 11.

options.text: Use a MenB-only dose instead of the missing MenACWY dose.
options.reason: A MenB-only vaccine covers serogroup B and does not provide the missing A, C, W, and Y protection. An indicated MenABCWY combination product is a separate possibility and is not ruled out by this statement.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes: immunizations, contraindication and precaution awareness, Vaccine Information Statements, and injection planning (P108–P115; the note does not supply the schedule).

CDC — Child Immunization Schedule Notes, United States, 2025: DTaP, IPV, MMR, varicella, MenACWY, MenB, and residential-college recommendations used for this explicitly July 2, 2025 exercise (not a blanket 2026 schedule or school-law certification).

CDC — Meningococcal Vaccine Recommendations: MenACWY at ages 11–12 with a booster at 16, plus MenACWY, MenB, and MenABCWY serogroup and product distinctions (page dated March 30, 2026; not a school-law source).

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: School-Age Child: Injury prevention; General Safety promotion and injury prevention.
questions.stem: During anticipatory guidance for a 10-year-old, which caregiver statement most clearly requires correction?
questions.clue: Correct seat-belt fit does not make the front and back passenger positions equally safe for a child.
questions.rationale: Independence should increase with development while evidence-based protection remains in place. Correct the specific unsafe practice rather than discouraging all autonomy.
questions.difficultyReason: Identify the single unsafe transportation statement among routine prevention plans.

options.text: "We use a helmet on every bicycle ride, including short rides."
options.reason: Consistent helmet use supports injury prevention.

options.text: "We review an emergency contact plan before allowing time at home without me."
options.reason: Planning and assessment of readiness support safer independence.

options.text: "We check who supervises swimming rather than assuming another adult is watching."
options.reason: Defined active supervision reduces water-injury risk.

options.text: "A properly fitted seat belt makes the front seat as safe as the back."
options.reason: Children younger than 13 should ride in the back seat; proper belt fit does not eliminate front-airbag risk.

questions.objective: Escalate spreading lesions with new systemic findings
questions.stem: A child with localized impetigo has used prescribed topical mupirocin for two days. Today the lesions are spreading, the surrounding skin is increasingly warm and tender, and the child has a new fever. What should the nurse advise?
questions.clue: New fever accompanies spreading warmth and tenderness despite treatment intended for localized lesions.
questions.rationale: The whole trend matters: localized impetigo is now spreading with new systemic and inflammatory findings. Prompt same-day reassessment allows the clinician to evaluate the diagnosis, severity, and need for a different treatment plan. Technique review, antipyretic comfort care, or marking a border may contribute information but should not delay that reassessment. The item does not diagnose sepsis, determine the causative organism, select a systemic antibiotic, or require a particular emergency disposition.
questions.difficultyReason: The findings are aligned rather than competing, but the learner must evaluate deterioration during topical treatment and escalate appropriately. This supports level 2.

options.text: Arrange prompt same-day clinical reassessment before changing the prescribed treatment.
options.reason: The new fever and spreading local inflammation show deterioration despite a localized-treatment plan. Reassessment is needed to evaluate severity and whether the plan must change.

options.text: Confirm the application technique and continue the same plan until the scheduled follow-up because two treatment days are too soon to judge.
options.reason: Technique review can be useful, but it does not make new fever and spreading warmth or tenderness appropriate for delayed routine reassessment.

options.text: Treat the fever for comfort and plan to contact the prescriber if the tenderness remains after the fever resolves.
options.reason: Comfort care does not explain or evaluate the combined systemic and local deterioration. The decision to seek reassessment should not depend on fever resolution first.

options.text: Mark the current redness and call tomorrow if it spreads past the line after another prescribed topical dose.
options.reason: Border monitoring may help describe change, but the child already has spreading lesions, increased warmth and tenderness, and fever that warrant prompt assessment now.

questions.objective: Interpret nits after treatment without unsafe repeat exposure
questions.stem: A child received a head-lice product yesterday. Its label states that it does not kill all eggs and directs a second application on day 9. No live crawling lice are seen today, but attached nits remain. Which caregiver statement shows correct understanding?
questions.clue: The supplied product is not fully ovicidal and explicitly directs a second application on day 9; no crawling lice are present today.
questions.rationale: Head-lice products differ in whether they kill eggs and whether retreatment is needed. For a product that explicitly directs a day-9 second application, the caregiver should avoid extra medication today, continue checking and combing as directed, and follow that product plan unless a clinician changes it. Remaining nits alone prove neither cure nor immediate treatment failure, and the absence of visible crawling lice after one day does not cancel a required follow-up dose. Day 9 is case-specific, not a universal schedule for every pediculicide.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner interprets residual nits using the supplied product action and timing rather than equating nits with failure or cure. This product-dependent application supports level 2.

options.text: I will give no extra dose today, continue checking and combing as directed, and follow the product's day-9 plan.
options.reason: The product-specific plan anticipates surviving eggs and supplies the repeat timing. Remaining nits without live crawling lice do not justify an additional dose today.

options.text: I will repeat the same product today because attached nits show that the first application failed.
options.reason: Nits can remain after treatment, and this product already specifies later retreatment because it does not kill all eggs. Their presence alone is not proof of immediate failure.

options.text: I will cancel the day-9 dose because not seeing crawling lice today proves that the eggs are no longer viable.
options.reason: Absence of visible crawling lice one day later does not establish that all eggs are nonviable. The supplied product directions still call for retreatment.

options.text: I will move the repeat dose to day 5 so the next application occurs before any nits can hatch.
options.reason: Retreatment timing depends on the product. Moving the dose earlier without guidance substitutes an assumed life-cycle rule for the actual label instructions.

Course lecture topic context — Week 7 Children & Integumentary, slide 7: pediculosis (text-layer locator only; no product schedule or diagnosis).
Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapter 30, printed pp. 198–199: head lice, treatment and environmental context (older fixed product intervals and doses excluded).

CDC — Treatment of Head Lice: follow the medicine instructions; egg-killing activity and retreatment differ by product; non-ovicidal products may require retreatment at 7–9 days; and check or comb as directed (page dated November 12, 2024; the item's day 9 is fictional product-specific guidance).

questions.objective: Coordinate the prescribed household scabies plan
questions.stem: An 8-year-old has clinician-diagnosed scabies and an age-appropriate topical prescription with written application instructions. The caregiver is preparing the household plan. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: A complete plan coordinates contacts, prescribed pediatric application, recent-item cleaning, and reassessment while distinguishing residual itch from new infestation findings.
questions.rationale: Scabies control requires multiple independent decisions. Household members and close contacts are treated together as directed because symptoms can be delayed. The child uses the actual pediatric prescription for coverage and contact time rather than a universal adult application rule. Clothing and bedding used during the three days before treatment are hot-washed and hot-dried. Continued itching alone can persist after successful treatment, while new burrows, a new pimple-like rash, or signs of infection warrant reassessment. The case supplies no infant dose, bagging interval, or fixed universal retreatment schedule.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies distinct contact, application, environmental, and response-assessment instructions within one prescribed household plan. This supports level 2 without relying on SATA format alone.

options.text: Treat household members and close contacts at the same time as directed, even when some have no symptoms.
options.reason: Symptoms can be delayed, and simultaneous contact management reduces reinfestation and continued household transmission.

options.text: Apply the child's product to every body area named in the pediatric instructions and leave it on only for the prescribed contact time.
options.reason: Application sites and contact time depend on the child's actual prescription and instructions; adult neck-down shorthand should not replace them.

options.text: Hot-wash and hot-dry clothing and bedding used during the three days before treatment began.
options.reason: Current scabies guidance targets clothing and bedding used during the three days before treatment and recommends hot washing and drying.

options.text: Contact the clinician if new burrows, a new pimple-like rash, or signs of skin infection appear after treatment.
options.reason: New infestation findings or possible secondary infection differ from ordinary residual itching and warrant clinical reassessment.

options.text: Keep the family dog separated from the child throughout treatment because pets commonly carry human scabies between household members.
options.reason: Animals do not spread human scabies. A pet can have a different mite infestation, but routine pet separation does not control the child's human scabies.

options.text: Interpret continued itching in the first days as evidence that another application should be scheduled now.
options.reason: Itching can continue for weeks after mites and eggs are killed. Itching alone in the first days does not prove treatment failure or authorize an immediate repeat application.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 7 Exam 2 Integumentary Instructor Notes: scabies, pediculosis, and infestation care (P73–P94; no pediatric dose, universal coverage shorthand, or fixed repeat schedule).
Course lecture topic context — Week 7 Children & Integumentary, slide 6: scabies (text-layer locator only; no regimen or response algorithm).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, chapter 30, printed pp. 198–199: scabies, contact and environmental measures, and secondary-infection context (older product intervals, ages, doses, and universal application shorthand excluded).

CDC — Preventing Scabies: treat household members and close contacts together, hot-wash and hot-dry items used during the three days before treatment, and recognize that animals do not spread human scabies (page dated December 18, 2023; the three-day window is not a drug-retreatment interval).

CDC — Treatment of Scabies: follow the prescribed application sites and contact time; persistent itching can continue after treatment; and new burrows, rash, or skin sores warrant reassessment (page dated January 12, 2024; no infant regimen or universal repeat schedule).

questions.objective: Correct an unsafe generalized skin-care routine
questions.stem: A child with atopic dermatitis has very dry skin and a current flare. The prescription directs a topical corticosteroid to named inflamed areas for the current course but gives no whole-body maintenance instruction. The caregiver gives long hot baths and applies the corticosteroid over the entire body every day, including clear skin. Which teaching is most appropriate?
questions.clue: The routine combines drying heat with medication use that extends beyond the sites and course in the current prescription.
questions.rationale: Eczema care combines gentle bathing, prompt moisturizing, and individualized anti-inflammatory treatment. The caregiver should replace long hot baths with lukewarm bathing, pat rather than rub, moisturize promptly, and use the topical corticosteroid at the sites and schedule specified in the current plan. Generalized dryness does not authorize applying the corticosteroid outside the named areas in the current prescription. This is not a universal ban on clinician-directed intermittent maintenance therapy; any maintenance plan remains individualized.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must correct both barrier-damaging care and overgeneralized medication use while preserving individualized maintenance exceptions, supporting level 2.

options.text: Use lukewarm baths, moisturize promptly, and apply the corticosteroid only as currently prescribed; ask before changing maintenance use.
options.reason: This corrects the drying bath routine, supports the skin barrier, and returns medication use to the individualized prescription without banning clinician-directed maintenance.

options.text: Use lukewarm baths, wash the entire body with mild fragrance-free cleanser each time, then moisturize promptly and apply the corticosteroid as prescribed.
options.reason: Using cleanser over the entire body at every bath is unnecessary; cleanser should be mild, fragrance-free, and used only when needed. The remaining steps fit the plan.

options.text: Use lukewarm bathing and moisturizer, but apply the corticosteroid to all dry skin each day because dryness predicts the next flare.
options.reason: Barrier care is appropriate, but generalized dryness is not permission to extend a prescription to untreated sites or create a maintenance regimen without clinician direction.

options.text: Use lukewarm baths and the prescribed corticosteroid, but wait until the skin is completely dry before applying moisturizer.
options.reason: Waiting for complete drying misses the prompt post-bath sequence used to retain moisture; the bathing temperature and prescribed medication use are otherwise appropriate.

refs.label: Course scope — Week 7 Exam 2 Integumentary Instructor Notes: atopic dermatitis and daily skin care (P141–P154; no steroid potency, dose, site, duration, or maintenance regimen).
Course lecture topic context — Week 7 Children & Integumentary, slide 2: dermatitis and eczema (text-layer locator only; visual context was not used for diagnosis or treatment).

American Academy of Dermatology — Pediatric atopic dermatitis guideline announcement: moisturizers, topical corticosteroids for flares and maintenance, and bathing followed by moisturizer (dated April 7, 2026; announcement only, not the full JAAD guideline or an individualized prescription).

American Academy of Dermatology — Atopic dermatitis: Self-care: use warm rather than hot water, mild fragrance-free cleanser only when needed, gently pat partially dry, apply prescribed topical medicine, and moisturize promptly (page date not established; no fixed bath duration or medication regimen).

questions.objective: Escalate new joint symptoms despite improving plaques
questions.stem: An adolescent with psoriasis reports that prescribed skin care is improving the plaques. During the past 10 days, however, several finger joints have become swollen and stiff each morning, making it harder to open containers. The adolescent denies injury and fever. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The plaques and joints are giving different signals: the skin is improving while new swelling, morning stiffness, and loss of function have appeared.
questions.rationale: Psoriasis can be associated with inflammatory joint disease. New swollen or tender joints, morning stiffness, and reduced function should be reported and assessed promptly even when skin lesions are improving. The nurse should preserve the current prescribed skin plan unless the prescriber changes it. These findings raise concern for possible joint involvement but do not by themselves establish a diagnosis or authorize a new systemic regimen.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must separate improving skin findings from a new musculoskeletal problem and choose timely assessment without overdiagnosing or independently changing treatment, supporting level 2.

options.text: Arrange prompt clinical assessment of the new joint symptoms and continue the current skin plan unless the prescriber changes it.
options.reason: New joint swelling, stiffness, and functional change in a person with psoriasis warrant prompt assessment for possible joint involvement. Improving plaques do not make the joint findings unimportant, and the nurse should not independently diagnose arthritis or replace the prescribed skin plan.

options.text: Wait until the next routine visit because improving plaques show that the psoriasis is adequately controlled.
options.reason: Skin improvement does not exclude associated joint disease. Delaying assessment could postpone evaluation of symptoms for which early recognition matters.

options.text: Limit use of the affected hand for one week and report the symptoms only if the swelling remains after rest.
options.reason: Rest alone does not address the combination of new swelling, morning stiffness, and functional limitation. The symptoms should be assessed promptly rather than observed for an additional week.

options.text: Stop the prescribed skin care because joint symptoms indicate that the plaque treatment is causing the new problem.
options.reason: The findings do not establish that the skin treatment caused the joint symptoms. The safe response is assessment without an independent medication or care-plan change.

Week 7 Children & Integumentary lecture — slide 3: psoriasis heading and photo label (topic locator only; the original image was not used for joint-management guidance).

American Academy of Dermatology — Psoriatic arthritis: Signs and symptoms: people with psoriasis should report swollen or tender joints and stiffness; a swollen joint may be an early sign, and early assessment and treatment can help prevent joint damage (page-update date not established).

questions.objective: Stabilize losses and electrolyte disturbance before anesthesia
questions.stem: A 5-week-old with ultrasound-confirmed pyloric stenosis is NPO with IV access after progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting. Urine output is improving after initial fluids, but the mucous membranes remain dry; potassium is 2.9 mEq/L and bicarbonate is elevated. Pyloromyotomy is tentatively scheduled this morning. Which action should the nurse anticipate next?
questions.clue: Urine output is improving, but dry mucosa, hypokalemia and elevated bicarbonate show that the preoperative deficits are not yet fully corrected.
questions.rationale: Pyloromyotomy is definitive treatment, but early management prioritizes correction of dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities and acid-base disturbance before anesthesia. An improving urine-output trend is not enough to declare readiness while other deficits remain. The infant should remain NPO and receive the prescribed IV plan with clinical and laboratory reassessment. The item does not select a potassium rate, fluid recipe or universal laboratory target.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must weigh one improving hydration cue against remaining clinical and laboratory deficits and sequence stabilization before anesthesia, supporting level 2.

options.text: Continue prescribed IV correction and reassess hydration, electrolytes, and acid-base status before anesthesia.
options.reason: One improving finding does not establish readiness. Dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and metabolic alkalosis should be corrected and reassessed before anesthesia when clinically feasible.

options.text: Prepare for anesthesia now because improved urine output shows that the preoperative deficits are resolved.
options.reason: Improving urine output is useful but does not override the remaining dry mucosa, low potassium and elevated bicarbonate.

options.text: Begin oral rehydration while IV correction continues because vomiting has paused since admission.
options.reason: A temporary pause in vomiting does not remove the gastric outlet obstruction or the preoperative NPO plan. Correction should follow the prescribed IV strategy.

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound before continuing IV correction because narrowing severity determines the fluid requirement.
options.reason: The diagnosis is already confirmed, and fluid correction is guided by the infant's clinical and laboratory deficits rather than postponed for another image.

Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne — Clinical Practice Guidelines: Pyloric stenosis: correct dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and acid-base abnormality before surgery when clinically feasible (last updated March 2024; the page's fluid recipe, potassium threshold, and universal anesthesia targets are excluded).

questions.objective: Recognize a changed abdominal pattern requiring escalation
questions.stem: A child with confirmed appendicitis is NPO and awaiting appendectomy. After several hours of right-lower-quadrant pain, the child reports sudden relief. Thirty minutes later, the pain is generalized, the abdomen is rigid, and the pulse has risen from 96/min to 128/min. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.clue: The decisive finding is not the temporary relief alone; it is the subsequent generalized pain, rigidity and rising pulse.
questions.rationale: Sudden pain relief can occur after appendiceal perforation, but pain relief alone is not diagnostic. Here it is followed by generalized pain, abdominal rigidity and tachycardia, an aligned deterioration pattern that warrants immediate surgical-team notification and continued prescribed preoperative support. Analgesia, laboratory data and routine handoff may still be part of care, but they must not delay escalation of the changed pattern.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner interprets a short clinical sequence and prioritizes escalation over several otherwise reasonable care steps, supporting level 2.

options.text: Notify the surgical team immediately about the changed abdominal and pulse findings, and maintain NPO status.
options.reason: Brief relief followed by generalized pain, rigidity and tachycardia is a deterioration pattern concerning for perforation with peritonitis and requires immediate surgical escalation.

options.text: Continue the existing plan and report the change during operating-room handoff because surgery is already scheduled.
options.reason: A scheduled operation does not make the new deterioration routine. The team needs the change now so the urgency and support plan can be reassessed.

options.text: Give the prescribed PRN analgesic and wait for its effect before deciding whether to call the surgical team.
options.reason: Analgesia may be appropriate, but it should not delay reporting rigidity, generalized pain and tachycardia in a child awaiting surgery.

options.text: Obtain a repeat white-blood-cell count before notifying the surgical team so perforation can be confirmed.
options.reason: A laboratory result does not confirm perforation by itself and should not delay escalation of the new peritoneal and systemic findings.

Course lecture topic context — Week 7 GI Dysfunction, slide 7: appendicitis (text-layer heading only; no diagnostic or escalation protocol).

Supplemental reading — ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11, printed pp. 145–146: appendicitis deterioration and peritonitis context (no laboratory confirmation rule, antibiotic regimen, imaging sequence, or operative approach).

questions.objective: Reassess an earlier procedure plan after new instability
questions.stem: At a referring emergency department, a stable 9-month-old with confirmed intussusception has been accepted for transfer to a pediatric center for air-enema reduction. Just before departure, the infant becomes lethargic, febrile, and hypotensive, with a rigid abdomen. The emergency clinician activates the hospital's resuscitation orders. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.clue: The child was an enema candidate, but new shock and a rigid abdomen now conflict with that earlier plan while urgent definitive transfer is still needed.
questions.rationale: Air-enema reduction can be appropriate for a stable child with intussusception, but shock, peritonitis, perforation or other instability contraindicate that pathway. The nurse should pause the routine enema plan, begin ordered resuscitative support and immediately coordinate with the surgical and receiving teams. Pausing an unsafe procedure does not mean preventing emergency transfer for definitive care. The item does not specify an enema pressure, fluid dose, antibiotic or operative technique.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must revise a previously appropriate procedure and transfer plan after new shock and peritoneal findings while preserving emergency definitive transfer, a genuine level-3 conflict.

options.text: Pause the enema pathway, begin ordered resuscitation, and coordinate urgent surgical transfer under a revised plan.
options.reason: Shock and peritoneal findings make the prior enema plan unsafe. Resuscitation and rapid surgical-team coordination are required, while transfer for definitive care should proceed under the revised plan.

options.text: Continue transfer for the enema while providing IV support en route because rapid reduction may reverse the instability.
options.reason: Providing circulation support is appropriate, but shock, rigidity and suspected peritonitis contraindicate proceeding on the routine enema pathway.

options.text: Cancel transfer and observe locally until vital signs normalize before contacting the receiving surgical team.
options.reason: The routine enema plan should pause, but urgent resuscitation and early receiving-team coordination should not wait for normalization or block definitive transfer.

options.text: Ask the receiving radiology team to perform a diagnostic-only enema before deciding whether reduction is safe.
options.reason: The new shock and peritoneal findings contraindicate the enema pathway itself; labeling it diagnostic does not remove that risk.

Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne — Clinical Practice Guidelines: Intussusception: resuscitation precedes reduction; shock, peritonitis, perforation, or instability contraindicates the enema pathway; suspected cases require surgical-team discussion and transfer support (last updated February 2026; no dose, pressure, or operative protocol).

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Hirschsprung's disease: Potential for enterocolitis.
questions.stem: The pediatric nurse receives four GI-related reports. Which child requires the first bedside assessment?
questions.clue: Fever, distention, diarrhea, and poor perfusion occur in an infant at risk for enterocolitis.
questions.rationale: Prioritize systemic illness and impaired perfusion over diagnostic labels. In Hirschsprung disease, new diarrhea can be a danger sign rather than relief of constipation.
questions.difficultyReason: Prioritize systemic enterocolitis signs over three stable gastrointestinal reports.

options.text: A child with treated constipation who passes a soft stool without blood and has normal vital signs.
options.reason: This suggests a response to the current plan rather than acute deterioration.

options.text: An infant with uncomplicated reflux who is gaining weight and sleeps supine on a firm, flat surface.
options.reason: Growth and safe sleep are reassuring in this report; reflux does not require prone or inclined sleep.

options.text: An infant with Hirschsprung disease who now has fever, increasing distention, explosive diarrhea, and poor perfusion.
options.reason: This suggests Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis with possible sepsis; diarrhea does not exclude obstructive disease.

options.text: A child after successful intussusception reduction who is alert, pain-free, and has normal perfusion.
options.reason: Continued monitoring is required, but this report is stable compared with suspected enterocolitis.

questions.objective: Prioritize evaluation and antidote preparation when unknown ingestion time makes a reassuring lab flag unreliable
questions.stem: A 14-kg toddler is in the emergency department after possible acetaminophen ingestion. Neither the amount nor ingestion time can be established. The child is alert and breathing comfortably. Acetaminophen is detectable, but the report labels the result within its therapeutic reference interval; initial AST and ALT are within reference limits. Which actions are appropriate during the initial emergency evaluation? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: A therapeutic reference flag answers a different question from overdose risk when the time of exposure is unknown.
questions.rationale: Interpret the result in exposure context, not from its label alone. Unknown timing prevents using an assumed ingestion clock; normal initial AST/ALT do not justify delaying evaluation. Carry out prescribed testing and the promptly determined antidote plan with clinical monitoring. No dose, bag schedule or automatic stopping rule is being tested. The lab reference flag is a fictional case detail, not a universal therapeutic cutoff.
questions.difficultyReason: Reconcile a detectable result labeled therapeutic and currently normal liver tests with an unknown ingestion time. Reject a routine-reference-range interpretation and an invalid nomogram clock before choosing care. Provisional author estimate, not calibration.

options.text: Use the time the child was found beside the bottle as the ingestion time when interpreting the nomogram.
options.reason: Discovery time does not establish ingestion time. A guessed clock cannot make an unknown-time exposure suitable for timed nomogram interpretation.

options.text: Obtain the prescribed hepatic, coagulation and renal studies needed to assess risk and guide follow-up.
options.reason: Current and follow-up laboratory assessment supports evaluation beyond a reference-range flag or a single early liver-test result.

options.text: Request prompt toxicology/prescriber review and prepare to administer prescribed N-acetylcysteine during evaluation of the unknown-time exposure.
options.reason: The unknown-time pathway warrants prompt antidote evaluation; the drug label supports immediate initial treatment in that context. Do not wait for liver injury to become evident.

options.text: Defer toxicology contact until an acetaminophen sample drawn four hours after emergency-department arrival becomes available.
options.reason: The known-ingestion sampling interval is not a four-hour waiting period from arrival. Delaying expert evaluation leaves the actual elapsed time unresolved.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Contact Dermatitis; Poison Ivy, Oak and Sumac.
questions.stem: A school-age child develops itchy streaks on the forearms after clearing vines. The child is breathing comfortably, and the clinician identifies poison-ivy contact dermatitis. Which home-care action best prevents continued contact with the irritant?
questions.clue: The rash followed contact with vines, and contaminated objects can retain the irritant.
questions.rationale: Separate removing the cause from relieving the symptoms. Gently wash exposed areas and contaminated items, then follow the prescribed symptom-care plan. Report infection signs or a severe reaction.
questions.difficultyReason: Identify removal of a known contact irritant rather than confuse symptom relief with decontamination.

options.text: Wash exposed skin gently and clean contaminated clothing and equipment.
options.reason: Urushiol remaining on skin or objects can cause further exposure. Gentle cleansing removes it without adding skin injury.

options.text: Cover the contaminated gardening gloves with a towel and reuse them tomorrow.
options.reason: Covering the gloves does not remove the oil. Clean contaminated equipment before reuse.

options.text: Wash exposed skin and clothing, then air-dry the unwashed gardening tools before reusing them.
options.reason: Air-drying does not remove residual plant oil from tools. Clean contaminated equipment before reuse.

options.text: Apply the prescribed anti-itch medicine but leave the clothing unwashed.
options.reason: Symptom relief does not remove residual irritant from clothing.
