questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Injurious Agents/Poisons: Acetaminophen.
questions.stem: A child with a potentially toxic acetaminophen ingestion has already reached the emergency department. Poison specialists recommend an antidote under the hospital protocol. Which medication should the nurse recognize as the acetaminophen antidote?
questions.clue: The question asks for the antidote, not a decontamination treatment.
questions.rationale: Recognize the purpose of the medication before preparing it. The poison team determines whether treatment is needed using the exposure history, timing, laboratory findings, and clinical state. Do not wait for symptoms before evaluating a potentially toxic ingestion.
questions.difficultyReason: Distinguish the named antidote from a decontamination agent and antidotes for other exposures.

options.text: N-acetylcysteine.
options.reason: N-acetylcysteine supports detoxification of the toxic acetaminophen metabolite and is the antidote used when indicated.

options.text: Activated charcoal.
options.reason: Charcoal is selected gastrointestinal decontamination in some exposures; it is not the acetaminophen antidote.

options.text: Naloxone.
options.reason: Naloxone reverses opioid effects, not acetaminophen toxicity.

options.text: Calcium gluconate.
options.reason: Calcium gluconate is used for selected electrolyte and toxicologic indications, including magnesium toxicity, not as the acetaminophen antidote.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Umbilical cord prolapse.
questions.stem: During orientation, a nurse asks why the presenting part is manually elevated when an umbilical cord prolapse occurs. Which explanation best describes the purpose of this temporary bedside maneuver?
questions.clue: A compressed cord threatens the fetal circulation.
questions.rationale: Understanding the mechanism explains why relief must be maintained during emergency preparation and transfer until a safe handoff or birth. The team prepares definitive delivery in parallel.
questions.difficultyReason: Explain the mechanism of a specified emergency maneuver rather than choose between competing emergencies.

options.text: Relieve pressure on the cord so fetal blood flow can continue while urgent birth is arranged.
options.reason: Compression can interrupt fetal circulation. Decompression is a bridge to definitive delivery, not a treatment that eliminates the emergency.

options.text: Push the cord back into the uterus so normal labor can resume.
options.reason: The goal is pressure relief, not repeatedly manipulating or replacing the cord.

options.text: Increase uterine contractions to shorten the first stage of labor.
options.reason: Increasing contractions can worsen cord compression and is not the purpose of elevation.

options.text: Reduce fetal oxygen demand by preventing further descent during contractions.
options.reason: Elevation relieves mechanical pressure on the prolapsed cord; it does not reduce fetal oxygen demand.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Abruptio placentae.
questions.stem: A patient at 34 weeks is admitted after blunt abdominal trauma. BP is 110/70 mmHg, compared with 138/86 on arrival; pulse has risen from 88 to 116/min. The patient reports constant abdominal pain, the uterus stays firm, and recurrent late decelerations have appeared. No vaginal bleeding is seen. A colleague suggests waiting for ultrasound before activating hemorrhage resources. Which response is best?
questions.clue: Several trends deteriorate together despite absent vaginal bleeding and a systolic BP still above 90.
questions.rationale: Prioritize the combined maternal-fetal pattern. Concealed hemorrhage can be substantial before profound hypotension or visible blood appears. Activate the appropriate team, ensure IV readiness, and reassess response while clinicians determine definitive management.
questions.difficultyReason: Integrate maternal and fetal trends despite absent external bleeding and a deceptively normal-range systolic BP.

options.text: Escalate the clinical pattern now and prepare maternal resuscitation and urgent obstetric care while diagnostic assessment proceeds.
options.reason: Relative BP decline, tachycardia, uterine findings, and fetal deterioration suggest concealed abruption. Visible bleeding and imaging confirmation are not required before escalation.

options.text: Continue monitoring until the systolic BP is below 90 mmHg, then activate hemorrhage resources.
options.reason: Waiting for an absolute hypotension cutoff ignores a concerning trend and can delay care while compensation is failing.

options.text: Prioritize ultrasound confirmation before IV preparation because the current systolic BP is within the usual range.
options.reason: Imaging can inform care but must not delay assessment and resuscitation for clinical deterioration.

options.text: Address the late decelerations with position change alone and postpone maternal reassessment until the tracing improves.
options.reason: Repositioning can occur promptly, but the concurrent maternal pattern requires coordinated reassessment and preparation, not fetal-only treatment.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Operative vaginal birth: trauma, lacerations and hematoma.
questions.stem: After an assisted vaginal birth, a patient reports increasing deep perineal pressure. The fundus is firm, a straight catheter has just drained the bladder, and lochia remains small. Pulse rises from 82 to 112/min. Another nurse offers a choice of interventions. Which should the primary nurse prioritize?
questions.clue: The usual atony and bladder explanations do not fit the stated assessments.
questions.rationale: Reassess the likely source when findings conflict with the routine postpartum pathway. Evaluate pain location, tissue swelling, and perfusion while obtaining prompt obstetric review and preparing indicated hemorrhage care.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner integrates assisted birth, increasing deep pressure, scant visible bleeding, and rising pulse, but the firm fundus and just-emptied bladder explicitly remove the two principal alternatives. That is intermediate focused application, not a level-3 reconciliation of genuinely competing evidence.

options.text: Assess the perineum and perfusion and promptly notify the obstetric clinician about possible concealed genital-tract bleeding.
options.reason: Focal pressure and an increasing pulse despite a firm uterus and empty bladder suggest a hematoma or other trauma-related bleeding.

options.text: Repeat bladder catheterization because urinary retention is the most likely cause of postpartum pressure.
options.reason: The bladder was just emptied. Repeating the intervention does not address the new pain and circulation trend.

options.text: Massage the fundus continuously while waiting to see whether the pressure improves.
options.reason: A firm uterus makes atony less likely. Fundal massage alone will not treat a concealed hematoma.

options.text: Give the next prescribed oral analgesic and reassess only after its expected peak effect.
options.reason: Analgesia may be needed, but waiting for its effect would delay evaluation of a possible hemorrhagic complication.

questions.objective: Reconsider an earlier successful route when recurrent symptoms conflict with a standing order
questions.stem: A 3-hour-old infant of a parent with diabetes had an initial low glucose that improved after feeding. The infant now has recurrent apnea, a weak suck, and a bedside glucose of 28 mg/dL. Airway support is underway, but a standing feeding order remains active. What should the nurse advocate for next?
questions.clue: The earlier route worked under different conditions; current apnea and weak suck now conflict with the standing oral order.
questions.rationale: The nurse must reassess both treatment effectiveness and route safety. This infant has recurrent symptomatic hypoglycemia and can no longer feed safely, so airway support continues while oral feeding is withheld and the neonatal IV-glucose pathway is activated immediately. Confirmation and cause evaluation may occur concurrently, and gel may be used only as a team- or protocol-directed bridge rather than as a reason to delay parenteral rescue.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies symptomatic hypoglycemia and a now-unsafe oral route to interrupt a standing feeding order and activate immediate IV rescue. The prior feeding response adds context, but the current cues align rather than create a genuinely competing advanced decision.

options.text: Withhold oral feeding, continue airway support, and activate the neonatal plan for immediate IV glucose and reassessment.
options.reason: The infant is now symptomatic and cannot feed safely. The earlier response to feeding does not justify reusing that route when apnea, weak suck, and recurrent low glucose require immediate parenteral rescue and neonatal reassessment.

options.text: Repeat the standing oral feeding, continue airway support, and check whether glucose improves as it did previously.
options.reason: The infant's route safety has changed. Repeating the formerly effective feed despite apnea and weak suck risks aspiration and delays the immediate treatment needed for symptomatic hypoglycemia.

options.text: Obtain laboratory confirmation, maintain airway support, and wait for the result before changing the treatment route.
options.reason: Laboratory confirmation can proceed according to the pathway, but acute treatment should not wait in a symptomatic newborn with a documented low bedside value and unsafe oral route.

options.text: Use dextrose gel as the only rescue, keep the feeding order active, and reconsider IV treatment after another low value.
options.reason: Gel may be a protocol-directed temporary bridge while IV access is obtained, but it should not be the sole plan that delays IV therapy for symptomatic hypoglycemia or preserves an unsafe feeding order.

questions.objective: Reconcile an LNG handout with a UPA-specific combined-pill restart and follow-up plan
questions.stem: A patient took ulipristal today after intercourse without contraception four days ago. The patient has an eligible combined-pill prescription but has not restarted it. The handout is labeled levonorgestrel and says, 'Restart hormonal contraception today; use backup for seven days.' The nurse is correcting the written plan using CDC guidance. Which instructions belong in that plan? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: The medicine taken is UPA; both the restart instruction and the meaning of an early negative test depend on timing.
questions.rationale: Reconcile the medication name with the written instructions and have the patient explain the revised plan back. Do not use the immediate LNG restart instruction for UPA or let an early negative test provide false reassurance. Specify the method, delay, backup endpoint and follow-up clearly. Condom use may still be indicated for STI prevention beyond the pregnancy-backup period.
questions.difficultyReason: Apply product-specific teaching and testing limitations to the supplied mismatch. Merely presenting a wrong handout does not by itself establish advanced reasoning.

options.text: Restart the combined pill no sooner than five days after today's ulipristal dose.
options.reason: Starting progestin-containing contraception too soon can interfere with UPA's effect. The combined-pill prescription does not remove the delay.

options.text: Use a combined vaginal ring today instead of pills to avoid the hormonal restart interaction.
options.reason: A combined ring also contains hormones covered by the restart guidance; changing the delivery route does not remove the interaction.

options.text: Use condoms or abstain during the delay, then for seven days after restart or until the next menses, whichever occurs first.
options.reason: Protection is needed during the delay and after restart. The post-restart instruction retains CDC's earlier-next-menses qualification.

options.text: Arrange pregnancy testing if no withdrawal bleed occurs within three weeks after today's ulipristal dose.
options.reason: The three-week follow-up is anchored to EC use. Lack of bleeding warrants testing rather than assuming treatment succeeded.

options.text: Use a negative urine pregnancy test today to exclude pregnancy from intercourse four days ago.
options.reason: A test today cannot exclude pregnancy arising from very recent intercourse. It does not replace the later follow-up plan.

questions.objective: Resolve discordant postoperative report and behavior with fear
questions.stem: A 4-year-old who was calm before surgery now guards the incision and refuses to cough or move. The child can communicate by pointing and speaking but says, "It does not hurt," after hearing an adult say that reporting pain could mean another injection. A caregiver asks the nurse to accept the answer. Which approach best guides the next care decision?
questions.clue: The child's denial follows an injection threat and conflicts with new guarding and refusal to move.
questions.rationale: The nurse should not choose between the child's words and observed behavior as if either were automatically conclusive. The stated injection fear can suppress reporting, so it should be explored with honest, concrete language. A self-report method suited to the child's abilities remains important, while guarding, function, caregiver observations, and other assessment findings provide additional context. Findings guide the existing ordered plan, and pain is reassessed after intervention. The scenario does not establish dishonesty, a numeric pain intensity, a medication route, or a dose.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate discordant self-report, postoperative behavior, functional change, a specific fear, caregiver pressure, and the need for reassessment. That competing-cue reasoning supports a provisional advanced estimate.

options.text: Clarify the injection fear, obtain self-report with a suitable tool, include guarding as additional evidence, and reassess after ordered care.
options.reason: The denial, behavior, and stated fear conflict. Clarifying the fear preserves the child's voice while a developmentally appropriate tool and behavioral evidence support assessment and later reassessment.

options.text: Score the guarding with a behavioral tool and use that score in place of asking the child again because fear makes self-report unreliable.
options.reason: Behavior is important additional evidence, but it should not automatically replace usable self-report. The nurse should explore how the injection concern affected the answer.

options.text: Document the no-pain statement, interpret guarding as an expected postoperative behavior, and defer another pain assessment until routine rounding.
options.reason: Expected postoperative discomfort does not resolve the discrepancy. New guarding, movement refusal, and fear-linked denial warrant timely clarification and assessment.

options.text: Ask the caregiver to estimate the pain, treat that estimate as the main report, and avoid discussing the injection concern with the child.
options.reason: A caregiver can contribute observations, but proxy judgment should not displace a communicative child's account or leave the known fear unexplored.

questions.objective: Negotiate independence after skill success but inconsistent use
questions.stem: A 15-year-old correctly self-administers a prescribed once-daily medication. The written plan permits self-administration during overnight visits only when the medication stays in its original labeled container and is taken at the prescribed evening time; any timing change requires prescriber review. The supply is available, but the adolescent missed four of the last six sleepover doses because friends might notice. The caregiver wants to give every dose, while the adolescent wants no check-ins. No acute symptoms are present. Which plan best addresses the evidence?
questions.clue: Technical performance is correct, but adherence fails in a defined peer setting under explicit medication timing and storage constraints.
questions.rationale: One correct demonstration establishes ability, not dependable self-management across settings. The nurse should assess the adolescent's specific peer concern, include the adolescent and caregiver in a feasible plan, keep transport and timing within the written treatment requirements, and use proportionate verification until reliability improves. A generic reminder misses the named barrier, moving the dose requires prescriber review, and imposing an outside supervisor without discussion can undermine participation. The case supplies no missed-dose instruction and does not authorize a regimen change.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner integrates demonstrated skill, repeated real-world failure, peer visibility, opposing autonomy preferences, and treatment-specific timing and storage constraints. Those competing considerations support a provisional advanced estimate.

options.text: Explore the peer concern, then use labeled transport, a reminder, and short-term caregiver confirmation within the written plan; reassess reliability.
options.reason: The adolescent has the technical skill but not reliable implementation in the identified setting. A negotiated, time-limited support plan addresses the barrier while respecting the stated storage and timing constraints.

options.text: Keep independent administration, add a phone reminder, and review at the next routine visit because the correct demonstration shows readiness.
options.reason: The demonstration proves technique, not reliable use at sleepovers. A reminder alone does not assess the stated peer concern, and the recent pattern warrants nearer follow-up and proportionate support.

options.text: Move the prescribed evening medication to the afternoon on overnight days so the caregiver can administer it before departure.
options.reason: Advancing the prescribed evening time without prescriber review violates the written plan and transfers the task instead of building reliable self-management within its constraints.

options.text: Keep the prescribed timing and use the friend's parent as the dose supervisor at every overnight visit, then review adherence at the next appointment.
options.reason: Adult verification may sometimes be appropriate, but making a friend's parent the standing supervisor does not explore the adolescent's preferences and can intensify the stated peer-visibility barrier.

questions.objective: Distinguish improving post-treatment itch from new infestation evidence
questions.stem: Two weeks after completing the prescribed scabies treatment, a child's original lesions are healing, itching is less intense, and no new burrows or rash are present. Household contacts completed coordinated treatment. The caregiver asks whether another application should be given today because nighttime itching remains. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: Every objective trend is improving: old lesions are healing, itch is less intense, contacts were treated, and no new burrows or rash are present.
questions.rationale: Persistent itching can continue for several weeks after scabies treatment and is not, by itself, evidence of live mites or treatment failure. The child's improving lesions, decreasing itch and lack of new burrows or rash support following the existing aftercare plan rather than adding an unprescribed application. Reassessment remains appropriate if new lesions appear, symptoms worsen, or itching persists beyond the expected period. The response neither promises permanent cure nor assigns a definite cause to residual itching.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a longitudinal but aligned improvement pattern to avoid overtreatment while retaining conditional follow-up, supporting level 2 rather than level 3.

options.text: Do not add an unprescribed application today; continue directed aftercare and seek reassessment for new lesions or prolonged symptoms.
options.reason: Residual itching can continue for several weeks despite successful treatment. Healing lesions, improvement and no new burrows support monitoring without an extra application, while new or persistent findings still require reassessment.

options.text: Request a different scabies medication now because residual nighttime itching means the first plan failed.
options.reason: Itching at two weeks does not by itself establish treatment failure, especially when lesions are healing and no new burrows or rash are present.

options.text: Wait for a new burrow before seeking reassessment, even if the itching stops improving over the next several weeks.
options.reason: New burrows are not the only reason for follow-up. Itching that persists beyond the expected post-treatment period or symptoms that worsen also warrant reassessment.

options.text: Repeat the prior application today because treated contacts make extra dosing unlikely to cause harm.
options.reason: Completed contact treatment reduces one transmission pathway but does not authorize an extra medication application or establish that unprescribed use is harmless.

questions.objective: Interpret perfusion improvement despite continuing stool losses
questions.stem: A toddler hospitalized with acute infectious diarrhea received a prescribed isotonic IV bolus for poor perfusion. The child is now alert and warm with capillary refill of 2 seconds, tolerates small sips of oral rehydration solution without vomiting, and then passes a large watery stool. The ongoing-fluid order directs replacement of measured losses by the currently tolerated route. The caregiver asks whether the stool means the bolus failed. Which response and plan are best?
questions.clue: The perfusion target improved, while a new stool creates a separate replacement need.
questions.rationale: Explain that the IV bolus treated poor perfusion rather than stopping the diarrheal illness. The child's alertness, warmth, and capillary refill indicate improvement, but the new stool is an ongoing fluid loss. Continue reassessment and replace measured losses according to the existing order and current oral tolerance, changing route only when the clinical status, tolerance, or team plan requires it. No universal repeat-bolus rule or fluid dose is inferred.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner distinguishes a favorable resuscitation response from continued disease losses and applies current oral tolerance to the ordered replacement route. All findings align and no competing cue, linked calculation, or failed response is present, so level 2 is more appropriate than the historical level 3.

options.text: Explain that circulation improved; reassess hydration and replace the measured stool loss with ordered oral rehydration while tolerated.
options.reason: Alertness, warmth, and improved capillary refill show a favorable perfusion response. Diarrhea can continue after resuscitation, so the nurse should reassess and replace the new measured loss using the ordered route the child currently tolerates.

options.text: Request another rapid IV bolus now because the large stool shows that the initial resuscitation was incomplete.
options.reason: A new stool represents an ongoing loss, not proof that the circulation failed to respond. Another rapid bolus should depend on reassessment of perfusion and hydration rather than stool occurrence alone.

options.text: Continue the maintenance plan without separate loss replacement because the improved perfusion findings show adequate hydration.
options.reason: Current improvement does not prevent a new deficit if losses continue. The order distinguishes maintenance from replacement of measured ongoing losses, so reassessment and replacement remain necessary.

options.text: Use IV replacement for the stool loss despite current oral tolerance because the initial response followed IV therapy.
options.reason: The route for initial resuscitation does not automatically determine the route for subsequent losses. The child currently tolerates oral rehydration, and the order directs use of the tolerated route with reassessment if that changes.

questions.objective: Reconcile apparent visual improvement with rising bilirubin and weaker feeding
questions.stem: A 38-week infant with a positive direct antiglobulin test is receiving phototherapy under an age-in-hours and risk-adjusted plan. The skin appears less yellow, but a repeat serum bilirubin has risen and feeding is weaker. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Visual appearance conflicts with both an objective serum trend and a new functional finding during treatment.
questions.rationale: Treatment response is assessed with serial serum bilirubin measurements and the infant's clinical state, not skin appearance alone. The nurse should report the rising value and weaker feeding, continue and verify ordered phototherapy, reassess feeding safety, and examine for neurologic change. A positive DAT identifies antibody coating but does not independently prove hemolysis severity or establish an exchange threshold, and a third value is not required before reporting the current change.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner reconciles discordant visual, laboratory, and functional cues during active treatment and separates appropriate reassessment from premature threshold escalation and unsupported delay, supporting provisional level 3.

options.text: Report the rising serum bilirubin and weaker feeding promptly to the neonatal team.
options.reason: The objective treatment-response trend and new functional change warrant prompt team reassessment even though the infant looks less yellow.

options.text: Continue ordered phototherapy while verifying that prescribed light delivery and skin exposure are being provided.
options.reason: Phototherapy effectiveness depends on treatment delivery. The nurse should continue the current order while checking that the prescribed therapy is actually reaching the infant during reassessment.

options.text: Perform a focused assessment of feeding effectiveness and current ability to feed safely.
options.reason: Weaker feeding is a new functional change that can affect intake and may accompany worsening illness. It requires direct reassessment rather than attribution to appearance or treatment routine.

options.text: Assess for neurologic changes in arousal, tone, cry, and posture while escalation is being considered.
options.reason: A focused neurologic reassessment helps identify clinical deterioration that must be integrated with the measured bilirubin trend and feeding change.

options.text: Begin exchange-transfusion preparation because a positive test and rising bilirubin establish that threshold treatment has failed.
options.reason: A positive direct antiglobulin test does not by itself prove the degree of hemolysis, and a rising value alone does not establish an exchange indication. The team must compare measurements with age, gestation, risk factors, trajectory, thresholds, and clinical status.

options.text: Wait for a third serum value before reporting because three measurements are needed to identify a treatment trend.
options.reason: Serial values support trajectory assessment, but the current rise and weaker feeding already justify prompt reporting. Requiring a third value would create an unsupported delay.

questions.evidenceFamily: contextual hereditary-cancer result interpretation before risk-plan change
questions.objective: Interpret a negative hereditary-cancer panel in its family-testing context before changing an existing family-history-based surveillance plan.
questions.stem: An adult with no personal history of breast or ovarian cancer receives the result of a multigene hereditary-cancer panel. Her mother and maternal aunt have had breast cancer, and her maternal grandmother had ovarian cancer. No relative with cancer has undergone genetic testing, and no familial pathogenic variant is known. The panel detected no pathogenic variant. She has no new symptoms and asks the nurse to cancel the family-history-based surveillance plan her specialist previously arranged. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: Ask what a negative result establishes when the test was not aimed at a pathogenic variant already identified in the family, then connect that limit to the requested plan change.
questions.rationale: The panel did not identify a pathogenic variant, but no family variant had first been established. In an unaffected person from a strongly affected family, this result does not exclude all inherited or familial risk. The existing family-history-based plan should therefore remain in place while the genetics and clinical teams interpret the result and discuss whether testing an affected relative could clarify the family's risk. If a pathogenic variant had already been established in the family and targeted testing showed that the patient did not inherit it, the family-variant interpretation would differ, although overall cancer risk would not be zero.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate a negative multigene result with a strong breast-and-ovarian-cancer family pattern and the absence of a previously identified familial pathogenic variant, then choose among premature relaxation, suspension pending more testing, rigid history-only continuation, and conditional preservation of the existing plan. No single cue establishes both the result's meaning and the immediate care consequence.

options.text: Keep the plan pending genetics interpretation; the negative panel does not erase the family-history concern, and affected-relative testing may clarify risk.
options.reason: This response uses all three decision-changing facts: the broad panel is negative, the family pattern remains concerning, and no family variant exists against which the patient's result can be interpreted as targeted noninheritance. It preserves the clinician-directed plan while the result and possible affected-relative testing are reviewed.

options.text: Ask the specialist to use population-level surveillance now; the negative panel makes the family cancer pattern less relevant to ongoing planning.
options.reason: A negative panel is most useful for excluding a specific inherited variant when that variant is already known in the family. Here no familial variant has been established, so the negative result does not by itself remove the family-history-based concern or justify lowering the plan.

options.text: Pause the current plan until an affected relative completes testing; risk-based surveillance should wait until a familial variant is identified.
options.reason: Testing an affected relative may improve family interpretation, but current guidance does not make ongoing family-history-based follow-up contingent on first finding a familial variant. Suspending the existing plan would discard the strong family history during the period of uncertainty.

options.text: Keep the current plan without genetics review; family history already determines future surveillance, so testing an affected relative would add little.
options.reason: Family history continues to guide risk-based follow-up, but the negative result still requires contextual interpretation and affected-relative testing may make the family's result more informative. Treating the current plan as fixed would ignore information that could legitimately change later planning.

questions.objective: Recognize jaundice in the first 24 hours as a trigger for prompt objective bilirubin measurement.
questions.stem: At 8 hours after birth, the nurse notes yellowing of the face and sclera in an alert 39-week newborn. Vital signs are stable, feeding is effective, and no bilirubin measurement has been obtained. Which action should the nurse take?
questions.clue: Jaundice has been observed before 24 hours of age, when current guidance calls for prompt objective bilirubin measurement even if the newborn otherwise appears well.
questions.rationale: Obtain a TcB or TSB measurement as soon as possible and document the time jaundice was first observed. Current AAP guidance specifically directs prompt measured assessment when jaundice is noted before 24 hours because an identifiable cause is often hemolytic and missing significant early hemolysis can be harmful. The finding is a surveillance trigger, not proof of hemolysis and not an automatic phototherapy order. Visual assessment supplements rather than replaces objective bilirubin screening.
questions.difficultyReason: One explicit observation maps directly to one current-guidance action: jaundice noted at 8 hours of age requires a prompt TcB or TSB measurement. The learner does not calculate a threshold, interpret a DAT, compare serial values, choose treatment, or integrate competing cues. The two cue-removal entries below only define when this early-onset rule applies; they are not offered as Level 3 branches.

options.text: Obtain a TcB or TSB measurement promptly and document when the jaundice was first observed.
options.reason: Jaundice noted before 24 hours is a direct current-guidance trigger for bilirubin measurement as soon as possible; the otherwise reassuring assessment does not remove that trigger.

options.text: Continue visual checks and obtain bilirubin at the routine universal screening time instead of measuring it now.
options.reason: Routine universal screening remains important, but jaundice already observed before 24 hours requires a prompt measurement rather than waiting for the ordinary screening time.

options.text: Begin phototherapy immediately because jaundice before 24 hours confirms a hemolytic disorder.
options.reason: Early jaundice raises concern for hemolysis but does not prove its cause or establish a treatment indication. Treatment decisions require objective bilirubin assessment and the applicable clinical context.

options.text: Obtain a DAT first and measure bilirubin only if the DAT result is positive.
options.reason: A DAT can be indicated in selected etiologic evaluations, but the observed early jaundice itself triggers prompt bilirubin measurement. A DAT result is not a prerequisite for measuring bilirubin.

questions.objective: Select a person-centered emergency-contraception access plan when the patient's preferred continuing copper-IUD option and an immediately available pill follow different access paths.
questions.stem: A patient arrives 96 hours after the first and only episode of intercourse without contraception this cycle. She wants emergency contraception and ongoing pregnancy prevention. After assessment, the clinician confirms that UPA and a copper IUD are medically appropriate and time-valid today. The current clinic can provide UPA until it closes in 90 minutes but cannot place an IUD. A referral clinic may have a cancellation for copper-IUD placement within the next four hours and will confirm availability within 30 minutes; the patient can attend if a slot is secured. After counseling, she says, "I would rather use one method for today's need and ongoing contraception, but I do not want to leave today without emergency contraception." Which plan should the nurse coordinate?
questions.clue: Treat a possible device opening as unresolved access while preserving the patient's opportunity to choose an available time-valid method.
questions.rationale: At 96 hours, both clinician-approved methods remain within their current emergency-contraception timing windows, and same-day copper-IUD placement would also provide continuing contraception. The patient has expressed two priorities rather than dictating the operational sequence: she favors one dual-purpose method but does not accept the risk of leaving without emergency contraception. Because the referral can resolve its same-day availability before the current clinic closes, the nurse can keep the UPA pathway available while confirming whether the preferred device is genuinely accessible. If the slot is secured, the patient can select the clinician-approved copper-IUD path; if not, the nurse should return to the informed UPA option before current access closes. Giving UPA before the callback and adding the copper IUD if placement opens is permissible for an eligible patient, but it commits this patient to two methods when a short access check can preserve both single-method paths and her stated preference.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must manage two time-valid, clinician-approved methods while actual access to the preferred dual-purpose method remains provisional. The patient's two priorities compete: avoid a separate ongoing method if same-day device placement is real, yet avoid leaving the encounter without emergency contraception. The learner must sequence a bounded access check while preserving the available pill fallback and return the final choice to the patient. Removing possible same-day device access selects the pill pathway; omitting the patient's stated priorities removes the unique basis for the contingent plan; replacing them with an informed preference for UPA selects the pill pathway even if device access becomes available.

options.text: Keep UPA available while confirming today's IUD opening; if placement is secured, coordinate the preferred dual-purpose method, otherwise revisit UPA before clinic closure.
options.reason: The 30-minute access check can finish while the current clinic's UPA pathway remains available. This sequence turns a possible device opening into a verified option, protects against leaving without emergency contraception, and lets the patient choose using actual access information rather than an assumed appointment.

options.text: Coordinate UPA use now and end the referral search; confirmed pill access meets today's need while ongoing contraception is addressed at follow-up.
options.reason: This is a safe fallback if same-day device access is unavailable or if the patient selects UPA. In the actual case, the referral can clarify access before UPA availability closes, so committing now would discard the patient's dual-purpose preference without first resolving the feasible access question.

options.text: Send the patient to the referral clinic without confirmation and return UPA to stock; possible device access and the dual-purpose goal favor that pathway.
options.reason: The dual-purpose preference matters, but a possible cancellation is not actual placement access. Releasing the confirmed pill pathway before the referral answers could leave the patient without either time-valid method, contrary to the second priority she stated.

options.text: Coordinate UPA use now but keep the referral inquiry active; if copper-IUD placement opens, use the device today for ongoing contraception as well.
options.reason: Current guidance permits starting a nonhormonal contraceptive method after UPA, so this is not a contraindicated sequence. It nevertheless commits to two methods before the access question resolves, contrary to the patient's stated one-method preference, even though UPA remains available during the callback.

questions.objective: Integrate an indicated neonatal resuscitation maneuver with temporary protected positioning for an open myelomeningocele.
questions.stem: A 32-week newborn with an open lumbar myelomeningocele is apneic and positioned side-lying under a radiant warmer. The sac membrane is intact and covered with the prescribed sterile, moist, nonadherent dressing. During face-mask ventilation, the team has corrected airway position and mask seal, used a two-handed mask hold, cleared visible secretions, and adjusted inflation pressure. The chest still does not move, and the ECG heart rate remains 80/min without increasing. The unit has no laryngeal mask approved for this newborn's gestational age. A protocol-specified foam mattress with a cut-out that keeps the defect free from pressure is ready. Which action should the nurse take?
questions.clue: Ventilation remains ineffective after corrective steps, so an alternative airway is needed; the open lesion requires the directly supported temporary cut-out setup rather than ordinary supine contact.
questions.rationale: Use the cut-out foam mattress for temporary supine positioning, assist with endotracheal intubation and ventilation, and resume side-lying protection when supine access is no longer needed. Current AHA/AAP guidance makes effective ventilation the priority and supports placement of an alternative airway when the heart rate remains below 100/min and does not increase after ventilation; the stem closes the laryngeal-mask route for this specific 32-week newborn. A current Sydney Children's Hospitals Network guideline states that when supine positioning is unavoidable for urgent intubation of a neonate with myelomeningocele, a foam mattress with a cut-out should be used temporarily. The same guideline and current NHSGGC guidance preserve prone or side-lying positioning as the default because pressure on the defect and exposed neural tissue must be avoided. A heart rate of 80/min does not yet supply the current chest-compression trigger, so the immediate problem is ineffective ventilation rather than a compression decision.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must respond to two independent constraints that change the preferred option. Persistent ineffective face-mask ventilation with a heart rate below 100/min requires an alternative airway, while the open lumbar lesion makes standard flat-surface supine positioning unsafe. Removing only the documented ventilation failure leaves continued protected face-mask ventilation and reassessment as the preferred plan; removing only the lesion facts leaves standard supine positioning for intubation. The current 2025 myelomeningocele guideline directly supports a temporary cut-out foam mattress for unavoidable supine urgent intubation, so the combined decision no longer depends on a fictional apparatus assertion.

options.text: Use the cut-out mattress for temporary supine positioning, assist with endotracheal intubation, and resume side-lying when supine access is no longer needed.
options.reason: This plan addresses both constraints with a directly supported setup: ineffective corrected mask ventilation prompts an alternative airway, and the temporary cut-out mattress prevents ordinary supine pressure on the open defect before protected positioning resumes.

options.text: Keep the newborn side-lying and continue face-mask ventilation with chest-movement and heart-rate reassessment instead of placing an alternative airway.
options.reason: This preserves lesion protection and would fit a case without documented failure of mask ventilation. Here, chest movement and heart-rate improvement remain absent after the corrective sequence, so continuing the same interface delays the indicated alternative airway.

options.text: Move the newborn to standard supine airway position on the flat warmer and assist with endotracheal intubation and ventilation.
options.reason: This promptly addresses ineffective ventilation and would fit a newborn without a posterior open lesion. In this case, the flat surface omits the temporary cut-out protection that current myelomeningocele guidance specifies when urgent supine intubation is unavoidable.

options.text: Use the cut-out mattress for supine intubation and keep the newborn supine after effective ventilation to minimize handling of the secured tube.
options.reason: The supported cut-out setup makes necessary supine intubation possible, but the exception is temporary. Once supine access is no longer required, airway-device handling can be coordinated while returning to the default pressure-avoiding prone or side-lying position.

questions.objective: Identify and clarify an unresolved oxytocin order, concentration, and pump-history discrepancy before possible resumption.
questions.stem: During a labor-unit handoff, oxytocin remains paused while the nurse completes the required medication reconciliation. The patient-specific active order is oxytocin 6 milliunits/min by smart pump, with calculated rates rounded to the nearest whole mL/hr. The obstetric clinician has documented that resumption at the active ordered dose may proceed after reconciliation; no titration is requested, and the current maternal, fetal, and contraction assessments meet this patient's prescribed continuation parameters. The earlier bag was labeled oxytocin 20 units in 500 mL. Its pump history shows 9 mL/hr from 1045 to 1100 and 12 mL/hr from 1100 until the pause at 1115. The medication record and active order show 6 milliunits/min throughout, with no dose-change entry. A pharmacy-issued replacement bag, already authorized for this patient, is labeled oxytocin 15 units in 500 mL. The incoming handoff proposes 12 mL/hr. Unit policy requires any unexplained order, label, medication-record, or pump-history mismatch to be clarified before administration. Which recommendation should the nurse make?
questions.clue: A current-only calculation reconciles the replacement bag with the active order, but the required check also includes the earlier bag, pump history, and unchanged dose record.
questions.rationale: Keep the infusion paused and use the supplied unit clarification process to resolve the unexplained pump-history entry with the responsible practitioner or staff before administration. The earlier concentration was 40 milliunits/mL: 9 mL/hr delivered 6 milliunits/min, but 12 mL/hr delivered 8 milliunits/min. The replacement concentration is 30 milliunits/mL, so the proposed 12 mL/hr would deliver the ordered 6 milliunits/min. That correct current calculation does not resolve why the earlier history shows an 8-milliunit/min exposure while the order and medication record remained at 6. This case does not establish a general resumption or titration rule.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must calculate both concentrations, reconstruct two delivered dose-rates from the pump history, calculate the proposed replacement-bag dose, and reconcile those results with an unchanged active order and medication record. The proposed 12 mL/hr is correct for the replacement concentration, so a current-only check supports the plausible nonkey; only the linked historical calculation exposes the unresolved discrepancy that keeps administration paused. Literal omission of a required record makes the evidence incomplete, while omission of the discrepant interval changes the decision only when the remaining history is explicitly known to be complete.

options.text: Keep the infusion paused and clarify the history; 12 mL/hr matches 6 milliunits/min now but previously delivered 8 milliunits/min.
options.reason: The replacement bag contains 30 milliunits/mL, making 12 mL/hr equal 6 milliunits/min. The earlier bag contained 40 milliunits/mL, so its 12 mL/hr history equals 8 milliunits/min and conflicts with the unchanged 6-milliunit/min order and medication record. The supplied unit process requires that discrepancy to be clarified before administration.

options.text: Complete the reconciliation and prepare 12 mL/hr for possible resumption because the replacement bag delivers the active 6 milliunits/min dose.
options.reason: The replacement-bag calculation is correct, which makes this a plausible current-only conclusion. It is still unsafe under the supplied policy because reconciliation is not complete while the earlier 8-milliunit/min pump interval remains unexplained against the unchanged 6-milliunit/min order and medication record.

options.text: Keep the infusion paused and correct the proposed rate because this replacement bag would deliver 8 milliunits/min at 12 mL/hr.
options.reason: This applies the earlier bag's 40-milliunit/mL concentration to the replacement bag. The replacement contains 15,000 milliunits in 500 mL, or 30 milliunits/mL; at 12 mL/hr it delivers 360 milliunits/hr, which equals 6 milliunits/min.

options.text: Program 9 mL/hr because retaining the previously correct volume rate prevents a dose change when the concentration changes.
options.reason: Volume rate cannot be carried across a concentration change. With 30 milliunits/mL in the replacement bag, 9 mL/hr delivers 270 milliunits/hr, or 4.5 milliunits/min, rather than the ordered 6 milliunits/min.

questions.objective: Recognize why one glucose measurement cannot substitute for serial evidence within an already indicated newborn monitoring pathway.
questions.stem: A clinically well term newborn of a parent with gestational diabetes is already enrolled in the nursery's glucose-monitoring pathway. The pathway documented for this case calls for a series of measurements during transition. After the first feeding, the first bedside glucose result meets the pathway's current goal. Which interpretation of that result is most accurate?
questions.clue: Only one time point is available; a trend describes what happens across multiple time points.
questions.rationale: Document the first result as one reassuring point within the supplied monitoring pathway. It cannot establish whether glucose remains within the pathway goal across transition because no later measurements are available. The item does not ask whether this newborn qualified for screening, whether monitoring can stop, or which treatment route to use. No universal glucose value, testing count, interval, duration, or stopping rule is implied.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner recognizes one direct measurement principle: a single glucose result is one point, not a serial transition pattern. Pathway entry, clinical stability, and the need for a series are supplied, and no care-plan, stopping, treatment-route, or threshold decision is required. This is estimated Level 1 foundational recognition.

options.text: Treat it as one point in the series; it does not establish transition over time by itself.
options.reason: A single result describes one moment. The supplied pathway calls for serial measurements, so later results are needed before the record can show a pattern across transition.

options.text: Treat it as a stable transition pattern because this first postfeeding result meets the pathway's current goal.
options.reason: Meeting the goal at one postfeeding check is reassuring for that point, but one value cannot show that the result will remain stable over later checks.

options.text: Treat it as evidence that feeding will maintain the pathway goal through the remainder of the transition.
options.reason: The measurement follows one feeding, but it does not establish the effect of later feeds or the glucose pattern through the rest of transition.

options.text: Treat it as the newborn's established baseline because the newborn remains clinically well during this single measurement.
options.reason: Clinical well-being is important, but it does not turn one point measurement into an established longitudinal baseline or transition pattern.

questions.objective: Reassess a hyperemesis plan after treatment when improved nausea-vomiting symptoms conflict with persistent inadequate oral intake and continuing weight loss.
questions.stem: At 11 weeks, a patient returns to an ambulatory pregnancy day unit for a second visit after community measures did not control hyperemesis symptoms. The clinician-prescribed day-unit treatment has been tolerated. The same validated HELP assessment used before treatment now shows substantial improvement, and the patient reports much less nausea and retching. However, since the prior visit the patient has retained only occasional sips and no meal. Weights measured on the same calibrated clinic scale across the last three visits continue downward, with further loss today. The patient is alert, vital signs are stable, and assessment identifies no new pain, bleeding, fever, syncope, or separate acute complication. The team is considering discharge back to the community plan. Which recommendation should the nurse make?
questions.clue: The symptom-response measure is improving, but oral intake and the comparable weight series show that physiologic and nutritional recovery are not yet aligned with symptom relief.
questions.rationale: Preserve the symptom-control component that is producing a measured response, but postpone discharge and bring the persistent oral-intake failure and downward weight trajectory to the team for reassessment of intake support and the appropriate care setting. Current RCOG guidance treats validated symptom response, ability to eat and drink, examination, weight, and other objective findings as related but distinct parts of reassessment; improved nausea and retching do not establish adequate oral nutrition or hydration. Stable observations make this a plan-reassessment problem rather than a supplied emergency sequence. Urinary ketones are not used because the same guidance rejects ketonuria as a dehydration or severity indicator and as a basis for hydration or treatment decisions. That exclusion does not rule out a separately supported metabolic illness.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must reconcile improvement in a validated symptom-response measure with continued failure of oral intake and a worsening serial weight trajectory after treatment. The first domain supports preserving the current symptom-control component; the other two prevent discharge and require reassessment of intake support and care setting. Stable observations remove a separately controlling emergency without resolving the discordance. Literal omission of either principal response domain makes a different part of the plan indeterminate, while replacing that domain with its opposite changes the recommended plan.

options.text: Preserve the symptom-control component, postpone discharge, and request team reassessment of intake support and the appropriate care setting.
options.reason: The improved HELP response supports keeping the symptom-control component active, while persistent minimal intake and further serial weight loss show that discharge readiness has not been established. Team reassessment preserves the observed benefit without treating symptom relief as complete nutritional or hydration recovery.

options.text: Preserve the symptom-control component, support discharge, and reassess intake and weight at the next planned community visit.
options.reason: This appropriately recognizes the measured symptom improvement but gives it too much weight. The patient has not demonstrated adequate oral intake, and the comparable weight series is still moving downward, so discharge should not proceed before those unresolved domains and the care setting are reassessed.

options.text: Treat the symptom-control component as ineffective, postpone discharge, and request a replacement plan because intake and weight remain poor.
options.reason: Persistent intake and weight concerns justify postponing discharge and reassessing the whole plan, but they do not erase the separately documented improvement in the validated symptom response. The team should preserve that benefit while addressing the nonrecovering domains rather than label the symptom component ineffective.

options.text: Preserve the symptom-control component, continue the present day-care plan, and defer team reassessment unless vital signs become abnormal.
options.reason: Stable vital signs help show that no separate emergency sequence is supplied, but they do not resolve the persistent inability to maintain intake or the downward weight trend. Waiting for abnormal vital signs would leave clinically relevant nonresponse unreviewed.

questions.objective: Validate the analytical comparability and histology-specific pathway context of a post-molar hCG series before acting on a specialist abnormal-trend interpretation.
questions.stem: After uterine evacuation, pathology confirms a complete hydatidiform mole. The patient remains in the pre-normalization portion of the GTD center's surveillance plan. The complete local chart series is: July 25, 820 IU/L, North Hospital laboratory, platform L1; August 1, 420 IU/L, North/L1; August 8, 162 IU/L, North/L1; August 15, 128 IU/L, South Hospital laboratory, platform L2; August 22, 101 IU/L, South/L2; and August 29, 79 IU/L, South/L2. Because the transfer changed both laboratory and platform, the center completed a case-specific review using retained material from all six dates. Its R1 reanalysis is: July 25, 818 IU/L; August 1, 417 IU/L; August 8, 160 IU/L; August 15, 158 IU/L; August 22, 160 IU/L; and August 29, 159 IU/L. The center laboratory's final technical verification states that every R1 result met its validated process requirements and that the six R1 measurements are analytically comparable for longitudinal interpretation. The existing center plan states that, during complete-mole pre-normalization surveillance, a comparable sustained plateau is routed promptly for GTD specialist management review while prescribed surveillance continues unless the service changes it. No case-level trend classification, diagnosis, treatment order, or surveillance change is documented. Which interpretation and action should the nurse communicate?
questions.clue: The local chart crosses methods and appears to keep falling; the verified one-method center series falls first and then remains essentially unchanged across its final four dates.
questions.rationale: Use the center series because the patient-specific laboratory verification closes the analytical-comparability question for these six R1 results. That series falls from 818 to 160 IU/L and then remains essentially unchanged at 160, 158, 160, and 159 IU/L. In the supplied complete-mole pre-normalization pathway, that sustained plateau supports prompt GTD specialist management review. Continue the prescribed surveillance while awaiting service direction. Do not use the lower South/L2 values to infer continued decline across a method change, reopen a comparability determination the center laboratory has completed, independently defer testing, diagnose gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, select treatment, or reconstruct a universal numerical trend rule.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must reconcile two discordant complete representations of the same post-evacuation trajectory. The mixed North/L1-to-South/L2 chart appears to keep falling, whereas the patient-specific center reanalysis is explicitly verified as one analytically comparable R1 series and shows a steep initial decline followed by four essentially unchanged results. The record supplies the complete-mole pre-normalization pathway rule but no case-level trend classification. The learner must select the valid series, interpret its direction, apply the pathway's specialist-review boundary, and preserve surveillance authority. The result values now perform the reasoning work; neither a signed specialist conclusion nor a missing metadata field discloses the answer.

options.text: Interpret the comparable central series as a plateau, request prompt GTD specialist management review, and continue prescribed surveillance pending direction.
options.reason: The final four R1 results remain essentially unchanged after the earlier decline, and the laboratory has explicitly verified the complete R1 series as analytically comparable. The supplied complete-mole pre-normalization pathway therefore reaches its prompt specialist-review boundary. Continuing prescribed surveillance preserves the current plan until the service issues changes.

options.text: Interpret the comparable central series as continued decline, continue prescribed surveillance, and keep specialist review at its existing planned timing.
options.reason: The center series declines sharply at first but does not continue downward across the final four dates. Calling 160, 158, 160, and 159 IU/L continued decline misreads the analytically comparable series and fails to activate the supplied sustained-plateau review branch.

options.text: Treat analytical continuity as unresolved, continue prescribed surveillance, and obtain GTD-center and laboratory clarification before changing specialist review timing.
options.reason: Clarification would be appropriate if continuity had not been established. Here the center laboratory's final technical verification explicitly states that all six R1 results are analytically comparable under its validated case-specific process. Contacting the center remains permissible, but another comparability determination is not the unresolved decision in this complete record.

options.text: Interpret the comparable central series as a plateau, request prompt GTD specialist management review, and defer surveillance samples pending direction.
options.reason: The trend interpretation and prompt specialist review are appropriate, but the supplied plan says prescribed surveillance continues unless the service changes it. The nurse should not independently defer samples while awaiting management instructions.

questions.objective: Apply serial glucose and feeding-adequacy evidence to continue a supplied monitoring and feeding plan for a stable at-risk newborn.
questions.stem: A late-preterm newborn is receiving prescribed feeding support and scheduled prefeeding glucose checks under a case-specific nursery pathway. For a clinically stable newborn who can feed safely, the pathway requires the nurse to reassess the current plan using the entire recent glucose series together with observed feeding adequacy. It reserves rescue-branch review for documented instability, unsafe feeding, or a result in its rescue category. The current series contains two results classified by the pathway as low-but-feedable followed by one result in its goal category. During three observed feeds, the newborn remained alert and coordinated sucking, swallowing, and breathing but tired early twice, with incomplete milk transfer. No result entered the rescue category, and no apnea, cyanosis, or other instability developed. Which recommendation should the nurse include in handoff?
questions.clue: One current result improved, but the pathway asks for the series and feeding assessment to be interpreted together.
questions.rationale: Continue the current feeding support and scheduled prefeeding checks while handing off the complete serial and feeding record. The latest goal-category result is reassuring, but it does not erase the earlier low-but-feedable results or establish that feeding is adequate; two observed feeds still ended with early fatigue and incomplete transfer. Conversely, the newborn's stable appearance does not replace serial glucose evidence. The preserved coordination of sucking, swallowing, and breathing and the absence of apnea, cyanosis, or a rescue-category result keep this case outside the supplied rescue branch. This is a bounded application of a fictional case pathway, not a universal monitoring, feeding, rescue, or stopping protocol.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must apply a supplied case-specific interpretation rule to two observation streams rather than copy a branch action from the stem. The most recent glucose result is reassuring, but the entire current series still includes low-but-feedable results and the feeding record shows repeated incomplete transfer. The learner must preserve the current nonrescue plan without using one improved point to close the feeding concern, stable appearance to erase the serial record, or feeding fatigue alone to declare the oral route unsafe. The findings are aligned and the rule is supplied, so this is estimated Level 2 application rather than advanced competing-cue reasoning.

options.text: Continue current feeding support and scheduled checks; report the full glucose series and repeated incomplete transfer as unresolved evidence in both domains.
options.reason: This applies both records without overreading the newest point. The serial record still includes low-but-feedable results, and feeding is not yet established despite a safe oral route. Neither finding activates the supplied rescue branch, so the current prescribed plan and complete handoff remain appropriate.

options.text: Continue scheduled checks but return to routine feeding; report the latest goal-category result as showing that the earlier feeding fatigue has resolved.
options.reason: The latest result is one reassuring glucose point, not a feeding assessment. The newborn still tired early with incomplete transfer during two observed feeds, so the record does not support treating feeding adequacy as established or withdrawing its prescribed support.

options.text: Continue feeding support but move glucose checks to routine care; report stable appearance as outweighing the earlier low-but-feedable results in the series.
options.reason: Clinical stability supports the current oral plan and keeps the newborn outside rescue care, but it does not cancel measured serial evidence. The current series still contains low-but-feedable results, so replacing the scheduled checks with routine care is not supported by the supplied pathway.

options.text: Continue feeding support and scheduled checks while requesting rescue-branch review; report repeated fatigue as evidence that oral feeding has become unsafe.
options.reason: This option preserves both current interventions, so completeness does not distinguish it from the key. Its interpretation is unsupported: the newborn remained alert and coordinated feeding without apnea or cyanosis, and no rescue-category result or other instability was documented. Fatigue shows inadequate endurance, not an established unsafe route in this case.
